      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Side B's command: the Duke of Brunswick commanded the main army, with the King present. On the evening before the battle the Duke, very weak and exhausted, thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen and still believed he had to deal only with a detached corps of about 6000 French at Naumburg; the next day's movement was arranged with Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull and Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist present, no one from the division Oranien being there and General Blücher not yet arrived. In the morning the march set off in the fog; Möllendorf had Schmettau's main body follow its advanced guard immediately, and Höpfner thinks the eagerness to get at the enemy and catch the French cavalry beyond the defile was the main reason that the usual caution was dropped, the enemy and the ground left unreconnoitred and the lifting of the fog not awaited, Möllendorf vying with the youngest and the impulse reaching even the Duke. General Blücher, who found the King at the head of Schmettau's division and asked for instructions, was referred to the Duke and told only that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen and must be thrown back; on meeting French infantry he sent to the Duke asking for more cavalry and more troops to strike a decisive blow. After the first clash the Duke thought it doubtful to march on before the fog lifted, but Möllendorf believed they must march on without loss of time and the King, assuming they had not met considerable forces, agreed. The enemy was thought too strong to attack at once with the division Schmettau alone, so the division Wartensleben was first to come level, and the Duke made Colonel Scharnhorst responsible for everything on the left wing; the Duke sent the division Wartensleben to the right to take the height right of Hassenhausen, believing that if his infantry gained a footing there victory was certain, Möllendorf ordered the regiment Prinz Louis to take the village with the bayonet, and the Duke had called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot through both eyes; Schmettau was mortally wounded. Then all general arrangements ceased: the King took over the command definitively, but Möllendorf and every leader, aide-de-camp and staff officer gave orders as well, which was especially ruinous to the cavalry, led forward squadron by squadron. The King, displeased that the division Oranien had not come up sooner, ordered its battalions to reinforce the left wing of the fighting troops and then both wings, as the division Wartensleben could not hold much longer right of Hassenhausen. The reserve, first meant to march by Eckartsberga on Laucha, was ordered to follow the division Oranien through Auerstädt; when Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed once more to General Arnim, in Kalkreuth's absence, to march by Reisdorf to Eckartsberga and decide the battle by turning the enemy's right, the general would not depart from the order he had received, and Kalkreuth took no notice of Major Jagow's proposal to move part of the reserve on Lisdorf. The King, from the height of Eckartsberga, having given up hope of throwing the enemy back on Kösen, ordered the retreat, first toward Sömmerda and then on Weimar, to unite with Prince Hohenlohe and renew the battle the next day; he countermanded General Blücher's attack with the cavalry and had General Kalkreuth lead the army back (OCR from 'In the morning'). Höpfner's reflections say that on the Prussian side the passage from the march disposition to a plan of battle was wholly lacking: no one knew what to do and the troops went into the fight without knowing what was wanted; with an orderly plan the reserve would not have been split up nor 8 battalions spent covering the right flank, and the reserves would have marched by Eckartsberga to turn Davout's right. They also call it unwise to have let General Blücher attack the infantry his cavalry met in the fog, and say that after the Duke's mortal wound all unity in the arrangements for continuing the battle was lost, every general, staff officer and adjutant commanding on his own, and that the battle was given up before the reserves had been used (OCR from 'They also').",

      "rationale": "Höpfner's page images (pp. 364 and 485) and his narrative and reflections from the OCR. The decisions on the field — the march in the fog, the commitment of the divisions one by one, the King's assumption of command, the handling of the reserve and the order to retreat — were the Prussian commanders' own, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner's reflections also blame the organisation of the army command, which set beside the Duke a council headed by the King himself instead of leaving him the whole responsibility (OCR). The Duke's mortal wound is also in Davout's report and the 5th Bulletin (claim side-b-losses-reported). English renderings (ours): 'at this arrangement Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull, Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist and the Duke's aides-de-camp were present'; 'of the division Oranien nobody was present; General Blücher, who had been ordered to headquarters, was also still missing'; 'the Duke thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen, but spoke at great length about the position to be taken beyond the Unstrut, and still believed he had to deal with a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg'; 'the Duke was extremely weak; the hardships of the preceding days, the mental exertions and anxieties about the situation of the army, had exhausted his strength' (p. 364); 'the eagerness to get at the enemy, and the hope of capturing or destroying the enemy cavalry that had gone over the defile, was probably the main reason that the caution otherwise observed was lost from view, the reconnaissance of the enemy and of the ground left undone and the lifting of the fog not awaited, but rather everyone pressed forward, in which the old Field Marshal Möllendorf vied with the youngest, and this impulse communicated itself even to the otherwise so deliberate Duke'; 'the advanced guard of the division Schmettau set off, and since, by the general view of things, it was thought that no interval from the advanced guard was needed, Field Marshal Möllendorf, arriving, ordered that General Count Schmettau should follow immediately with the main body of the division'; 'for his own person the general [Blücher] went forward and found the King at the head of the division Schmettau with the regiment Alvensleben'; 'on asking for instructions he was referred to the Duke, and received only the information that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen already, which had to be thrown back'; 'Colonel Scharnhorst, who had made the same discovery [an enemy infantry line close at hand], met the general [Blücher] there, who at once sent his adjutant, Rittmeister Count Goltz, back to the Duke to report to him that he — the general — was outflanking the enemy, and to ask for more cavalry and more troops in general, with which he then meant to strike a decisive blow'; 'the Duke had, as mentioned, thought it doubtful to continue the march before the fog had lifted. Field Marshal Möllendorf, on the other hand, believed they must march on without loss of time, and the King joined the latter opinion, since he assumed that they had not run into considerable enemy forces. The division Schmettau had therefore had to set off again'; 'the enemy was thought too strong to attack at once with the single division, and so one wished first to let the division Wartensleben, which was on the march, come level'; 'the Duke sent him [Scharnhorst] to see what the musket fire meant, and had made him responsible for everything that went on on the left wing'; 'when this division had reached the height of Gernstädt, the Duke sent the order to turn off the road to the right, deploy, and advance through the hollow between Rehhausen and Tauchwitz, in order to take the height to the right of Hassenhausen. The Duke was of the view that if he succeeded in gaining a firm footing on that height with the infantry, he was sure of victory'; 'Field Marshal Möllendorf ordered the regiment Prinz Louis of the division Wartensleben to take the village with the bayonet'; 'the Duke had called on the grenadier battalion Hanstein on the left wing of the division Wartensleben to take the village, when he sank from his horse shot through both eyes'; 'General Count Schmettau was busy leading a regiment forward again on the right wing of his division when he was wounded, but hid his condition until he received a second, mortal wound'; 'now all general arrangements ceased. The King did indeed take over the command definitively, but Field Marshal Möllendorf, every single leader, every aide-de-camp, general staff officer etc.'; '[each] likewise made arrangements, which had an especially ruinous effect on the use of the cavalry, which was led forward and used squadron by squadron by everyone who wished to help here or there, so that all common direction of this arm ceased and, despite its superiority, it could nowhere gain a significant effect'; 'immediately afterwards the King had come, had expressed himself very displeased that the division [Oranien] had not come up sooner, and had ordered the left wing of the fighting troops to be reinforced with all battalions;'; 'while one was still busy deploying, a second order of the King had come: to reinforce both wings of the fighting troops, since the division Wartensleben would not be able to hold much longer to the right of Hassenhausen'; 'the two reserve divisions of General Count Kalkreuth were, according to the first arrangement, to march on Laucha'; 'a peasant from Auerstädt had offered to lead them by Reisdorf, Mallendorf, Eckartsberga and Lisdorf into the old road to Laucha, but the general had first had this way reconnoitred by a column guide, to whom it had not seemed wide enough, and when the fire began at Hassenhausen while the reserves still stood behind Auerstädt, it was thought necessary to bring them up for immediate support, and it was ordered that they should follow the division Oranien and, together with the ... battalion of Blücher hussars and part of the Württemberg hussars, halt as general reserve with Gernstädt before them'; 'when it was further noticed that, with the disorder in Auerstädt, a considerable time would also pass before the infantry of the reserve could pass the village, Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed to the division com-'; '-mander General Arnim, in the absence of General Count Kalkreuth, once more to march by Reisdorf to Eckartsberga etc., from where the battle could be decided by turning the enemy's right wing, but the general would not depart from the order he had received,'; as in claim side-b-engaged for Jagow's proposal, Kalkreuth's silence and the retreat order; 'it was the King's intention, under the protection of such a position, to have the retiring troops take the road by Buttstädt to Sömmerda, and to direct the corps of Hohenlohe, Rüchel and Weimar there as well'; 'the King believed, however, that Artern might well already be occupied by the enemy, and since he had no knowledge of the fate of Hohenlohe's and Rüchel's corps, he now decided not to go back on Sömmerda either, but on Weimar, in order to unite with Prince Hohenlohe at the Ettersberg and renew the battle the next day'; 'the general [Blücher] asked the King to allow him to fall upon the enemy with the cavalry; then he meant to play him another considerable trick'; '[so] the King also sent an aide-de-camp to the general with the order to refrain from the attack';       "id": "davout-decision",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Marshal Davout's decision: on the 13th, at the time a Prussian patrol threw back a French chasseur patrol, Davout was on the road from Kösen to Hassenhausen with his suite to reconnoitre the ground, and from the height behind Hassenhausen he saw the march of the advanced guard of the division Schmettau and part of the division itself; on his return to Naumburg he had the pass of Kösen occupied by the 25th line infantry regiment and assembled his generals. Napoleon's orders, dated 10 in the evening of the 13th from the heights by Jena, reached him only toward 3 in the morning of the 14th: Napoleon, resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on him to direct himself on Apolda to act in its rear, leaving him the road; in the 5th Bulletin Davout had been ordered to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy marched on Naumburg or to go to Apolda and take the enemy in the rear if he stayed in his position. Davout proposed that Marshal Bernadotte debouch behind him as far as Kösen and take command of the united corps of about 56,000 men, but Bernadotte understood the order otherwise and believed he must march to Dornburg. Davout had kept his generals at his quarters that night, and when the orders came they left at once to set their troops in motion (OCR). By the 3rd corps's journal there was no other road toward Erfurt by Auerstädt and Apolda, as the Emperor had ordered, so it was important to seize the head of the defile in order to deploy; by the marshal's orders given in the night, because of the distance of the 1st division, the movement was made by the left, and General Gudin with the 3rd division crossed the Saale on the bridge of Kösen at half past 6, Gudin's report having the division leave its position at Neuflemming at 4 in the morning and its head cross the defile at 6. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league away, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner says that at Kösen, as at Jena, everything depended on reaching a point on the plateau of the left bank before the Prussians (OCR).",

      "rationale": "Read from the page images (pp. 365, 614, 615, 670, 672 and 673) and the OCR as marked. That he met the Prussian main army at Hassenhausen was not his choice (claim posture). Foucart's note to the journal's 'orders given in the night' refers to p. 670, where the 3rd corps set off immediately and the 3rd division was crossing the bridge at half past 6; the orders themselves are not in the passages read.       "id": "side-a-losses-reported",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side A's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the 1st division lost 98 officers and 2,181 men killed or wounded, the 2nd 20 and 900 and the 3rd 134 and 3,500, 252 officers and 6,581 men in all, and with the losses of the cavalry, artillery, engineers and staff about a third of the 3rd corps was put out of action. Davout reported that the Emperor had lost many brave men, among them General Debilly and Colonels Vergès, Higonet, Viala and Nicolas, with several others wounded, that several regiments had lost most of their officers, and that the number of wounded was very considerable. The 5th Bulletin, whose account covers Jena and Auerstedt together, estimates the French loss at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, regrets among the generals only General Debilly, and names among the colonels killed Vergès of the 12th line infantry regiment, Nicolas of the 61st, Viala of the 85th and Higonet of the 108th. Höpfner writes that the enemy himself gave his loss as 270 officers and 7000 men.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Read from the page images (pp. 683, 684, 672, 673, 614, 619, 620 and 471). Bodart's 7,100 with 252 officers (claim bodart-losses) lies between the journal's three divisions and Höpfner's figure. The Bulletin's 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, 4,000 or 4,100 for both fields (our arithmetic), are fewer than the journal's 6,833 for the 3rd corps's infantry divisions alone. The Bulletin's dead colonels are not divided by field in the passages read; Vergès, Nicolas, Viala and Higonet are the four Davout names. Foucart's note to the journal's cavalry losses, a table of the losses of the 3rd corps's three chasseur regiments (p. 684, note 1), and the ordonnateur Chambon's letter to Davout on the wounded at Naumburg (p. 684, note 3) were read only in the OCR and are not restated, and the fuller details Davout's report promised were not looked for (open questions). English renderings (ours): the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'officers | men'; 'the 1st division lost, killed and wounded together | 98 | 2,181'; 'the 2nd — — | 20 | 900'; 'the 3rd — — | 134 | 3,500'; '[total] | 252 | 6,581', the dashes being ditto marks (p. 683); 'adding to these the losses of the cavalry, the artillery, the engineers and the staff, about a third of the 3rd corps was put out of action' (p. 684); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); 'Your Majesty has lost many brave men, among whom I shall cite General Debilly, Colonels Vergès, Higonet, Viala, Nicolas, and several others wounded'; 'several regiments have lost most of their officers; the number of the wounded is very considerable' (p. 672); 'in the coming days I shall have the honour of sending Your Majesty the details needed to make known to it the brilliant conduct of all its officers and soldiers' (p. 673); the 5th Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); as in claim side-a-command for Davout's corps (p. 619); 'on our side we have to regret, among the generals, only the loss of General Debilly, an excellent soldier'; 'among the colonels killed, Colonels Vergès, of the 12th regiment of line infantry;'; 'Nicolas, of the 61st of the line; Viala, of the 85th; Higonet, of the 108th'; 'our loss is estimated at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded' (p. 620); Höpfner, 'the enemy had completely stopped the pursuit, since his troops were very exhausted and had suffered great losses'; 'he himself gave his loss as 270 officers and 7000 men' (p. 471).",

      "id": "side-b-losses-reported",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side B's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the enemy lost 115 pieces of cannon, about 15,000 men killed or wounded and 3,000 prisoners, and at the end abandoned 20 pieces of cannon to General Petit. Davout reported that the victory remained with his corps together with almost all the enemy artillery, that the number of prisoners was not very considerable because his little cavalry could not exploit the infantry's successes, that the Duke of Brunswick was gravely wounded in the head and the wound thought mortal, that Prussian generals were wounded, among them Prince August, the King's uncle, and that the Guards on horse and on foot suffered much. The 5th Bulletin's results for Jena and Auerstedt together are 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, among them more than 20 generals including Lieutenant-General Schmettau, 25 to 30 colours, 300 pieces of cannon and more than 20,000 killed or wounded, with Field Marshal Möllendorf wounded and the Duke of Brunswick killed. Höpfner holds a statement of the Prussian loss at Auerstädt impossible because of the uninterrupted retreat until the army's complete dissolution, and says the men's loss may be inferred from the officers': 1 field marshal, 3 generals, 7 staff officers and 36 other officers, 47 officers in all, were killed or died of wounds — the Duke of Brunswick, Lieutenant-General Count Schmettau and Major-Generals Quitzow and Greiffenberg — and 1 field marshal, 5 generals, 34 staff officers and 181 other officers, 221 in all without the general staff and adjutants, were wounded; 57 guns were lost without the battalion guns, and nearly half the infantry that stood against Hassenhausen was killed or wounded. His narrative calls the loss in prisoners great in the retreat of the left wing by Poppel and very considerable in the retreat by Reisdorf, and his reflections call it very considerable among the Prussians beaten in front; for single units he gives losses for the Irwing dragoons and the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg (OCR from 'His narrative', figures not restated).",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Read from the page images (pp. 673, 683, 682, 672, 614, 619, 620, 471 and 472), with the losses in prisoners and the single units from the OCR. The journal's 3,000 prisoners and 115 cannon equal Bodart's, and its about 15,000 killed or wounded are 5,000 more than Bodart's 10,000 (our arithmetic; claim bodart-losses). Höpfner's 57 guns without the battalion guns are about half the journal's 115 (our arithmetic). Höpfner's officers killed and wounded make 268 (our arithmetic), of whom 10 are field marshals and generals, as in Bodart. The Bulletin's results cover Jena (B372a) and Auerstedt together and the prisoners taken in the pursuit to the day of writing; Davout's 'not very considerable' prisoners are his own field on the day, against Höpfner's loss in prisoners 'great' and 'very considerable' (OCR); the journal counts 3,000. Schmettau is among the prisoners in the Bulletin but among the dead in Höpfner and among the fallen generals in Bodart (claim bodart-commanders), and the Bulletin has the Duke of Brunswick killed where Davout's report of the 14th calls the wound thought mortal and Höpfner lists him among those killed or dead of their wounds. English renderings (ours): the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'the enemy lost 115 pieces of cannon, about 15,000 men killed or wounded and 3,000 prisoners' (p. 683); 'the enemy abandoned this fine and last position with such haste that he left 20 pieces of cannon in the power of General Petit' (p. 682); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claims foucart-side-b and foucart-side-a for the victory and the prisoners; 'the Duke of Brunswick was gravely wounded in the head; his wound is regarded as mortal'; 'Prussian generals were wounded. Among these is counted Prince August, the King's uncle'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the Guards (p. 672); the 5th Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'the results of the battle are 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners,' (p. 619); 'more arrive every moment; 25 to 30 colours; 300 pieces of cannon; immense magazines of subsistence'; 'among the prisoners are more than 20 generals, several of them lieutenant-generals, among others Lieutenant-General Schmettau'; 'the number of the dead is immense in the Prussian army; it is reckoned that there are more than 20,000 killed or wounded'; 'Field Marshal Möllendorf has been wounded; the Duke of Brunswick has been killed; General Rüchel has been killed; Prince Henry of Prussia, gravely wounded' (p. 620); Höpfner, 'as for the battle at Jena, so also for that at Auerstädt, because of the uninterrupted retreat that followed until complete dissolution, a statement of the loss on the Prussian side is impossible'; 'here too, therefore, the loss of the men may be inferred from the loss of officers'; 'there remained [dead] or died of wounds 1 field marshal, 3 generals, 7 staff officers, 36 other officers, together 47 officers'; his footnote, '1) there remained [dead] or died of their wounds: Field Marshal Duke of Brunswick, Lieutenant-General Count Schmettau, Major-Generals Quitzow and Greiffenberg' (p. 471); '[there were] wounded: 1 field marshal, 5 generals, 34 staff officers, 181 other officers, together 221 officers, without the general staff and adjutants'; 'in artillery 57 guns were lost, without the battalion cannon'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the infantry at Hassenhausen (p. 472); 'but even so the loss in prisoners was great'; 'but the loss in prisoners was nevertheless very considerable'; 'the consequence was that the loss in prisoners on the part of the Prussians beaten in front was very considerable, and the thought of a retreat over the Unstrut was given up. —'; 'the dragoon regiment Irwing had through canister and musket fire a loss of ... officer and ... men in dead, ... officers, ... men and ... horses in wounded' (OCR); as in claim side-b-engaged for the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg (OCR).",

      "value": "Auerstädt is a village in the Prussian province of Saxony, 22 km north of Jena (Bodart). In the 3rd corps's journal the ground beyond the Saale is high and offers fine plateaus, cut here and there by brooks, small ravines and some sunken roads and dotted with many villages, crowned to the north by higher knolls covered with clumps of wood; the Saale is not fordable and its left bank is very steep; the great road from Naumburg to Weimar and Erfurt passes through Kösen, where there is a stone bridge over the Saale, and beyond it one must climb a long, steep slope to the plateau of Hassenhausen. Höpfner calls the defile of Kösen an unassailable post, scarcely 1½ Meilen from the division Schmettau's camp before Auerstädt, and says that, with the road as it then was, the slightest infantry or artillery detachment could have made the climb from the Saale to the plateau impossible (the last OCR). A fog so thick that objects could not be made out at pistol range rose half an hour before daybreak (the journal) and cleared gradually (Höpfner; both OCR). Hassenhausen formed the pivot of Davout's position, with no new hold for his corps until behind the Saale if it were lost, and Höpfner judges that taking it would have decided the battle, since the French had very little cavalry and without the village could no longer hold the plain between it and the Saale; the French in it stood covered up to the neck in the hollow roads, in the houses and behind the hedges, and the Prussians came early into the French fire, which the village's gardens covered (OCR). Battalions of the division Friant, detached by Davout on their arrival, manoeuvred in the Prussian left flank and rear on ground where they had nothing to fear from the superior Prussian cavalry (Höpfner), and Davout put his cavalry on his right, the only part of his line where it could act; the Prussian outflanking movement came first against that wing, where the plain was more open and the folds of ground on the way from Poppel toward Spielberg let the columns climb under cover (Foucart's notes; all OCR).",

      "value": "Side A: all the 3rd corps's artillery, reserve included, consisted of only 44 pieces of different calibres (the journal); Davout had little cavalry, not enough to profit from the infantry's successes, the grand-duc de Berg having withdrawn the dragoon division Sahuc the day before; and by Davout's later complaint his cavalry general, Viallanes, despite his entreaties left the marshal's quarters, where the generals were to spend the night, without his knowledge and could not be found when the orders came, so that his cavalry, instead of debouching first, debouched three hours later (OCR). About 7 in the evening, with cartridges lacking and the units much weakened, Davout took position, and the cartridges were to be replaced in the night. Side B: the Prussian divisions reached their bivouacs late, in the cold, dark night, and wood, straw and food could not be brought in under proper supervision, which ended in the plundering of the villages nearby; the troops had cooked and drawn bread, the filled bread wagons were left behind on the Duke's order, and the King's gift of brandy reached few of the troops (OCR). Höpfner's reflections on Auerstädt say the troops went into battle the next morning exhausted and dispirited, without straw, wood and food, and his reflections on both battles that in the rich country the army could not bring itself to requisition and let men and horses go hungry (OCR). On the field the battalion guns of the division Wartensleben stuck in part in the hollow it crossed between Rehhausen and Tauchwitz; guns of the battery Riemer, assigned to the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben, which the King personally ordered forward against Poppel as the division Oranien came up, overturned in the road ditch, and those that could follow had only a few rounds with them, the ammunition wagons not having come up; and with several Prussian battalions the ammunition was already shot off when Morand's division attacked (OCR).",

    {
      "id": "side-b-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Side B's information: on the day before the battle a Prussian patrol under Lieutenant Böhmer met a French patrol between Auerstädt and Kösen, threw it back and took a chasseur, who stated that General Davout had taken Naumburg the day before with his division; it seemed certain that chasseur regiments had crossed the defile of Kösen, and reports put infantry with guns at the pass and bridge of Kösen and more infantry at Naumburg, all of Davout's corps, but on the whole the news of the enemy was contradictory, and the troops arrived too late for any proper reconnaissance of the ground and the enemy; in the night no further news of the enemy and no significant outpost reports reached headquarters at Auerstädt, so everything ordered for crossing the Unstrut at Freiburg and Laucha stayed in force (all OCR so far). The Duke still believed he faced a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg, and the statements of the head forester at Auerstädt did not change his view. In the morning the Duke remarked to Colonel Scharnhorst that it was a very doubtful thing to advance so, not knowing what was before them (OCR); when the Prussians met the enemy in the fog they believed it only a detachment, and Höpfner holds that once it was certain that a considerable enemy corps was arriving the march dispositions should have been dropped. Later the Prussians judged the enemy far stronger than he was, because they had themselves lost heavily and he had husbanded his forces, and saw the divisions of their main body destroyed while the enemy still showed fresh forces and perhaps further reinforcement from Kösen (OCR). By the account of an officer taken prisoner and brought to the King, which Colonel Blein heard, the King, told that Davout's corps was only 25,000 to 26,000 men, called it French bragging and said there were certainly more than 50,000; and he did not yet know that Hohenlohe and Rüchel had been completely defeated at Jena the same day when he appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.",

The figures of the prisoner's statement and of the reports on Kösen and Naumburg are read only in the OCR (not restated). 'this man states: that General Davout took possession of Naumburg yesterday with his division, ... men strong'; 'on the whole the news of the enemy coming in was contradictory'; 'it seemed certain: that ... regiments of chasseurs had crossed the defile of Kösen and in the'; 'that the pass and the bridge of Kösen were occupied by about ... men of infantry and ... cannon, Naumburg by about ... men of infantry, and that all these troops belonged to the corps of Marshal Davout';       "value": "Side A's objectives: Napoleon, resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on Davout to direct himself on Apolda to act in its rear, leaving him the road; if Bernadotte was with him they were to operate together, though Napoleon hoped Bernadotte had taken the position at Dornburg assigned to him, an order Höpfner says Bernadotte had not received. Foucart notes that had the 3rd corps not found the King's army on its way it would have reached Apolda about noon, having heard the cannonade since the morning (OCR).       "id": "side-b-objectives",
      "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side B's objectives: by Höpfner's reflections the Duke did not wish to fight but to march off to the left, cross the Unstrut and place himself again directly before the French, the main army marching off while Prince Hohenlohe was to cover the right flank of its march and then follow (OCR). The disposition for the main army's march announced a retrograde movement, to unite with Duke Eugen of Württemberg and to free the army's rear again, for which the division Schmettau was to set off at once and march to Kösen, taking the pass if it was not strongly held (OCR); Höpfner holds that the division could well have reached that unassailable post on the 13th, as the disposition had prescribed, but the march to Auerstädt was thought long enough and the Duke did not think it urgent. His reflections say the course of the battle had been prepared by the arrangements of the 13th, among them that the division was not sent forward to Kösen that afternoon to occupy the pass and so make sure that the next day's march on Freyburg would not be disturbed: with the pass held, he says, the battle of Auerstädt became impossible (OCR from 'among them'). When a prisoner's report on Davout came in, the Duke had the troops of the main army hasten their march and be ready to engage the enemy that same day, the King intending to attack him at once (OCR). For the next day, as arranged late in the evening at Auerstädt, the army was to set off at daybreak in the same order of march, the division Schmettau following the road to Kösen, its cavalry and advanced guard throwing themselves on the enemy cavalry and an infantry brigade taking and occupying the post of Kösen, the division holding the heights of Kösen until the whole army had passed behind it and defiled across the Unstrut, while the two reserve divisions marched by Eckartsberga straight on Laucha (OCR). In Goltz's account the main army meant to cross the Unstrut between Freyburg and Laucha on the 14th to join the reserve corps approaching the Saale. Höpfner's reflections add that the battle was fought not only to win a victory but to open the retreat across the Unstrut toward the Saale and the middle Elbe, which obliged the Prussians to dare the utmost (OCR). After the battle the King, still hoping to join Prince Hohenlohe and General Rüchel, appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.",

      "value": "Both sides attacked. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league off, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner calls it, on both sides, a matter of dispositions after a chance encounter ('Rencontre'), both being surprised by running into a considerable opponent; the heads of both armies met at Hassenhausen, which the French occupied, and the division Gudin and the Prussian division Schmettau reached it at about the same time (the last OCR). The Prussians attacked: General Blücher's cavalry attacked the French infantry at Hassenhausen and was repulsed by the squares; the King ordered the division Schmettau to attack, and Schmettau's and Wartensleben's divisions attacked Hassenhausen but could not take it, the Duke having called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot; Prince Wilhelm's cavalry charged Morand's division, which received it in square (OCR). The French attacked: while Gudin's division held at Hassenhausen, Friant's went on turning the enemy, advancing between Spielberg and Zeckwar against the Prussian left; Davout sent Morand's division against the King's last effort to break the French left, and Morand outflanked the Prussian army and took it in flank; Davout then had the centre advance (OCR); at the end General Petit, ordered to attack the last Prussian position before Eckartsberga with 400 men, climbed the height with the bayonet without returning the fire and took 20 pieces of cannon.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Coded both_attacked: a meeting engagement, in which the Prussian main attacks on Hassenhausen and the French main attacks by Friant's and Morand's divisions, the advance of the centre and the final attack before Eckartsberga fell on different parts of the field; neither side fought from a position taken up before the meeting, and the French defence of Hassenhausen and the Prussian reserve's stands before Eckartsberga were parts of a battle that both sides fought by attacking. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. The meeting came from marches set by orders, Napoleon's to Davout and the Prussian disposition to take the post of Kösen (claims davout-decision and side-b-objectives), but the attacks were decided on the field by Davout, the Duke and the King, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claim davout-decision for the debouch and the battle engaged at once (p. 672); Höpfner, 'it was a matter here, on both sides, of the arrangements after a Rencontre, for both parties were surprised by running into a considerable opponent' (p. 485); as in claim side-b-engaged for the first and third moments, and in claim hoepfner-side-a for Gudin and Schmettau; 'second moment. General Blücher attacks the enemy infantry at Hassenhausen with some cavalry and is repulsed. The enemy division Friant arrives'; 'the unshaken French squares received him coolly'; 'the King gave the division Schmettau the order to attack, which was begun in echelons from the left wing'; as in claim side-b-command for the Duke's wound (OCR); the journal, '[rein]forced by another numerous corps of cavalry, at whose head was Prince Wilhelm of Prussia'; 'the Prince charged the division Morand several times, but all the units, formed in square, received him coolly with cries of Vive l'Empereur!'; 'the division Gudin was defending itself with advantage level with Hassenhausen, while General Friant with the greater part of his division continued to turn the enemy, advanced between Spielberg and Zeckwar, and was already troubling the Prussians' left flank with a well placed and well directed artillery'; as in claim side-a-command for the King's last effort, Morand and the centre; '[Morand] outflanks and takes the Prussian army in flank; at the same time General Friant, placed likewise on the heights to the right of Poppel, was already outflanking the enemy's left wing' (OCR); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); as in claim side-a-command for the last division and Petit's orders (OCR and p. 682); 'General Petit received the fire of the Prussian artillery and that of the musketry without replying; his troops climbed the hill with the bayonet forward, while General Grandeau arrived on the right of this hill with the greater part of the 111th, followed by General Friant and his division'; 'the enemy abandoned this fine and last position with such haste that he left 20 pieces of cannon in the power of General Petit' (p. 682).",

### B373b: KAPITULATION von Erfurt (15./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p373, as printed:

```text
1806 15./10. KAPITULATION von Erfurt
(Stadt in Preußen, Provinz Sachsen, 20 km westl. von Weimar).
Die Franzosen unter Großherzog Murat zwingen 10.000 Preußen unter Gen.-Lt. Pz. v. Oranien zur Übergabe. Die preußischen Truppen durften mit Kriegsehren ausziehen, mußten jedoch auf dem Glacis die Waffen niederlegen und sich kriegsgefangen geben. Den Offizieren (worunter 1 GFM., 6 Gen.) wurde gegen die ehrenwörtliche Verpflichtung, vor ihrer Auswechslung nicht gegen Frankreich zu dienen, freier Abzug bewilligt. Die Franzosen fanden in Erfurt 65 Geschütze vor.
```

      "value": "Höpfner: the Prince of Orange had arrived in Erfurt, and after him Field Marshal Möllendorf, who had the prince assemble the generals and staff officers on the Petersberg; towards noon Möllendorf gave the definite order for the baggage to leave at once for Langensalza and the cavalry and the infantry to follow at set hours. General Larisch at once left his position on the Galgenberg with the infantry and fell back in disorder to the town. Having received the King's order to march to Sömmerda, Larisch resolved to carry it out at once, but the prince had him halt and, on the Petersberg, repeated the order, since getting through was no longer possible; when Larisch appealed to the King's order, the prince gave the strict order that he stay in Erfurt with the troops and have the walls manned. The commandant, Major Prüschenk, at first meant to defend himself seriously but soon changed his mind; Möllendorf attended only the start of the negotiations. The prince dictated the points of the capitulation to Major Lossau of the general staff. Höpfner judges that not defending the town was in order, but that it would then have been a duty to take the troops out at once to continue the retreat under the Duke of Weimar's protection, and that the surrender of the Petersberg was irresponsible: against a regular attack it could have held out 19 days.",

      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Erfurt on 15 October: the Prussian troops marched out with the honours of war, laid down their arms on the glacis and became prisoners of war; the officers, among them a field marshal and six generals, were released on their word not to serve against France until exchanged. Höpfner says the capitulation was concluded in the night to the 16th; men from the Bayreuth country were sent home and the rest treated as prisoners of war. The terms the major general sent Murat as the only capitulation His Majesty could grant were that the troops march out with the honours of war, file through the middle of the French army and lay down their arms, the soldiers keeping their booty and the officers their baggage; all were to be prisoners of war, the soldiers and even the generals to be sent to France, though the Emperor left Murat latitude to let the officers go home on their undertaking not to serve before their exchange. ### B374a: TREFFEN bei Halle (17./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 17./10. TREFFEN bei Halle (4.)
(Stadt in Preußen, Provinz Sachsen, an der Saale, 32 km nordwestl. von Leipzig).
Sieg der Franzosen (14.500 Inft., 1.500 Kav. = 16.000 M.) unter Marschall Bernadotte über die Preußen (18 Btln., 20 Esk. = 11.500 Inft., 2.200 Kav., 62 Kan. = 13.700 M.) unter Gen. d. Kav. Hz. E. v. Württemberg.
Frz. Verl.: ca. 800 M. (6 Stb.-, 28 Ob.-Offz.) tot u. verw.
Preuß. Verl.: 1.000 M. tot u. verw. 4.200 „ Gefg. zus. 5.200 M. (113 Offz.) = 37% 11 Kan., 4 Fahnen.
[Offiziersverlust table not transcribed]
```

      "value": "Höpfner: the Duke, though informed of the beaten army's retreat, could not bring himself to leave Halle, believing he must first gather all his troops and holding the King's order to keep large stores ready at Halle for the army; so the retreat was not begun and even the baggage stayed with the corps. At Major Bergen's repeated urging that the corps must march off to the Elbe, the Duke called the division generals to his quarters in Halle; the march back was discussed, and they had just agreed on it when a trumpeter reported the dragoons surprised at Passendorf. The Duke attached little weight to it and rode to the Saale bridge still taking it for a reconnaissance; he went forward over the high bridge with the bridge post, reinforced by the guard, and a gun, then gave General Hinrichs the command at the bridge, returned to the town and ordered the camp's tents struck. Fortunately, in Höpfner's words, the Duke became aware of the danger in time and hurried in person with the grenadier battalions Vieregg and Schmeling to the Ober-Steinthor, where the French were already pressing forward, and the enemy were thrown back to the Unter-Steinthor.     {
      "id": "halle-ground",
      "dimension": "terrain",
      "value": "Bodart places Halle in the Prussian province of Saxony on the Saale, 32 km north-west of Leipzig. Bernadotte wrote that to cross all these obstacles one had to file along a dyke exposed to all the enemy's fire.       "id": "side-b-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Höpfner: the King's order reached the Duke on his journey to Halle; on the onward journey he heard the cannonades of Jena and Auerstedt and concluded, from the King's letter and the fire receding, that the enemy's turning movement had been beaten off; half a day then passed without his receiving news of the previous day's battles, and the reports that came in contradicted each other; then came a report of Davout at Naumburg and Weißenfels, and a wounded officer of the regiment Renouard told him of the main army's defeat. He was also informed of the beaten army's retreat by the Halberstadt chamber, and in Höpfner's view sufficiently informed of the army's state by General Tschammer. ### B374b: KAPITULATION von Spandau (25./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 25./10. KAPITULATION von Spandau
(Befestigte Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, 9 km westl. von Berlin).
Die preußische Garnison (1.000 M.) unter Major v. Benekendorf ergibt sich ohne Schwertstreich an die Franzosen unter Marschall Lannes.
```

    {
      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Major Benekendorf, the commandant, wrote to the King that the citadel was secure against a coup de main and that, failing other orders, he would leave the enemy only the ruins of the fortress. The commandant's reply to the summons made to him, a copy of which went with Lannes's letter, was that the fortress would not surrender but would not oppose the passage of the French troops entering by the Potsdam gate and leaving by the Charlottenburg gate, provided they did not approach the fortress, its bridges and its gates. In Höpfner's account the commandant called a council of war in which all the members but the engineer captain Meinert voted to surrender, though no shot had yet been fired, citing the bad state of the works, the insufficient ammunition and garrison and the harm a defence would do to the King's interest and the inhabitants'. He declared to the parlementaire his readiness to surrender, the judge-advocate was to draw up the points of capitulation, and during this work he is said to have waved his handkerchief to the post at the drawbridge to let it down. He was later sentenced to be shot, and pardoned by the King to fortress imprisonment for life. Bertrand reported that a young officer said only that they had the King's order to defend themselves and would die, and that the commandant is old.",

      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Spandau on 25 October: the garrison surrendered without a fight to the French under Lannes. ### B374c: KAPITULATION von Prenzlau (28./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 28./10. KAPITULATION von Prenzlau
(Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, am Ausfluß der Ucker aus dem Uckersee, 120 km nordöstl. von Potsdam).
Die Franzosen unter Großherzog Murat nötigen die preußische Armee unter Gen. d. Inf. Fürst Hohenlohe zur Kapitulation, wonach 10.000 M. (wor. 400 Offz.) in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten, 45 Fahnen, 64 Geschütze, 1.800 Pferde den Franzosen in die Hände fielen.
```

      "value": "Höpfner: General Tschammer was charged with the defence of the approaches to Prenzlau; his companies and battalion guns covered the Berliner-Damm while two companies held the Berliner-Thor. He told the first parlementaire that he would continue his march without firing first, but whispered to General Hirschfeld that they were surrounded, and let Colonel Massenbach ride back with the parlementaire to see the enemy for himself. An officer of his suite, whose name was not established, ordered the grenadier battalion Dohna and the Wobeser dragoons back behind the town; Major Dohna left the gate despite Colonel Böhmke's order, and what caused this retreat Höpfner could not establish. Massenbach reported that they were not yet turned but might be in a few moments, that the Stettin road was open to the enemy and the enemy in the town, and urged that only pride and ambition could sacrifice the 7—8000 men still under the Prince's command; he assured General Hirschfeld that they were enclosed. Hohenlohe paid little attention to Captain Schöler's report and rode to meet Belliard; Hirschfeld was against any capitulation, and when Rittmeister Marwitz proposed falling on the small body standing in front, the Prince answered that Marshal Soult stood there. He reserved the terms for his generals and staff officers and obtained a longer truce. Before them he declared them surrounded and the road to Stettin cut, as Massenbach had seen for himself; Colonel Hüser, his chief of artillery, reported a want of ammunition, the guns having on average only 5—8 rounds, though he had only the battalion guns in view; the Prince called it his duty to accept the terms, all were silent, and he ordered the terms announced to the troops. Höpfner judges that the generals and staff officers were so blinded by Massenbach's false report and Hüser's misunderstood one that none rose to propose the most natural course, though most were men of the highest sense of honour, courage and talent.",

      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Prenzlau on 28 October: the French under Murat forced the Prussian army under Hohenlohe to capitulate. Murat wrote the same day that Hohenlohe and his corps were in his power: the officers were prisoners of war, keeping their swords and baggage and free to go home until exchanged; the troops laid down their arms, were prisoners of war and were sent to France. Höpfner gives the terms the Prince announced: the officers to keep their swords, horses and equipages and the men their knapsacks; the officers released on their word of honour not to serve until exchanged; the Guards and the King's regiment to be quartered at Potsdam; the NCOs and men of all other troops to go to France until exchanged; the arms not to be laid down but only stacked. The arms were stacked and the cavalry dismounted while the French shouted 'Vive l'Empereur!'.",

      "rationale": "The frozen frame outcome with Murat's letter, read from the page image, and the terms in Höpfner (OCR); no source read gives a different result. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; 'Sire, Your Majesty's orders are carried out. The Prince of Hohenlohe is in my power, as is his army corps'; 'the officers are prisoners of war, keep their swords and baggage and may return home until the exchange; the troops have laid down their arms, are prisoners of war and are sent back to France'; Höpfner, 'the officers keep their swords, horses and equipages, the common soldier his knapsack' (OCR); 'the officers are released on their word of honour not to serve until the exchange, and are free to go wherever they think fit' (OCR); 'to the royal Guards, as to His Majesty the King's regiment, although this is already captured, Potsdam shall be assigned as residence' (OCR); 'the NCOs and privates of all other troops shall be taken back to France until the exchange' (OCR); 'the muskets shall not be laid down but only stacked, the troops march off and leave them' (OCR); 'the thing was done! ### B374d: KAPITULATION von Stettin (29./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 29./10. KAPITULATION von Stettin
(Hafenstadt in Preußen, an der Oder, Hauptstadt von Pommern).
Vor 800 französischen Husaren unter Brig.-Gen. Gf. Lasalle kapituliert ohne Schwertstreich die von 5.300 Preußen (wor. 100 Offz.) mit 281 Kan. unter GM. v. Romberg besetzte Festung. Die Offiziere wurden auf Ehrenwort entlassen, die Mannschaft geriet in Kriegsgefangenschaft.
```

      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "The capitulation records that Lasalle summoned Fort Preussen and the town of Stettin in the name of the Grand Duke of Berg and repeated the summons with insistence after a first refusal. Höpfner: a hussar officer with a trumpeter rode at a trot to the governor, unescorted and without a blindfold, summoned him in the Grand Duke's name and urged that all resistance was vain, since the fortress was surrounded by 100,000 men and Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau; at 4 in the afternoon a second parlementaire declared that Lasalle stood with the advance guard ½ mile from the town, that the corps of Murat and Lannes would take the fortress the next morning with 30 to 40,000 men, and that if the governor did not surrender within 12 hours the town would have to pay ½ million Thaler besides the contribution to be demanded of it. The parlementaire accepted the governor's draft except the free withdrawal, and in the night brought it back translated into French with that condition changed to the garrison's disadvantage. Belliard, sent by Murat to Stettin to summon the commandant, found that Lasalle had begun the work and let him finish it, having the replies to the governor's demands put in; he approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order.       "rationale": "The capitulation's preamble, Belliard's letter and his approval, and Höpfner's account, all read from the page images. The parlementaires' figures are their claims, not counts.     {
      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: the governor was the 81-year-old General-Lieutenant Romberg and the commandant Major General Knobelsdorf, and General Rauch, director of the engineering academy and in charge of the works, was named vice-commandant by the King. The governor kept back no man of the troops passing through for fortress duty and refused General Bila II passage, which by Höpfner's account caused the capitulation of Anklam. Romberg answered the first summons with apparent calm that he knew his duty and would defend the fortress entrusted to him to the utmost, but as soon as the parlementaire had gone he dictated to the judge-advocate Dragaud a draft capitulation: the fortress to be handed over the next morning, the garrison to have free withdrawal and march off with all marks of honour; the commandant and vice-commandant joined in, the latter dictating the end of the draft. At the second parlementaire the governor lost all composure; everyone talked at once in the Frenchman's presence and no one thought of calling the prescribed council of war; the minister Ingersleben, who had come in uninvited, took the parlementaire to his residence so that they could deliberate, and those present unanimously resolved to surrender. The governor and both commandants signed the draft. When the garrison, knowing nothing of the negotiation, fired on enemy horsemen riding too boldly forward, the governor forbade the firing. Romberg was sentenced to death by court martial in 1809 but pardoned by the King. Belliard called him an old wreck of a governor who greeted the French with a few cannon shots and surrendered at discretion after making many difficulties.",

      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Stettin on 29 October without a stroke of the sword: the officers were released on their word of honour and the men went into captivity. The capitulation, dated at Stettin on 29 October 1806 at 6 in the evening and signed by Romberg as governor, surrendered the town and Fort Preussen to Lasalle. To the garrison's request for free exit with arms and baggage it answered that the garrison would march out with the honours of war, lay down its arms on the glacis and be prisoners of war sent to France, the officers prisoners on parole with passports to go where they wished, keeping their swords, baggage, horses and all that belonged to them; everything in the place belonging to the King of Prussia was to be handed over, the Prussian troops had until noon to settle their affairs, and the Berlin gate and a post on the Oder bridge were to be occupied by the French at 6 in the morning. Below the date the print sets the words 'seen and approved the present capitulation to be carried out' above Romberg's name, followed by Lasalle's, as brigadier general, at the headquarters of Möhringen on 29 October; whose approval the words record is not shown. Belliard approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order at half past eleven that evening. Belliard wrote that the commandant capitulated at 1 in the morning. Höpfner: the capitulation was carried out; at daybreak General Knobelsdorf led the garrison out by the Berlin gate, held like the Uckermünde gate by French cavalry, and it laid down its arms before 800 enemy cavalry and 2 guns. Lasalle reported that after he left, the garrison left on the glacis tried to take up its arms again, 500 having done so, until the elite battalion made them surrender again without firing a shot.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "The frozen frame outcome; the capitulation, Belliard's, Murat's and Lasalle's letters and Höpfner's account read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. The hours disagree and are kept as given: the capitulation is dated 6 in the evening of the 29th and Belliard approved it at half past eleven that night; Belliard reported that the commandant capitulated at 1 in the morning; Höpfner has the parlementaire bring back the French text in the night to the 30th and Lasalle enter the town at 6 in the morning before it was signed (claim side-a-command); Murat's covering letter is dated 2 in the morning, but Höpfner has him report at 5 in the morning. Articles 11 and 12, printed without replies, hand over the treasure in the place and name artillery and engineer officers to hand over and receive the magazines, munitions, maps and plans. Lannes wrote on 31 October that after the capitulation a rumour that the Russians were coming had made part of the garrison take up arms again, and that all was back in order (OCR). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; the capitulation, as in claim side-a-command for the preamble; 'art. 1. The whole present garrison, including the small staff and all soldiers not belonging to the garrison, shall obtain free exit with arms and baggage to go either to West and North Prussia or to Silesia'; 'reply. The garrison will march out with the honours of war, lay down its arms on the glacis, be prisoner of war and sent to France. The officers will be prisoners on parole and passports will be issued to them to go wherever they please'; 'reply. The officers will keep their swords, their baggage, their horses and all that may belong to them'; 'reply. Everything in the place belonging to His Majesty the King of Prussia will be handed over to the French troops'; 'reply. The Prussian troops will be granted until noon to arrange their affairs'; 'reply. The Berlin gate will be handed over to the French troops, who will have a post on the Oder bridge. These two posts will be occupied at 6 o'clock in the morning by the French troops'; 'art. 11. The treasure in the place will be handed over to the French troops'; 'art. 12. Artillery and engineer officers will be named on both sides to hand over and receive all the magazines, munitions, maps, plans, etc., in the place'; 'Stettin, 29 October 1806, at 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'seen and approved the present capitulation to be carried out. The Baron de Romberg, governor'; 'at the headquarters of Möhringen, 29 October 1806. The brigadier general, Lasalle'; as in claim side-a-command for Belliard's approval and the heading of his letter; 'I have the honour to report to you that the commandant of Stettin capitulated at 1 o'clock in the morning'; Murat, as in claim side-a-strength for the heading and the hussars at the gates; Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command for the night to the 30th and Lasalle's entry, and in claim side-a-strength for the march out; 'the Grand Duke of Berg reported to Napoleon at 5 o'clock in the morning: \"Your Majesty's hussars will take possession of the gates of the town\"'; Lasalle, as in claims side-b-strength-french for the heading and side-a-strength for the glacis; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor. Pasewalk, 31 October 1806'; 'the division of General Gazan with the brigade of General Claparède are at Stettin. After the enemy had capitulated, the rumour was spread that the Russians were coming, and part of the garrison had taken up its arms again. Everything has returned to order' (OCR).",

### B375a: KAPITULATION von Pasewalk (29./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 29./10. KAPITULATION von Pasewalk
(Stadt in Preußen, Pommern, an der Ucker, 37 km westl. von Stettin).
Vor der französischen Kavalleriebrigade Milhaud (700 Reiter) kapitulieren 4.200 Preußen, (worunter 185 Offiziere) mit 2.100 Pferden, 8 Kanonen, 1 Munitionswagen unter Brigadier Oberst v. Hagen, wonach die Offiziere auf Ehrenwort entlassen, die Mannschaften in Kriegsgefangenschaft abgeführt wurden.
```

      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Colonel Hagen, as the eldest of the column, called all the staff officers of the infantry and cavalry to a conference. Before it, Colonel Poser told the cavalry's staff officers that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated and the pass at Löcknitz was occupied, so that they would have to cut their way through; Major Thielan of the Heising regiment spoke first of the difficulties a break-through faced with men and horses exhausted and told Lieutenant Prittwitz, who declared a capitulation dishonourable, to be quiet; Colonel Winning of the Leib-Karabiniers consulted not only his officers but also called into counsel the sergeant-major of each squadron with NCOs and men, and that meeting resolved that they could not cut through but must capitulate. Several staff officers urged Poser to set out for Stettin as soon as possible. At the conference Hagen said he lacked the knowledge to judge whether the cavalry could march on; the Landrat Podewils proposed a safe route by Jägerbrück and Stolzenburg, and the colonel, by the context Hagen, paid no heed. Poser posted no field guards and ordered no patrols, only a chain of posts round the bivouac whose officers were to meet the enemy with a trumpeter and tell him negotiations were under way, and sent officer after officer to find the enemy, Count Matuschka with orders to tell him of their sad situation and bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to reconnoitre. When Prince Gustav of Mecklenburg-Schwerin reported the cavalry ever more enclosed and saw no way out but capitulation, Hagen, physically and morally exhausted and deeply bowed by Prenzlau, was confirmed in a resolve to capitulate that Höpfner says Poser seems to have prompted. Hagen and Poser signed a written mandate to capitulate for the two brigades with free withdrawal or, failing that, to surrender them into captivity. Höpfner finds no justification of any kind for the capitulation: the commanders thought of nothing but capitulation and sent officers in all directions to seek out the enemy and offer themselves.",

English renderings (ours): 'Colonel Hagen, as the eldest of the column, invited all the staff officers of the infantry and cavalry to a conference' (OCR); 'before the assembled staff officers of the cavalry had left the bivouac, Colonel Poser told them' (OCR); 'that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated and the pass at Löcknitz was occupied, so that they would have to cut their way through' (OCR); 'Major Thielan of Heising took the floor at the outset, set out the difficulties that the exhaustion of men and horses put in the way of a break-through, and told Lieutenant Prittwitz, who was present, to be quiet when the latter declared that a capitulation was dishonourable' (OCR); 'Colonel Winning, commander of the Leib-Karabinier regiment, asked not only the officers but also called into counsel from each squadron the sergeant-major, ... NCO and ... men' (OCR); 'and the decision of this meeting was that they could not cut their way through but must capitulate' (OCR); 'several staff officers urgently pressed Colonel Poser to set out for Stettin as soon as possible' (OCR); 'after all the staff officers had gathered in the evening at Colonel Hagen's in Pasewalk, he declared to the officers of the cavalry that he had not enough knowledge of their situation to be able to judge whether they were able to march on or not. Because of the difficulty of the crossing he advised against a march to the island of Usedom' (OCR); 'the colonel paid no heed to this statement' (OCR); 'Colonel Poser arranged that for the night no field guards were posted and no patrolling ordered, but only a chain of posts drawn round the bivouac of the cavalry, whose commanding officers received the instruction, if the enemy approached, to enter into no hostilities but to go to meet him with a trumpeter and inform him that negotiations were already under way' (OCR); 'at midnight Colonel Poser further sent off Lieutenant Count Königsdorf of the Henckel cuirassiers with a trumpeter and ... men' (OCR); 'when this officer came back without having perceived anything of the enemy, Colonel Poser sent Lieutenant Count Matuschka of the same regiment with the same escort, but with the errand to ride straight on until he came upon the enemy, to inform him of their sad situation, and to bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to make a reconnaissance' (OCR); 'he rode to Pasewalk to Colonel Hagen and reported to him: the cavalry was being more and more enclosed by the enemy' (OCR); 'Colonel Hagen asked the Prince what was to be done, as the cavalry's horses were too exhausted to accept a fight' (OCR); 'the Prince found a way out only in capitulation' (OCR); 'this view of the Prince strengthened in Colonel Hagen, who was physically and morally quite exhausted by the unspeakable hardships but deeply bowed by the capitulation of Prenzlau, the resolve already taken after the ... conference to capitulate as well, though Colonel Poser seems to have prompted the very idea' (OCR); 'if the capitulation at Prenzlau, where they knew a strong cavalry to be facing them and, by Colonel Massenbach's statements, could assume a strong enemy in their rear, where the troops had to cover a road of almost 4 miles across the plain in the face of the enemy in complete exhaustion and almost without ammunition, still had a trace of justification, the capitulation of Pasewalk had none of any kind'; 'they were informed early of the events at Prenzlau, and so knew of the enemy's approach; nevertheless no patrols are sent out to learn the enemy's position; no attempt is made, by spending their last strength, to forestall the enemy at Löcknitz; nor, if they believed they could not risk this attempt, do they take the trouble to inquire whether other roads than that by Löcknitz to Stettin were free; they pay no heed to the statement of the Landrat Podewils, who shows such a road; ### B375b: KAPITULATION von Boldekow (30./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 30./10. KAPITULATION von Boldekow
(Dorf in Preußen, Pommern, 14 km südl. von Anklam).
Die Franzosen unter Marschall Lannes nötigen die Bedeckungsmannschaft des Blücher'schen Artillerieparks unter Major v. Höpfner zur Kapitulation, wonach 25 Kanonen, 48 Munitionswägen, 800 Pferde in die Hände des Feindes und ca. 600 M. in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten.
```

      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Major Höpfner led the artillery column, which Blücher had urged to make particular haste. At Rheinsberg, when Prince Hohenlohe's expected orders failed to come and news arrived of a fight of Blücher's rear guard, he judged it unwise either to march on Fürstenberg or to spend the night at Rheinsberg, and marched by Alt-Strelitz towards Woldeck; at Bredenfelde, hearing that Pasewalk was in the enemy's hands, he turned to Friedland. There he told General Bila I that he meant to follow him to Anklam the next day, but Bila sent word that he should not march to Anklam but take his measures at his own discretion. In great perplexity the major called all the officers together to decide where to turn if they could march neither to Anklam nor to Stettin, and they resolved to march to Boldekow for forage. There, hearing that the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, they sent Lieutenant Braun II with a trumpeter towards Pasewalk to see how far the enemy had come; when the French officer came back with him, it was thought that a capitulation had to be made. Höpfner adds that no one thought of destroying the artillery material or of saving the men on the horses still found fit.",

### B375c: KAPITULATION von Küstrin (1./11. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 1./11. KAPITULATION von Küstrin
(Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, am Einfluß der Warthe in die Oder, 25 km nordöstl. von Frankfurt an der Oder).
Die preußische Besatzung (2.400 M. mit 92 Geschützen) unter Oberst v. Ingersleben ergibt sich ohne Schwertstreich an 1.500 Franzosen unter Brig.-Gen. Gauthier.
Die Besatzung wurde kriegsgefangen abgeführt, Offiziere auf Ehrenwort entlassen.
```

      "value": "Höpfner: Davout detached Gudin's division against Küstrin to seize its bridgehead if possible. After the fight at the bridgehead Gudin summoned the fortress and let the commandant know that he would bombard the town if surrender were refused; recalled that night, he left only the 85th regiment under General Gauthier. When the commandant's envoy, Lieutenant Thynkel, came to negotiate an armistice, General Petit seemed willing to negotiate, but Colonel Düplin of the 85th declared that unless the town were surrendered within 2 hours the bombardment would begin. Gauthier and Düplin received the commandant and told him that Stettin had fallen, Hohenlohe's corps was captured and Küstrin badly garrisoned, and that the bombardment would begin at once and not stop until the town was in ashes; the French general dictated the terms, and grenadiers crossing the Oder soon occupied the fortress. Davout then went to Küstrin in person (OCR passage). The 25th Bulletin: Davout had Küstrin invested and summoned.",

      "rationale": "Höpfner from the page images of pp. 324-328, with his sentence on Davout from the OCR; the Bulletin from the page image of p. 648. Höpfner does not say which general dictated the terms. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'with the main body of the corps Marshal Davout set out on the 28th from the area in front of Berlin, and on the 29th detached from Müncheberg the division Güdin with 12 guns on Küstrin, to seize the bridgehead there if possible'; 'General Güdin summoned the fortress and let the commandant know that he would bombard the town if the surrender were refused'; 'in the night before 1 November General Güdin received the order to set out at once for the main body of the 3rd corps at Frankfurt, as Napoleon would set part of Marshal Augereau's troops marching to Küstrin and assign them to invest the fortress'; 'General Güdin had to comply with the order, set out at daybreak on 1 November, and left behind only the 85th infantry regiment under General Gauthier'; 'Lieutenant Thynkel believed he had to obey, met the first French post at the far end of the suburb, and was taken to General Petit, who was about to have the posts relieved'; 'the general seemed willing to enter into negotiations, but was prevented from it by Colonel Düplin of the 85th regiment, who was present and declared: if the town were not surrendered within 2 hours, the bombardment would begin'; 'the commandant was received on the other side by General Gauthier and Colonel Düplin; it was put to him that Stettin had fallen, the Hohenlohe corps was captured, Küstrin badly garrisoned, the bombardment would begin at once and not stop until the town had been reduced to ashes. The commandant'; 'the French general dictated the points of capitulation, by which at noon on 1 November the gates were to be occupied by 3 companies of French grenadiers, the garrison was to lay down its arms, safeguards were to be granted to the members of the Chamber and the property of the inhabitants protected.     {
      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Colonel Ingersleben, the commandant, had been ordered on 17 October to make all defensive arrangements to secure the fortress against a forcible attack. In the fight at the bridgehead the Prussians escaped over the bridge he had already set on fire. That evening, when bugles sounded at the end of the Oder bridge, he told the engineer of the place, Lieutenant Thynkel, to go over and ask what the alarm meant and to threaten to burn the suburbs; when Thynkel objected to threatening or negotiating with the enemy, he sent the artillery lieutenant Wille to agree that if the enemy kept quiet he would not fire on the bridgehead. On the morning of 1 November he told his staff officers that he had sure news of a corps of 100,000 men approaching on the right bank, that no relief was to be expected and that the state of the garrison was known to all. Colonel Weyherr advised surrender rather than see the suburbs burned, Colonel Manteuffel agreed, trusting the commandant to act on his instructions, Colonel Boumann of the artillery said the commandant could do as he pleased, and Thynkel held that the fortress must and could defend itself, the main wall holding even without the outworks, and that a bombardment would not take it, the garrison having casemates. The commandant declared that he would not have the town burned and sent Thynkel to negotiate an armistice of 8 to 14 days; on Thynkel's report he said there was no time to lose and went himself, his wife's pleas being set aside by the Küstrin Kammerpräsident, who had gained great influence over him. Received by Gauthier and Düplin, he let himself be moved to capitulate, answering Thynkel's objections that he knew the Grand Duke of Berg was approaching with 100,000 men, after which no capitulation would be possible, and that he must not let the town be burned or its citizens made unhappy. Thynkel refused to sign. A court martial sentenced Ingersleben to be shot for proven cowardice; the King pardoned him to fortress imprisonment for life.",

'Colonel Ingersleben assembled the staff officers of the garrison on the morning of 1 November and put it to them that the enemy was before the gates of the fortress, and that he had received sure news that a corps of 100,000 men was also on the march on the right bank of the Oder; relief was not to be expected; the state of the garrison was known to all'; as in claim side-b-strength for Colonel Weyherr; 'Colonel Manteuffel of the regiment Zenge likewise voted for the surrender, relying on the honesty of the commandant to act according to the instruction given him'; 'Colonel Boumann of the'; 'artillery, who was present, answered: the commandant could do and leave undone what he would'; as in claim side-b-strength for Lieutenant Thynkel; 'the commandant objected that the garrison was not enough to man the outworks, to which Lieutenant Thynkel replied that even after abandoning the outworks the main wall could hold sufficiently'; ### B375d: KAPITULATION von Anklam (1./11. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 1./11. KAPITULATION von Anklam
(Stadt in Preußen, Pommern, an der Peene, 75 km nordwestl. von Stettin).
Vor der französischen Dragonerbrigade Becker (ca. 1.000 M.) strecken 2.200 Preußen (1.100 Inft., 1.100 Kav.) unter Gen. v. Bila die Waffen, wonach die Mannschaften in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten, die Offiziere gegen Ehrenwort entlassen wurden.
```

      "value": "Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures. Lasalle wrote on 30 October, citing a postillon, of a corps outside Anklam of guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers and dragoons, with many infantry and above all baggage and no guns, put at 6,000 men. Beker wrote on 31 October of a corps of 2,000 men, and then of a column of 3,000 men, 1,000 to 1,200 of them cavalry, commanded by 2 generals; on 2 November, writing that the capture was larger than it had first seemed, he gave an aide-de-camp's count: besides the 2 generals, 1,200 and some mounted cavalry and more than 1,500 infantry, including 1 battalion of 700 grenadiers, with 1 flag and 4 horsed guns. Murat wrote on 1 November that the corps was 3,000 to 4,000 men, with guns, 2 generals, 2 cavalry regiments and a strong detachment of a 3rd, and 1,400 or 1,500 horses to be received. The 25th Bulletin gives 4,000 prisoners of war, and Mathieu Dumas, as Höpfner quotes him, about four thousand, among them the hussars of the King's guard.",
