      "id": "magdeburg-ground",
      "dimension": "terrain",
      "value": "Bodart places Magdeburg, a town in Prussia and capital of the province of Saxony, on the Elbe. Höpfner: by the works undertaken since the end of April 1806 the main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had been palisaded, many works of the outer enceinte linked by palisades, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, so that with any serious resistance the fortress could be taken only by a formal attack; only the suburbs could not resist long, and the entrenchments near them were to hold the enemy only until the inhabitants had saved their belongings, after which the suburbs were to be burned, though their many massive ruins would still block the view. Buildings that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and Neustadt were pulled down from the 29th and the rest burned that night. On the right bank the garrison foraged towards the Herrenkrug, Kolbert set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester, and the French posts were pushed to 12—1500 paces from the glacis, with supports at Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau and reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern; on the left bank Marchand commanded the position upstream, with his quarters at Gr. Ottersleben, and Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt. Ney: the extent of the fortifications was immense; the bridges at Schönebeck and over the old Elbe at Plötzky let his corps cross without being disturbed; Friedrichstadt lay on the right bank, where Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester and the farms nearer the place; Colbert's posts stood one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and Vandamme's posts were entrenched within musket range of Neustadt; on 7 November Colbert, with his headquarters at Gommern, commanded on the right bank, Marchand was at Gross-Ottersleben and Vandamme had his headquarters at Olvenstadt, his left resting on the Elbe; works of the place protected Sudenburg and the Closterberg; and the musketry and cannonade of almost every night were between Neustadt and Diesdorf.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Location and works as described, read from the page images. No plan of Magdeburg was inspected (Ney's plan of the blockade, sent on 7 November, was not seen), and where each work stood is taken only from the narratives. Ney gives the distance of the posts in cannon ranges and Höpfner in paces; they are not converted. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, on the Elbe, capital of the province of Saxony)'; 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'the French posts on the right bank were now pushed forward to a distance of 12—1500 paces from the glacis, the supports in Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau, reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern'; 'on the left bank General Marchand commanded the position upstream and had his quarters in Gr. Ottersleben, General Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'the bridge at Schönebeck is perfectly established, as is the one over the old Elbe at Plötzky; this construction gives me the means of crossing the river with my army corps without the enemy being able in any way to disturb me'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'General Colbert's posts are at one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and the service is done so that nothing can come out of it. His main posts occupy Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs, Zippeleben and Pechau'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'if the works of the place that protect Sudenburg and Closterberg prevent us from keeping these 2 points, they will be set on fire, so that the enemy cannot draw any resource from them and is obliged to take in their population, which is already too considerable in Magdeburg for us not to hope for a general revolt if I receive some mortars to bombard the town'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'General Colbert, whose headquarters are at Gommern, commands on the right bank'; 'General Marchand is established at Gross-Ottersleben'; 'General Vandamme has his headquarters at Olvenstadt, resting his left on the Elbe'; 'musketry and cannonade are repeated almost every night between Neustadt and Diesdorf, which tired the garrison of Magdeburg extremely. I have signal rockets fired twice each'.",

      "value": "Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress had 577 guns and abundant ammunition but no miners; there was bread flour for 3 months and, in this trading town, no lack of grain, but the governor had neglected to bring in fresh meat and other provisions from the right bank in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October. The bearer of Ney's summons of 23 October reported little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces; the Emperor wrote on 7 November, after ordering Ney to bombard Magdeburg, that all the letters from Stettin asserted that 'the place' was not provisioned and lacked the most important things; the 29th Bulletin put much artillery, considerable magazines and many regimental chests in the fortress, but Ney wrote on 11 November that by his information the regimental chests had followed Prince Hohenlohe's corps on its passage through Magdeburg, and that no trace of the Prince of Hesse's treasure had yet been found. Side A (French): Ney wrote on 25 October that his corps's provisions were assured. He asked for mortars on 30 October, and on 2 November the 4 he had asked of General Clarke arrived with their supply (Höpfner has 4 mortars brought from Erfurt); General Marchand wrote that he had no means to have the ladders shod. The Emperor ordered on 7 November 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars sent from Wittenberg, noting powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden and 500 milliers of powder at Wittenberg; on 8 November Ney wrote that he had not thought he should countermand that artillery before the capitulation was signed, and would do so then.",

      "rationale": "Höpfner, Ney's and Marchand's letters, the Emperor's letter and the 29th Bulletin, read from the page images. Side B's stores were set before the investment; side A's mortars came from Ney's own requests and the Emperor's orders; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Old measures are kept as printed. The stores found at the capitulation are in claim side-b-losses. Whether the Emperor's guns had arrived by the capitulation is not shown. The sentence on the letters from Stettin does not name the place; it follows the order to bombard Magdeburg and is read as about Magdeburg only on that ground. The Bulletin's regimental chests and Ney's later information differ; both are kept. English renderings (ours): 'the fortress had 577 guns, abundant ammunition, 20,339 men of infantry, 2110 men of actual artillerymen, 510 men of cavalry, 1159 men of the pontoon and other trains, together 24,118 men and 6563 horses, so that a'; 'disproportionately small cavalry and no miners at all were present, a want by which an essential means of defence was withdrawn from the fortress'; 'of bread flour there was a stock for 3 months; of grain there could be no lack, given the great stores in this trading town; on the other hand the governor had neglected, in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, when the complete investment first took place, to supply himself from the rich country on the right bank of the Elbe with sufficient fresh meat and the other provisions, for which the confusion in the fortress until the complete departure of the Hohenlohe troops may at first have been to blame'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general.     {
      "id": "side-a-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Ney wrote on 2 November that he had intelligences in the place with persons who waited only for his bombs to force the governor to capitulate, and that despite the questioning of the deserters who arrived daily he had no very precise figure for the garrison. On 23 October General Wartensleben had told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to bring the governor to reason if a few shells were fired on the place (Höpfner gives Wartensleben's words to the French parlementaire from Ney's report). Ney had the Closterberg reconnoitred, and his engineers worked for 4 days on a plan of the blockade, which he sent on 7 November. His parleys over 2 days with civil and military officials of the town convinced him that a simple bombardment would bring the place down (3 November). It was known, he wrote, that the garrison was tired of its service; deserters and prisoners said it had only one night of rest, and the sick were said to number 1,800. Deserters kept coming in: 11 on 3 November, one on the 4th and 5 on the 6th. General Marchand judged on 2 November that Lieutenant General Kleist probably wanted only a plausible reason to surrender honourably, which only a few bombs thrown into the town could give him, and that until then an old soldier like him could not hear of surrendering a place such as Magdeburg. The Emperor wrote on 7 November that all the letters from Stettin asserted that the place, not named in the sentence, was not provisioned (claim means-and-supply). The French estimates of the garrison are in claim side-b-strength-french.",

      "rationale": "Side A's letters and report, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. Whether Ney's intelligences in the place were the officials he parleyed with is not shown. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I had the honour of writing to you on 30 October and asking you for some mortars to bombard Magdeburg; it would be all the more essential for me to have them at my disposal as the persons with whom I have intelligences in the place are only waiting for the moment when I have had bombs thrown, to force the governor, Count Kleist, to capitulate'; 'the strength of the garrison of Magdeburg is put today at 15,000 men; it has been impossible until now to obtain very precise information on this, despite the questioning to which the deserters, who arrive every day in fairly large numbers, have been subjected'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'General Wartensleben, sent by the King of Prussia to this governor, told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to succeed in making him listen to reason if a few shells were fired on the place'; 'for the rest the governor was a proud, hard man, feared by his subordinates, who at this time, however, had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who had stayed behind in the fortress, who seems early on to have wished for a speedy surrender and, according to Marshal Ney's report to Napoleon, is said to have told the French parlementaire, who complained to him of the old governor's obstinacy, as early as 23 October: \"First throw plenty of bombs and shells into the town, and the obstinate governor will surely change his mind.\"'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I have had the Closterberg reconnoitred; I hope to be able to carry it by a coup de main; at the same time Sudenburg and Neustadt will be escaladed'; 'it is known that the garrison is tired of its service; it will be still more so through the alarms that we give it from time to time'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'I shall have the honour of sending you within 3 days a plan of Magdeburg showing the camps and posts I have set up on both banks of the Elbe for the blockade of this place'; 'this work, on which the engineer officers have been busy for 4 days, will prove to Your Highness that the whole of the troops is not too numerous to blockade a place that holds many more men than is believed and that must be watched very closely, to deprive it of the resources in subsistence it could draw from its surroundings'; 'the parleys I have had for 2 days with civil and military officials of Magdeburg prove more than ever that a simple bombardment would make this place fall; I have at this moment the means of carrying it out and await only Your Highness's orders to do so'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'I have the honour to send Your Serene Highness the plan of the fortress of Magdeburg with the placing of the troops that form the blockade'; 'night. All these alarms exhaust the enemy, so that the deserters and prisoners say that the garrison has only one night of rest, during which it is often obliged to take up arms'; 'this extreme fatigue has caused much sickness; the number of men in hospital and with fever amounts, it is said, to 1,800'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'on the 3rd some detachments of the 3rd division were sent out during the night to carry any posts the enemy might have outside the place; they advanced up to the palisades without meeting anyone. — 11 deserters were received'; 'on the 4th one deserter arrived'; 'on the 6th 5 deserters arrived'; 'General Marchand to Marshal Ney. Benekenbeck, 2 November 1806'; 'in the circumstances in which Lieutenant General Kleist finds himself, it is probable that he asks only for a plausible reason to be able to surrender honourably; the only reason you can give him is to throw a few bombs into the town; until then an old soldier like him cannot hear of surrendering a place such as Magdeburg'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'all the letters from Stettin assert that the place is not provisioned and lacks the most important things'.",

    {
      "id": "side-b-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Höpfner: Ney sent the governor, through the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, the French Bulletin containing the capitulation of Prenzlau, and had the impossibility of relief put to him; his summons of the 5th again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of relief. The governor answered that he could agree to nothing until he had convinced himself of the army's dissolution by sending a Prussian officer. On 6 November Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, taken at Prenzlau, came in with Ney's envoys and gave the governor's meeting an account of the army's march to the Oder, and Kleist said Wedell had convinced him that relief was hopeless; the engineer of the place told him that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege. Ney wrote that he had had the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's corps and the surrender of Stettin brought into the town and spread there; that the governor wished to send an officer to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army before deciding on defence or capitulation; and that Baron de Williben, sent by the province's civil authorities to ask that the place not be bombarded, had tried in vain to convince Kleist that the obstinacy of the defence was pointless.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Side B's history and Ney's letters, read from the page images. Höpfner's footnote says Ney's report speaks of a former Oberstlieutenant and the records of the inquiry into the capitulation of Magdeburg of a Rittmeister Willisen; Ney's letter of 3 November calls Williben a former lieutenant colonel (claim side-b-strength-french). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney sent the governor of Magdeburg, through the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, the French Bulletin that contained the capitulation of Prenzlau, and had the impossibility of a relief represented to him'; 'Marshal Ney's report speaks of a former Oberstlieutenant, the records of the inquiry into the capitulation of Magdeburg of a Rittmeister Willisen'; 'on the afternoon of the 5th Marshal Ney summoned the fortress again, with the remark that by the bombardment he had only wanted to prove that he possessed the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes; at the same time he again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of a relief, and asked the governor to have regard for the unfortunate 25,000 inhabitants, who would be exposed to the misfortune of a bombardment to no benefit for the state' (pp. 333-334); 'the governor answered: he could not enter into anything until he had really convinced himself of the dissolution of the army by sending a Prussian officer; until that officer's return, however, he would conclude an armistice'; 'on 6 November the marshal sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard to Magdeburg, accompanied by Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, who had been taken prisoner at Prenzlau'; 'the governor at once assembled the generals present in Magdeburg and the commandant, laid before them the correspondence with Marshal Ney, had Major Wedell give an account of the events in the army on the march to the Oder, and announced his decision to capitulate'; 'the negotiations were continued. The engineer of the place represented to the governor that the fortress could not be taken by a coup de main, that despite its poor profile it could hold out in a regular siege for 4—5'; 'weeks after the opening of the trenches, that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege, which needed a considerable time, and that he should therefore not hurry anything at all'; 'it was all in vain. The governor answered that he held himself convinced by Major Wedell of the hopelessness of a relief, and must therefore capitulate out of humanity'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I have taken care to have the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's army corps, the surrender of Stettin, etc., brought into the town and spread there'; 'the governor expressed to me the wish to send one of his officers to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army, so as to take a decision either for the defence of the place or for the capitulation. I had agreed to this request on the condition that on this officer's return the town would capitulate. The governor has not spoken of it again'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'the governor renewed to me yesterday the request for a passport for one of his aides-de-camp, whom he wished to send'; 'to Berlin to make sure of the situation of the Prussian armies; he proposed a cessation of arms until this officer's return. I offered this passage on the condition that the town would surrender as soon as it was proved that there was no longer a Prussian army; this condition was not accepted'; 'Baron de Williben, former lieutenant colonel in the service of Prussia, president of the first circle of the administration of Magdeburg, who lives at Strassfurt, has been appointed commissioner by the civil authorities of the province to go to Berlin to Your Highness and, if possible, to His Majesty, to obtain that the place not be bombarded'; 'this officer has made vain efforts to convince Count Kleist that the obstinacy of the defence is pointless in the present circumstances; he claims that the place holds more than 16,000 men of all arms; I think this number exaggerated'.",

    {
      "id": "side-a-objectives",
      "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side A (French): on 23 October Ney set out to seize all the communications reaching Magdeburg on the right bank. On 2 November he asked the major general whether the Emperor intended the bombardment to be tried or a simple blockade, and whether he might use every means to reduce the garrison by force or by negotiation; on 3 November, whether to keep to a simple blockade, to bombard, or to negotiate an armistice of 15 days or a month so as to take half his troops to Berlin. His daily report of 2 November planned to carry the Closterberg by a coup de main and at the same time escalade Sudenburg and Neustadt, setting fire to Sudenburg and the Closterberg if the works of the place prevented holding them, so that the enemy could draw no resources from them and would have to take in their population, and hoped for a general revolt in the town if he received mortars; General Marchand urged him that the only aim was the taking of Magdeburg, for which bombs were needed, and that the Closterberg was not worth a hundred grenadiers if it would not hasten that by a quarter of an hour. The Emperor wrote on 7 November: bombard Magdeburg, with red-hot shot to set the town on fire; tell the governor that a siege train had arrived, that the town would be burned and sacked and that there would be no capitulation for the officers; and, if they ever doubted the capture of Küstrin and Stettin, he saw no objection to one of their officers going by Berlin to Küstrin and Stettin and back to Magdeburg to assure them of the position. He imagined that Ney would have Magdeburg before 15 November; his troops had entered Poland, the Russians had not yet entered it on 1 November and would probably be met in the first days of December, and he wished Ney rid of Magdeburg so as to be on the Vistula about that time. He ordered all wagons and baggage searched, saying Ney would find part of the Prince of Hesse-Cassel's treasure and many regimental chests at Magdeburg. By Höpfner, Ney told the governor on the 5th that the bombardment had only been meant to prove that he had the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes, and he expected to find the Elector of Hesse's treasure there. On 8 November Ney meant to leave the 6th light and the 15th dragoons at Magdeburg and set out for Berlin on the 13th, and promised every precaution so that the Hesse-Cassel treasure, if it was in the place, should not escape.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Ney's letters and report, Marchand's letter and the Emperor's, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. The aims came both from Ney and from the Emperor's orders, so the phase is left unresolved. The Emperor's letter of 7 November is dated after Ney's trial bombardment of the night of 4 to 5 November, and says he had already let Ney know that the bombardment should keep increasing; that earlier letter was not read, and when the letter of 7 November reached Ney is not shown. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'my responsibility requires me to ask Your Highness to answer the following questions with precise instructions'; 'is it the Emperor's intention that the bombardment be attempted, or must I confine myself to the simple blockade?'; 'am I authorised to use all the means in my power to reduce the garrison, either by force or by way of negotiations?'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'if the Emperor wishes me to leave the Vandamme division before Magdeburg and go to Berlin with the rest of my troops, I see no other means of fulfilling his intentions, without compromising that division, than to negotiate with the governor, Count Kleist, an armistice that would put this place in a state of blockade, without any kind of communication with the outside, for a fixed period of 15 days or a month. I could succeed in this negotiation'; 'I beg Your Highness to let me know which course I am to take: either to confine myself to a simple blockade, or to bombard the place, or finally to negotiate an armistice so as to withdraw half my troops and send them to Berlin'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I have had the Closterberg reconnoitred; I hope to be able to carry it by a coup de main; at the same time Sudenburg and Neustadt will be escaladed'; 'if the works of the place that protect Sudenburg and Closterberg prevent us from keeping these 2 points, they will be set on fire, so that the enemy cannot draw any resource from them and is obliged to take in their population, which is already too considerable in Magdeburg for us not to hope for a general revolt if I receive some mortars to bombard the town'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'General Marchand to Marshal Ney. Benekenbeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I think that before making any serious enterprise against the Closterberg one will have to think twice. If the occupation of that post cannot advance the taking of Magdeburg by a quarter of an hour, I think that one should not then risk losing a hundred or so grenadiers to carry it'; 'here the only result one can set oneself is the taking of Magdeburg. For that, bombs are needed. All the rest does nothing to advance the single aim'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'I am ordering General Lemarois, who is at Wittenberg, to send you 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars with their equipment and supply. We have powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden. You have gunners who can serve this matériel. Bombard Magdeburg'; 'I have let you know that the bombardment should always go on increasing. Serve the pieces with red-hot shot, so as to set fire to the town'; 'do not be slow to inform me that Magdeburg has surrendered or is on fire'; 'you will not fail to let the governor know that a siege train has reached you from Dresden; that with 100 pieces of artillery and the engineer and artillery officers you have, the place will soon be taken; that in 8 days you will have crossed the ditch and made the breach; that the town will be burned and sacked; that once it comes to that, there will be no capitulation for the officers; that this resistance is pointless, for my armies are on the Vistula, and that Küstrin and Stettin are taken'; 'if they ever doubted'; 'this capture, I would see no objection to one of their officers going by Berlin to Küstrin and to Stettin and coming back to Magdeburg to assure them of the position of things'; 'I imagine that you will have Magdeburg before 15 November'; 'my troops have entered Poland'; 'the Russians had not yet entered it on 1 November'; 'it is probable that we shall meet them in the first days of December'; 'you feel how much I wish you to be rid of Magdeburg, so as to be on the Vistula about that time'; 'you will find at Magdeburg part of the treasure of the Prince of Hesse-Cassel and many regimental chests. Let nothing escape you; to that end have all the wagons and baggage searched, and leave the officers only what truly belongs to them'; 'on the afternoon of the 5th Marshal Ney summoned the fortress again, with the remark that by the bombardment he had only wanted to prove that he possessed the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes; at the same time he again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of a relief, and asked the governor to have regard for the unfortunate 25,000 inhabitants, who would be exposed to the misfortune of a bombardment to no benefit for the state' (pp. 333-334); 'the marshal expected to find the treasure of the Elector of Hesse in Magdeburg and took every conceivable pains that it should not escape the hands of the French'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'my intention, unless Your Majesty orders otherwise, is to leave at Magdeburg the 6th light infantry and the 15th dragoons, which stayed at Brünswick, and to leave on the 13th with the rest of my army corps for Berlin'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'no measures will be neglected for the discovery and preservation of the objects that must belong to Your Majesty; above all I shall exhaust every precaution so that, if the Prince of Hesse-Cassel indeed has part of his treasure in the place, it cannot escape us'.",
      "citations": [
        {

          "quote": "J'ai l'honneur de rendre compte à V. A. que je fais établir un pont de bateaux à Schönebeck; aussitôt que cette opération sera terminée, je passerai l'Elbe pour m'emparer sur la rive droite de ce fleuve de toutes les communications qui aboutissent à Magdeburg."

          "quote": "Ma responsabilité exige que je prie V. A. de répondre par des instructions précises aux questions suivantes :"

          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 677 (transcribed from the page image)",

          "quote": "Si l'Empereur désire que je laisse devant Magdeburg la division Vandamme et que je me rende à Berlin avec le surplus de mes troupes, je ne vois d'autre moyen de remplir ses intentions, sans compromettre cette division, que de négocier avec le gouverneur comte de Kleist un armistice qui constituerait cette place en état de blocus, sans aucune espèce de communications avec le dehors pour une durée fixe de 15 jours ou d'un mois.           "quote": "Je donne ordre au général Lemarois, qui est à Wittenberg, de vous expédier 6 pièces de 24 et 2 mortiers avec armement et approvisionnement. Nous avons de la poudre et des bombes en quantité à Dresde. Vous avez des canonniers qui peuvent servir ce matériel. Bombardez Magdeburg."

          "quote": "Ne tardez pas à m'apprendre que Magdeburg est rendu ou en feu."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p766-figures-v1",
          "section": "p766",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 766 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Vous ne manquerez pas de faire connaître au gouverneur qu'il vous est arrivé un équipage de siège de Dresde; qu'avec 100 pièces d'artillerie et les officiers du génie et d'artillerie que vous avez, la place sera bientôt prise; que dans 8 jours vous aurez passé le fossé et pratiqué la brèche; que la ville sera brûlée et saccagée; qu'arrivé à ce point, il n'y aura pas de capitulation pour les officiers; que cette résistance est sans but, car mes armées sont sur la Vistule, et que Küstrin et Stettin sont pris."

      "id": "side-b-objectives",
      "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress had been readied so that, with any serious resistance, only a formal attack could take it, while the suburbs were to hold the enemy only until the inhabitants had saved their belongings and then be burned; but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence, would agree to nothing until an officer had confirmed the army's dissolution, and in the end said he must capitulate out of humanity, while the engineer held that the fortress could hold 4—5 weeks after the opening of the trenches and all the generals except Wartensleben were more or less averse to surrender. Höpfner says the inhabitants' disposition gave no suspicion that they would hinder the defence. Ney wrote that on 23 October Kleist gave his word not to thwart French movements out of range of his cannon; on 7 November, that the day after the trial bombardment the burghers had gathered under the governor's windows and threatened him with revolt if the place were not surrendered; and on 8 November, that there were two parties in the place, the magistrates and inhabitants wishing to capitulate and the officers insisting on resistance. The 29th Bulletin: after several houses were burned the inhabitants showed their discontent and the commandant asked to capitulate.",

      "rationale": "Side B's history with Ney's letters and the 29th Bulletin, read from the page images. Höpfner and the French documents differ on the inhabitants; both are kept. The governor's word of 23 October is Ney's report and is not in the Höpfner passages read. English renderings (ours): 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'the governor answered: he could not enter into anything until he had really convinced himself of the dissolution of the army by sending a Prussian officer; until that officer's return, however, he would conclude an armistice'; 'it was all in vain. The governor answered that he held himself convinced by Major Wedell of the hopelessness of a relief, and must therefore capitulate out of humanity'; 'the negotiations were continued. The engineer of the place represented to the governor that the fortress could not be taken by a coup de main, that despite its poor profile it could hold out in a regular siege for 4—5'; 'weeks after the opening of the trenches, that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege, which needed a considerable time, and that he should therefore not hurry anything at all'; 'except General Count Wartensleben, the senior general after the governor, all the generals had shown themselves more or less averse to the surrender of the fortress'; 'the disposition of the inhabitants of Magdeburg gave in no way any suspicion that, even in the greatest straits, they could in any respect hinder the defence'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'M. de Kleist has moreover given his word not to seek to thwart the operations of the French armies provided the movements take place out of range of his cannon'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general.           "section": "p330",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 330 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Magdeburg war trotz des früheren höchst verfallenen Zustandes und der fehlerhaften Konstruktion der Werke dennoch durch den seit Ende April 1806 unternommenen Korrekturbau und durch die Thätigkeit des Ingenieurs vom Platz, Hauptmann Kleist, dahin gebracht worden, daß die ganze Hauptfestung, die Stern- und Thurmschanze eine tüchtige Pallisadirung erhalten hatten, sämmtliche Barrieren eingehangen, die Barrikaden und Kommunikationsbrücken fertig, alle schadhaften und fehlenden Brustwehren in Ordnung gesetzt, viele Werke der äußern Umwallung durch starke Pallisadirungen zusammengehangen, ihre Saillants bonnetirt und die Gräben am Austritt nach der Elbe gesperrt worden waren, und überhaupt die Festung sich in einem Zustande befand, daß sie bei einer irgend ernsten Gegenwehr nur durch einen förmlichen Angriff erobert werden konnte."

    {
      "id": "posture",
      "dimension": "posture",
      "value": "Side A (French) attacked: Bodart has the French under Ney force the garrison to capitulate after a 12-day investment and a short bombardment, and the 29th Bulletin says Ney, charged with the siege, had the place bombarded. Ney bridged the Elbe to seize the communications on the right bank and summoned the place; by his daily report his troops drove the enemy's advanced posts under its cannon from the 26th to the 28th, completing the blockade, and Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester near Friedrichstadt in the night of 31 October to 1 November. Höpfner has the investment of the right bank completed on the 27th, only insignificant engagements until the 29th, Kolbert's attack on the Prussian outposts at 3 in the morning of 1 November, and on 4 November a French attack on the Neustadt, repulsed, followed in the night to the 5th by the bombardment and repeated vain attacks on the Neustadt. Ney's letter of 7 November has the enemy attempt a sortie between 8 and 9 that night and be sharply repulsed while 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place. Side B's sorties, among them the foraging sortie of 31 October, went back into the place or were repulsed, and by Ney's account took no prisoner.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Coded A_attacked: side A invested, bombarded and summoned the fortress, and side B capitulated; side B's sorties were counterattacks within the siege and do not make it an attacker. The phase is left unresolved: the passages read show Ney's own crossing, summonses, trial bombardment and attacks, and the major general's renewed order to bridge the Elbe, but no order from above to invest or attack Magdeburg; the Emperor's order to bombard is dated 7 November, after the trial bombardment, and says he had already let Ney know that the bombardment should keep increasing; that earlier letter was not read. Who attacked in the night of 4 to 5 November differs (Höpfner: the French, on the Neustadt; Ney: a Prussian sortie); both are kept. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'Marshal Ney, charged with the siege of Magdeburg, had this place bombarded. Several houses having been burned, the inhabitants showed their discontent, and the commandant asked to capitulate'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'I received today at 2 in the morning the letter you did me the honour of writing to me from Berlin on the 1st of this month, in which you renew the order to have a bridge of boats built over the Elbe'; 'Your Highness will have seen from my earlier letters that this bridge has existed opposite Schönebeck since 25 October'; 'only on the 27th did he complete the investment on the right bank of the Elbe, though still at a great distance from the place'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'did not interfere; in general it had so far come only to insignificant engagements'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'on 4 November the enemy attacked the Neustadt but was repulsed, and in the night to the 5th Marshal Ney had 12 bombs and also some shells thrown at the Altstadt and the Neustadt from the 4 mortars brought up meanwhile from Erfurt, and had the Neustadt attacked repeatedly in vain'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'great exactness reigns in the service, and the result is that the enemy, after attempting several sorties, has not managed to take a single prisoner from us'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms. The 3rd division was also under arms all night; the enemy attempted a sortie between 8 and 9 o'clock; he was sharply repulsed. 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place; one house was burned in the town and 2 others in the suburb of Neustadt'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'I am ordering General Lemarois, who is at Wittenberg, to send you 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars with their equipment and supply. We have powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden. You have gunners who can serve this matériel. Bombard Magdeburg'; 'I have let you know that the bombardment should always go on increasing. Serve the pieces with red-hot shot, so as to set fire to the town'.",

### B376d: KAPITULATION von Hameln (20./11. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p376, as printed:

```text
1806 20./11. KAPITULATION von Hameln
(Stadt in Preußen, Provinz Hannover, an der Weser, 40 km südwestl. von Hannover).
Die Franzosen (6.000 M.) unter Div.-Gen. Savary zwingen nach 14tägiger Blokade die preußische Besatzung (10.000 M. mit 129 Geschützen) unter GM. v. Lecoq zur Kapitulation, wonach die Garnison in Kriegsgefangenschaft abgeführt werden sollte. Nach Bekanntmachung dieser Kapitulation entstand unter der Besatzung eine Meuterei, welche mit der Desertion und Flucht des größten Teiles der Garnison auf das vom Feinde unbesetzte linke Weserufer endete, so daß nur ein schwacher Rest (600 M.) den Franzosen in die Hände fiel.
```

      "id": "bodart-commanders",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Bodart names General of Division Savary as side A's (French) commander and Major General v. Lecoq as side B's (Prussian). Höpfner: Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler was appointed commandant of Hameln in May, and Lecoq commanded his own corps, which reached 4000 men on 23 October and camped at the foot of the Klütberg from the 24th; at the Wehrberg Warte Lecoq drafted the capitulation and the commandant signed it, and Schöler refused to let Colonel Caprivi sign as well, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts. Savary announced his arrival as commander of the besieging corps on the evening of the 19th, sent by Napoleon's order of 18 November to take command of the blockading troops; the 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, already says that he had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner and the 32nd Bulletin, read from the page images. Bodart's choice of Lecoq rather than the commandant is kept as printed; the capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. The Bulletin is dated two days before the order of 18 November as Höpfner gives it; both are kept (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'immediately after the taking of possession Major General Strachwitz commanded in Hameln, but in May Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler, an old man of 75, physically and mentally wholly dulled, and therefore slow to decide and extremely anxious, was appointed commandant'; 'this was the state of things when General Hagken's detachment was drawn into the garrison on 23 October, and in exchange the 1st battalion of Oranien, 810 men strong, joined General Lecoq, whose corps thereby reached a strength of 4000 men'; 'on 24 October General Lecoq led his corps into a camp at the foot of the Klütberg, and had its entrenchment begun at once'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the colonel answered only with tears. When General Savary asked him to sign the capitulation as well, General Schöler refused this with the remark that the colonel did not need to sign, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'General Savary has been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division'.",

      "id": "side-a-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: the division Gobert, with the King of Holland present, drove the Prussian outposts back on 7 November and completed the investment on the left bank that day; on the 8th the enemy reconnoitred the fortress, and on the 9th threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr under a howitzer battery on the Ohrberg, attacked the post at the Afferde Warte and took up camps at Aerzen, the King's headquarters, and at Ohr on both banks; Rinteln and Hessen-Oldendorf were occupied and Rinteln's guns brought before Hameln. On the 10th part of Mortier's corps appeared and its tirailleurs attacked the covered way at the Mühlen gate, and General of Division Loison brought a letter from the King summoning Lecoq to capitulate in return for free withdrawal and threatening to burn the town in 24 hours; the King approved free withdrawal to the Prussian King's army as the main point, referring the details to Loison and Colonel Brüne. On the 12th, complaining of the detention of General Brack, who by Höpfner had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext, the King summoned the fortress to surrender in two hours, sending the news of the fall of Magdeburg and Napoleon's army order on Ratkau; he refused to receive Lecoq and demanded that the garrison surrender as prisoners of war, and General Michaud, who commanded the advance guard, wrote that the commandant might send an officer to General Blücher but must then surrender, the garrison becoming prisoners of war. Michaud then announced that the King had left and he had taken the chief command, sending the Bulletins on the capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin; on the 18th General dü Monceau, who had relieved Michaud, wrote that Napoleon was angered at the Prussian generals' conduct and had ordered that no more capitulation be granted them if they did not surrender at once, and summoned them to negotiate. On the evening of the 19th Savary announced his arrival as commander of the besieging corps and refused the conditions put; at the meeting at the Wehrberg Warte on the 20th he told the Prussian generals in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, added the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated and wanted to dictate the terms, and the French rejected the 5th article of Lecoq's draft. Mortier wrote on 12 November that he had moved on Hameln by the King of Holland's order to surround it on the right bank and debouched by Hastenbeck on the evening of the 9th, and that on the 10th all the enemy posts were driven into the place and dislodged from the brick fort on the Hamel, at half range from the town. Höpfner: Napoleon had chosen the right man to reach the goal quickly.",

      "rationale": "Höpfner and Mortier's letter, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Hameln, so the claim is tagged commander-created; the changes of command followed orders from above (claim side-a-objectives). Dü Monceau's letter came 'on the same day' as the relief of Fort George's garrison on the 18th. Höpfner gives the letters of the King, Michaud, dü Monceau and Savary in summary and cites no document for them in the passages read. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, already has Savary charged with the blockade (claim bodart-commanders), while by Höpfner Napoleon's order sending him is of 18 November and he announced his arrival on the 19th; the dates are kept as given. Mortier's brick fort on the Hamel may be the inundation redoubt that Höpfner has abandoned on the commandant's order in the night to the 10th and occupied by the enemy, who later left it (claim side-b-command); the passages read do not establish it, so Mortier's 'dislodged' and Höpfner's abandonment are both kept. The 'right man' is Höpfner's judgement. English renderings (ours): 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'the enemy soon advanced with a cavalry brigade — a Dutch Guard dragoon regiment and a hussar regiment — and forced the Prussian officers to retreat on Kl. Berkel'; 'an enemy column was seen marching towards the Weser and going into bivouacs; and by the occupation of the wood between Berkel and Hemeringen the investment of the fortress on the left bank was completed that same day'; 'it was the division Gobert to which the troops that appeared at Gr. Berkel belonged; the King of Holland was present in person'; 'on 8 November General Lecoq reconnoitred the enemy and the enemy the fortress, which led to an insignificant cannonade'; 'on the 9th the enemy, under the protection of a howitzer battery set up on the Ohrberg, threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr, for which the boats had been brought downstream'; 'the Prussian post at the Afferde Warte was at once attacked in superior force and, though reinforced from the fortress, pushed back to the barrier'; 'the enemy now took up camps at Aerzen, where the King of Holland's headquarters was, and at Ohr on both banks of the river'; 'Rinteln and Hessen-Oldendorf were occupied by him. In the former place the Hessian garrison had been disarmed and the guns on hand brought before Hameln'; 'on 10 November part of Mortier's corps also appeared before Hameln'; 'an enemy column moved from Rehrsen to the Baßberg and attacked the covered way with tirailleurs, who posted themselves in the gardens and garden houses in front and for a long time kept up their fire with the garrison of the covered way at the Mühlen gate'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'he was very kindly received; the King approved the main point: that the garrison could go by the nearest road to the King's army; but referred him for the details to General Loison and Colonel Brüne'; 'it was the enemy General Brack whom Major Beaufort had found with the commandant, and who had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'to impress them still more, the news of the fall of Magdeburg and the army order in which Napoleon praises the marshals who had pursued Blücher's corps and forced it to capitulate at Ratkau were attached to the summons'; 'at Ohr he met General Michaud, who commanded the enemy advance guard and had him announced to the King of Holland'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. General Lecoq rejected this condition, but allowed a French officer to accompany him to Hameln with a letter from General Michaud to the commandant, where he was let in in the evening without blindfold'; 'the letter contained nothing but the repetition of the news from the theatre of war already communicated in the morning, with the addition that after such events it was unreasonable still to want to defend the fortress, but that the commandant was permitted to send an officer to General Blücher to convince himself of the truth of what had been communicated, though after this officer's return the fortress must then be surrendered and the garrison become prisoners of war'; 'General Michaud announced by a parlementaire that the King of Holland had left for another destination, and that he, the general, had taken over the chief command. At the same time he sent the Bulletins that announced the unhappy capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin'; 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'on the same day, in the afternoon, the Dutch Colonel Stedtmann, who had already been in Hameln once as a parlementaire and spoke German fluently, came to the fortress again with the Prussian officer whom General Lecoq had sent to repay the enemy general the board costs of the captured officers, and brought the commandant a letter from General dü Monceau, who had relieved General Michaud in the command'; 'the letter contained the notice that Napoleon was angered in the highest degree at the conduct of the Prussian generals and had ordered that they be treated with the utmost severity, and that no capitulation be granted them any more if they did not surrender the fortress forthwith'; 'to this was joined the summons to negotiate with Colonel Stedtmann, or to send a plenipotentiary officer with him to Hessen-Oldendorf'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'at first the Prussian generals refused the meeting, but at last agreed to fix the rendezvous for the 20th at 9 o'clock in the morning at the Wehrberg Warte'; 'the French general received the Prussian generals very brusquely, told them in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, that later nothing more would be ag-'; 'reed to; he repeated the story of all the misfortune that had struck the Prussian state, and added the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the 5th article of the draft capitulation, as General Leeoq had drawn it up, commended the officers who belonged to provinces that might be ceded at the peace to the favour of the new monarch with regard to their maintenance in case of invalidity; it was rejected by the French as inadmissible'; 'Napoleon had chosen the right man to reach the goal quickly'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'I moved on Hameln, by the King of Holland's order, to surround that strong place on the right bank of the Weser'; 'on the evening of the 9th I debouched by Hastenbeck; on the 10th, in the course of the day, all the enemy posts were driven back into the place and dislodged from the brick fort situated on the Hamel, at half range from the town'.",
