      "value": "Bodart names Marshal Davoust as side A's commander and Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin as side B's. In Höpfner, Prince Gallizin posted the Russian troops before Golymin, where General Dochtorow, commander of the 7th Division, had stayed behind to take him in, and where Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz joined him at 3 in the afternoon; Marshal Augereau's corps, the Grand Duke of Berg with the cavalry reserve and 2 divisions of Marshal Davout's corps advanced on Golymin from three sides. The major general's orders of 26 December from Lopaczyn went separately to Marshal Augereau, the Grand Duke of Berg and Marshal Davout.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 122-124 and 126; Foucart pp. 458, 459 and 461). The commands were set before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. Bodart's Davoust is Davout, and his Gallitzin Höpfner's Gallizin. Whether any one commander directed side A is disputed (claim side-a-command); the marshals' and the Grand Duke's decisions on the field are in claim side-a-decisions, and side B's in claim side-b-command. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Gen.-Lt.' is General-Leutnant and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations; Höpfner, 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the same day on which Marshal Lannes was in action against General Bennigsen's main forces at Pultusk, Marshal Augereau, on the strength of an order of Napoleon's from the headquarters at Lopaczyn, had had to set the division Desjardins in motion at 7½ in the morning from Golaczyzna near Sonsk on the Sonna on Golymin, into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there, and was to have the division Heudelet follow at 9 o'clock unless orders changing this arrived'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg was to march with the available cavalry reserve, as it seems, via Slubowo to Golymin, and the light cavalry and 2 divisions of Davout's corps to the same place via Strzegocin, so that the French thus advanced against Golymin from three sides';       "value": "Whether anyone directed side A as a whole. The editor writes that the combat of Golymin was fought against columns in retreat coming from different directions, by army corps that joined in a common action, but without any general direction during the whole of the engagement. A line in Foucart's small type after the 3rd corps's journal says that Marshal Davout received no order from the Grand Duke during the whole affair, and the journal has Marshal Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy an hour after nightfall nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps, the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack making any concert impossible. The major general's letter of 9 in the morning told the Grand Duke of Berg that, having arrived at Golymin, he would push Marshal Augereau's corps beyond Golymin if possible, while Marshal Davout's would stay at Golymin with one of its divisions on the high road to Pultusk. The Grand Duke reported that he linked up entirely with Augereau, separating himself from Davout, who held the wood throughout without being troubled by the enemy, and that he would have Davout told to be under arms at 6 the next morning and move on Golymin. The editor writes that the 7th corps bore the whole effort of the day, and that the reserve cavalry served as the link between the 3rd and 7th corps and above all prevented the enemy from enveloping Marshal Augereau.",

    {
      "id": "side-a-decisions",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Side A's decisions on the field, each attributed to the commander the passages name. Marshal Davout, learning that General Morand had seen the column reported at Bielice, at once had the division Friant march; by the editor's note he had put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours, for fear that the enemy corps seen toward Bielice would debouch near Strzegocin to reach Pultusk behind the 3rd division, until Morand had recognised the Russian column on the march; and he sent General Daultanne the order before noon to join him with the 3rd division, and the order was repeated. General Morand had the wood attacked and carried it, and about half past 3 directed the columns of the 1st brigade against the woods of Golymin; seeing the enemy withdrawing to the right, the marshal ordered General d'Honnières to turn the wood and advance on the road from Golymin to Pultusk (the 3rd corps's journal), and in Höpfner Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières with the cavalry under General Rapp toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat. Marshal Augereau, in Höpfner, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins and held back the second at the village when he became aware of his opponent, and the division Heudelet was to be pushed to the left on Watkowo on arriving, to lead the attack on Golymin from there; in the editor's account of the 7th corps the marshal, arriving as General Desjardins continued his division's march on Golymin, had its 2nd brigade (printed 'général Lefrauc', Lefranc later on the page) halt in the plain so as not to be outflanked, changed the direction of General Sarrut's brigade to between Watkowo and Golymin, ordered General Lefranc to carry the three pieces hampering the French movements, and ordered General Heudelet to make with his second brigade for the fire of Kalenczyn. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that he ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, that when the enemy moved by his right he followed with all his cavalry and linked up entirely with Augereau, separating himself from Davout, and that he then had Golymin reconnoitred.",
      "status": "supported",

      "rationale": "Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 473-477, 480-482 and 487-489; Höpfner pp. 124 and 125). It attributes each decision to the commander the passages name and none to a single commander for the whole (claim side-a-command). The journal's 'M. le Maréchal' is Davout, whom Höpfner names as sending the brigade d'Honnières forward, and the 'maréchal' of the editor's account of the 7th corps is Augereau, whom Höpfner names for holding back the second brigade (our reading). The 1st division is Morand's and the 2nd Friant's (our reading; claim side-a-strength). English renderings (ours): Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'yesterday¹, as I had the honour to report to you, a column of artillery, cavalry and infantry that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice'; 'informed that this column had been seen by General Morand, I at once had the division Friant march, which was in reserve for either the 3rd or the 1st division'; 'General Morand had the wood attacked that was' (p. 474); 'on the right of the plain occupied by Prince Joachim's cavalry, and carried it' (p. 475); 'before noon I sent General Daultanne the order to come and join us with the 3rd division. This order was repeated'; the editor, '1. For fear that the enemy corps seen toward Bielice would debouch near Strzegocin to reach Pultusk behind the 3rd division, the marshal had put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours. It was only when General Morand had' (p. 475); 'recognised the Russian column on the march that General Friant received the order to set out; so his division could debouch from Garnowo only at 5 in the evening' (p. 476); the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'about half past 3, the 1st brigade being formed, General Morand directed its columns to attack the woods of Golymin'; 'the marshal, seeing that the enemy was withdrawing to the right, ordered General d'Honnières to turn the wood and advance on the road from Golymin to Pultusk'; Höpfner, 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'Marshal Augereau, who on the bad roads could bring up his troops only little by little, but, as it seems, no artillery yet, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins, while he held back the second brigade at the village when he had become aware of his opponent'; 'the division Heudelet was to be pushed to the left on Watkowo on arriving, so as to make the attack on Golymin from there'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; but the marshal had its direction changed, ordering it to move between Watkowo and Golymin'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'during his march between Watkowo and Golymin, General Heudelet received the marshal's order to make with his second brigade for the fire of the burnt village of Kalenczyn'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'I then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and as he was setting about carrying out this order, the enemy faced about and the brigade Lasalle and that of General Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown'; 'then the enemy made a general movement by his right and sought to outflank Marshal Augereau's left'; 'then I followed the enemy's movement with all my cavalry; I linked up entirely with Marshal Augereau, separating myself from Marshal Davout, who constantly held the wood without being troubled by the enemy, who then rested his left on Golymin';       "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Side B's commanders' decisions, in Höpfner. Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, kept with him on the 25th the detachment cut off from General Sacken, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession; only toward evening did Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach him; the retreat was begun at nightfall, covered by detachments toward Pultusk and the Sonna, and he sent ahead to General Dochtorow to ask to be taken in with the 7th Division, as he was threatened from two sides. Dochtorow received the news at the moment when the field marshal's order to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk arrived; he had his division march off and stayed behind at Golymin in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in the prince. At Golymin, his troops being too exhausted to march on, Gallizin sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment to hold up the enemy when Colonel Kreuz reported the enemy cavalry approaching, and, though he soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of his troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow. He detached General Prince Tscherbatow to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn, posted the rest before Golymin with a reserve east of it astride the road to Makow, reinforced the Kostroma regiment, and sent forward two more battalions when the head of the division Morand threatened Tscherbatow's left flank; after they were thrown back he took them in and repulsed the following French in all further attacks by artillery fire. The troops kept in reserve, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively when Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières and General Rapp's cavalry toward Zawady. General Count Pahlen held the crossing at Lopaczyn on the 25th until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was blocked, retreated up the Sonna toward Ciechanowo, took up a position before the crossing at Sonsk to give the train time to file through, and united with General Tschaplitz at Ciechanowo; on the morning of the 26th both continued the retreat on Golymin, probably turning off to the left by Paluki after running into Durosnel's light cavalry brigade at Pomorze, and joined Gallizin on the Russian right wing at 3 in the afternoon. Toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, and Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, the artillery first, then the cavalry, the infantry and last the outposts.",

      "rationale": "Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102 and 122-126). Gallizin is side B's commander in Bodart (Gallitzin); these were his and his fellow generals' decisions within Bennigsen's and Kaminskoi's orders, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner names Gallizin's report in Plotho's Tagebuch, Danielewski's work and the French reports as his sources for the combat and calls his account only an attempt (claim hoepfner-side-b); he follows Danielewski against Gallizin's report for Dochtorow's force, and his 'wohl' marks the cause of Pahlen's detour as his inference. In his account Durosnel's and Wathier's light cavalry brigades, without artillery, attacked Pahlen at Sonsk several times without doing the Russians any particular harm. English renderings (ours): 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'at that time the detachment cut off from General Sacken, which had stood below Lopaczyn, namely the Dnieper Musketeer and Little-Russian Cuirassier Regiments, arrived at Slubowo on its march to Strzegocin'; 'the prince kept it with him, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession'; 'only toward evening did General Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach [printed 'ereichte'] the prince, and free him from a very painful situation'; 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'Prince Gallizin sent ahead to Golymin to inform General Dochtorow of his approach, and to ask him to take him in with the 7th Division, as he [was] from two sides by the enemy' (p. 101); 'threatened' (p. 102); 'General Dochtorow had received this news at the moment when the field marshal's order had arrived' (p. 122); 'to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk' (p. 123); 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); 'while, to cover the left wing, thus probably in the direction of Strzegocin, 3 squadrons of Pskov dragoons were pushed forward' (p. 124); 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'when the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment came under the fire of the enemy's skirmishers, it at once gave way, but Prince Tscherbatow led it forward again with the colour in his hand, and Prince Gallizin reinforced the regiment further with 1 battalion of the Taurian Grenadier Regiment'; 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as soon as Prince Gallizin had taken in the broken battalions, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'he finally saw himself compelled to begin the retreat up the Sonna in the direction of Ciechanowo'; 'when on the march he wanted to cross the river at Sonsk, he took up a position on the left bank in front of the crossing, to give the train time to file through'; 'in this position the light cavalry brigades Durosnel and Wathier came against him, but as they had not been able to bring artillery with them, they did not succeed, despite several attacks, in doing the Russians any particular harm,'; 'at Ciechanowo he united with General Tschaplitz, who, as mentioned, had had to advance from Golymin to Ciechanowo with the Pawlogrod Hussar Regiment and a horse battery of the 7th Division'; 'on the morning of 26 December both generals continued the retreat on Golymin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the march they had run into the light cavalry brigade Durosnel of Augereau's corps at Pomorze, and had probably been caused by this to turn off to the left on Paluki, so as to reach Golymin from there via Obiedzyn'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'first the artillery set off, then the cavalry followed, then the infantry, and last the outposts'.",

      "id": "bodart-winner",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart codes the engagement at Golymin on 26 December 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshal Davoust over the Russians under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin. The Grand Duke of Berg reported on 27 December that there had been several charges of cavalry and infantry, the French pushing the enemy and being pushed back in turn, but that in the end they forced him to yield the field of battle; that the enemy had vigorously disputed the ground and the affair lasted until 8 o'clock; that, when he then had Golymin reconnoitred, the enemy was driven out of it and out of a small wood, so that the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock; that the enemy seemed, by the few fires, to be retreating on Makow; and that Marshal Augereau's whole corps occupied Golymin, and Marshal Davout's whole corps, in front of Garnowo, the wood it had taken. In the 3rd corps's journal, when night had fallen, General Morand's troops took position at the edge of the woods within musket range of the road from Golymin to Pultusk, which was thus cut off from the enemy; the division Morand stayed under arms throughout, and the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and in a position to attack. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Lapisse pushed 2 companies into Golymin and, told that nobody was there, two battalions of the 16th light to cover the position; the 3rd battalion surprised and attacked a strong enemy column in retreat and took 160 men; the 16th then withdrew and took position behind Golymin, where it bivouacked; the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, the round shot, grapeshot and bullets falling on the French until 10 in the evening; and the marshal's headquarters was set up at the burnt village of Kalenczyn. The editor adds that the brigade Lapisse's reconnaissance of Golymin took place after 8 in the evening, as the Grand Duke says in his report, the Russians no longer passing through the village but going round it to reach the road to Makow, and, in a note citing the Grand Duke's report, that the combat ended only after 10 in the evening. General Corbineau learned at three quarters past 10 in the evening, from a returning patrol, that the enemy had withdrawn and that the French, Marshal Augereau's corps with part of the Grand Duke of Berg's cavalry, were masters of Kalenczyn. In Höpfner, toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest, and the head of the retreat reached Makow at midnight.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Bodart's heading and entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Foucart and Höpfner from the page images (Foucart pp. 476, 478, 480, 482, 483, 487, 489, 491 and 493; Höpfner p. 126). The sources read agree that side B retreated on Makow in the night and that side A held Golymin; Höpfner holds that the combat went on without a decision until dark (claim hoepfner-result). Corbineau's note bears only the hour; the editor dates it to the 26th, later than his letter of 10 in the evening. The 'maréchal' of the editor's account is Augereau (our reading; claim side-a-decisions). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'there were then several charges of cavalry and infantry; we pushed the enemy; he pushed us back in his turn; but in the end we forced him to yield the field of battle to us'; 'the enemy vigorously disputed the ground; both sides fought with the greatest fury; the affair lasted until 8 o'clock'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'; 'the enemy was occupying it; he was driven out of it, as well as out of a small wood that he was holding with 4,000 infantry and several pieces of cannon; so the action began again and ended only at 10 o'clock'; 'it seems to me that the enemy is retreating on Makow, to judge by the few fires we see, though we have noticed that a large column had none, which' (p. 482); 'further confirms his retreat' (p. 483); 'Sire, here is our position: the whole of Marshal Augereau's corps occupying Golymin; the division Klein and the brigade Milhaud, Buskowo; Nansouty, Garnowo; Lasalle covering Marshal Augereau's infantry'; 'the whole of Marshal Davout's corps in front of Garnowo, occupying the wood it had taken this morning;'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'when night had fallen, to avoid skirmishes, always uselessly murderous, General Morand's troops took position at the edge of the woods, within musket range of the road from Golymin to Pultusk, which was thus cut off from the enemy'; 'the division Morand stayed under arms throughout'; 'the 2nd division, which had been able to debouch only at nightfall, was forming and was in a position to attack'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'General Lapisse, 1st brigade of the 1st division, pushes 2 companies into Golymin; told that nobody is there, they want to occupy the village; then two battalions of the 16th light infantry are pushed forward to cover this position'; 'a strong enemy column that was making its retreat is surprised and attacked by the 3rd battalion of this regiment; the enemy fired a discharge of grapeshot at 40 paces; the liveliest musketry begins; this battalion takes 160 men'; 'the 16th withdraws and takes position behind Golymin, where they bivouac'; 'the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, after having, however, lost many men; in short, the round shot, the grapeshot, the bullets and the hail did not stop falling on us until 10 in the evening'; 'the marshal's headquarters was set up in the burnt village of Kalenczyn, between Buskowo and Golymin'; 'the reconnaissance of the village of Golymin by the brigade Lapisse took place after 8 in the evening, as the Grand Duke says in his report'; 'the Russians were no longer passing through the village, but going round it to rejoin the road to Makow'; '1. The combat ended only after 10 in the evening. (Report of the Grand Duke of Berg.)'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to His Majesty the Emperor, at Paluki'; 'three quarters past 10'; 'I learn this moment from a returning patrol that the enemy, who was between Kalenczyn and here, has withdrawn and that the French are masters of Kalenczyn; it is Marshal Augereau's corps that is there, with part of the cavalry of His Highness Prince Murat'; the editor, 'this undated note is of the 26th at three quarters past 10 in the evening, and later than the preceding one'; Höpfner, 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at midnight the head reached Makow, 2¼ Meilen away, and joined the rear guard of the 5th Division, Tutschkow'.",

      "value": "Höpfner gives a different result in his account of the combat at Golymin on 26 December. On the Russian right wing the first brigade of Augereau's corps went forward to the attack, and when the French continued the attack they came into the Russians' musket and canister fire and were repulsed; the advance of the second brigade seems to have had no better success, and the French advance over the broken ground before Golymin was soon checked, so that the combat gradually ran out into a skirmishing fight back and forth across the meadows until dark. Where the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps came up, the two Russian battalions sent into the woods were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin, but Gallizin, having taken them in, repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire. When Davout then sent the brigade d'Honnières with General Rapp's cavalry toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat, the Russian reserves, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively; the cavalry fight that followed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the French pursued the Russian cavalry they came under the fire of the infantry and artillery and had to return with great loss, Rapp being severely wounded; so the combat went on there too without a decision, despite the unequal forces, until dark. Toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow, and Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest; the news of the battle won at Pultusk, which reached General Buxhöwden's headquarters at Makow on the morning of 27 December, changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier.       "rationale": "Bodart's printed losses, read from the page image in the frame transcription; his officer-loss table for the engagement is not in the frame transcription. Bodart's Fénérols is the Grand Duke's Fénérolz. The explanatory pages transcribed (pp. 45-48) do not define the dagger; the Grand Duke's report says that Fénérolz was killed by a cannon shot.     {
      "id": "side-a-losses-reported",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side A's losses as reported. Marshal Davout wrote on 26 December that General Rapp had been put out of action by fire, his arm broken, that the light cavalry of the 3rd corps with the reserve cavalry had suffered much, and that General Morand had had men wounded by musketry and a horse killed. A loss line in Foucart's small type after the 3rd corps's journal gives the 1st division 9 men killed and 8 officers and 205 men wounded. General Rapp wrote on 27 December that a ball had broken his left arm above the elbow: as he advanced at a very slow walk on a mass of cavalry, it opened, and some platoons of infantry it had masked fired a volley that wounded only him. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that they suffered much from the enemy's artillery, that General Fénérolz was killed by a cannon shot, and that Marshal Augereau and Generals Lasalle and Milhaud had several horses killed under them. General Curély recalled that General Lasalle led the reunited brigade under the enemy cannon, where it stayed until midnight, its general having two horses killed under him and men and horses falling at every moment. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Lefranc's brigade, ordered to carry three pieces, was covered with grapeshot at 50 paces and stopped by a marsh; its column fell back hastily some 200 paces, and with General Lefranc wounded Colonel Habert took command of the brigade; on the 26th the 1st division had 34 killed and 326 wounded and the 2nd division 9 killed and 53 wounded. In Höpfner the French estimate their loss as equal to that of the Russians, but he thinks it probable that, in the disadvantageous situation in which they had to fight, they lost considerably more; in the cavalry fight the French, pursuing the Russian cavalry, came under the fire of the Russian infantry and artillery and had to return with great loss, General Rapp being severely wounded.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 473, 475, 476, 478-482, 484 and 486-489; Höpfner pp. 125 and 126). No total for side A is given in the passages read. The loss lines make 222 for the 3rd corps's 1st division and 422 for the 7th corps's two divisions (our arithmetic), without the reserve cavalry, the light cavalry and the 3rd corps's 2nd division; whether the 1st division's line counts General Rapp's dragoons is not shown, and the line names no source. Bodart's about 1,000 is compared in claim bodart-losses. Höpfner's view that the French lost more is his inference from their situation. English renderings (ours): Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Rapp moved to our right and, with his brilliant courage, although the ground was very marshy, wanted to cross swords; the enemy cavalry fell back; the Russian infantry did the same, but after firing; General Rapp was put out of action by the fire; his arm is broken'; 'the light cavalry of the 3rd corps, which was with the reserve cavalry, suffered much'; 'General Morand had men wounded by musketry and had a horse killed'; the line, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; '1st division. — Killed: men, 9. Wounded: officers, 8; men, 205'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'Sire, Marshal Davout will no doubt have reported to Your Majesty on the affair that took place yesterday' (p. 478); 'in front of Garnowo. There I received a ball that broke my left arm above the elbow...' (p. 479); 'I was advancing on this mass of cavalry in the hope of making it cross swords, still at a very slow walk, being unable to go faster; all of a sudden it opened to right and left, and some platoons of infantry that it masked fired a volley at us that wounded only me'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'the enemy in his turn was totally overthrown and driven back to his lines of infantry; it was then that we suffered much from the enemy's artillery'; 'Sire, I owe the greatest praise to the dragoon division; it was that which restored the affair four or five times; we have to regret General Fénérolz, who was killed by a cannon shot'; 'Marshal Augereau and Generals Lasalle and Milhaud had several horses killed under them'; Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The brigade having been reunited, General Lasalle led it under the enemy cannon. It stayed there until midnight without moving'; 'to give an idea of the loss this brigade suffered from the enemy cannon, in punishment for its retrograde movement: the general, who was at its head, had two horses killed under him; men and horses fell at every moment: nobody moved; not even a murmur was heard....'; the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'; 'the column fell back hastily some 200 paces; it was rallied, formed in square, and stayed in position in front of the burnt village, between Buskowo and Goly-' (p. 488); 'min.     {
      "id": "side-b-losses-reported",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side B's losses as reported. In Höpfner Prince Gallizin gives the Russian loss as 3 officers and 80 men dead, 16 officers and 473 men wounded and 203 men missing; in Höpfner's account of his retreat from Lopaczyn on the 25th, General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons. Marshal Davout reported on 26 December that the 1st division, on its march on Golymin, forced the enemy to abandon 13 pieces of ordnance. The 3rd corps's journal says that General Marulaz's chasseurs, the 1st division's advance guard, had taken 26 cannon, 80 caissons and 200 baggage vehicles that the Russians had abandoned in their retreat, as he came out of the village of Ostarzewo, and that the enemy, after a lively resistance, threw down his packs to charge with the bayonet but was forced to abandon the wood and the field of battle, leaving on it a great number of dead and 4,000 packs. General Rapp wrote on 27 December that the artillery the enemy had abandoned and the French had gathered up would be very difficult to get out of the places where it was. General Curély recalled that the cavalry of the right took from the enemy a good number of men and horses and two standards. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the 3rd battalion of the 16th light took 160 men, one piece of cannon and one caisson remained in French hands, the enemy lost many men before continuing his retreat, and the 1st division took 10 pieces of cannon in the affair. The report on General Durosnel's brigade, signed by him at Pomorze at 2 in the afternoon, says that the brigade took stragglers, ammunition caissons, carts loaded with flour and some baggage there at noon, and that two squadrons of the 7th chasseurs, sent after the enemy toward Gotskowo, had taken 4 pieces of cannon and several caissons on the road.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101, 102 and 126; Foucart pp. 473, 476-480, 484-487 and 489-491). Gallizin's figures make 83 dead and 489 wounded, 572 killed and wounded with 19 officers, and 775 with the missing (our arithmetic); Bodart's figures are compared in claim bodart-losses. The gun counts are not added: Davout's 13 pieces, Marulaz's 26 cannon, the 10 pieces of the 7th corps's 1st division and the one piece left in French hands, and the 4 pieces on the Gotskowo road may count the same guns more than once, and several were abandoned on the roads rather than taken in the fight (our reading). The 160 men are the only prisoners counted in the passages read; Curély's men and horses and the stragglers taken at Pomorze are not counted. Pahlen's gun was left before the engagement, and the guns and vehicles taken on the French march and on the Gotskowo road are reported with their place and time. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the Russians' loss is given by Prince Gallizin as 3 officers and 80 men dead, 16 officers and 473 men wounded, and 203 men missing'; 'General Count Pahlen had stayed behind at Lopaczyn with a rear guard — the 21st Jäger Regiment, the Sumy Hussar Regiment and a horse battery'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'on its march on Golymin the 1st division forced the enemy to abandon 13 pieces of ordnance'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'General Marulaz with his chasseurs, forming the advance guard of the 1st division, had taken 26 cannon, 80 caissons and 200 baggage vehicles that the Russians had abandoned in their retreat'; 'he was coming out of the village of Ostarzewo'; 'the enemy put up a lively resistance'; 'he ended by throwing down his packs to charge with the bayonet, but the fire and boldness of the skirmishers and the battalions forced him to abandon the wood and the field of battle, on which he left a great number of dead and 4,000 packs'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'Marshal Davout must also have reported to Your Majesty on the artillery that the enemy abandoned and that we have picked up; it will be very difficult to get it out of the places' (p. 479); 'where it is' (p. 480); Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; '« The cavalry of our right was not stopped in its charge, and it overthrew the enemy, who was also charging on his side. Our cav-' (p. 485); 'alry took from the enemy a good number of men and horses and two standards' (p. 486); the editor, 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'General Lapisse, 1st brigade of the 1st division, pushes 2 companies into Golymin; told that nobody is there, they want to occupy the village; then two battalions of the 16th light infantry are pushed forward to cover this position'; 'a strong enemy column that was making its retreat is surprised and attacked by the 3rd battalion of this regiment; the enemy fired a discharge of grapeshot at 40 paces; the liveliest musketry begins; this battalion takes 160 men'; 'one piece of cannon and one caisson remained in our hands'; 'the enemy continued his retreat under cover of night, after having, however, lost many men; in short, the round shot, the grapeshot, the bullets and the hail did not stop falling on us until 10 in the evening'; 'the 1st division took 10 pieces of cannon in this affair'; Durosnel, 'the light cavalry brigade commanded by General Durosnel arrived before Pomorze about 10 o'clock; a strong Russian column of cavalry and infantry was filing past there'; 'the brigade entered Pomorze at noon; it took stragglers there, ammunition caissons, carts loaded with flour and some baggage'; 'two squadrons of the 7th chasseur regiment were detached after the enemy as far as Gotskowo, in accordance with His Majesty's orders [printed 'ordes']. On the road they took 4 pieces of cannon and several' (p. 490); 'caissons. The report of their arrival at Gotskowo has not yet come in' (p. 491); 'Pomorze, 26 December 1806, 2 in the afternoon'; 'the brigade general,'; 'Durosnel'.",

      "id": "golymin-ground",
      "dimension": "terrain",
      "value": "Golymin is a market town in Russian Poland, 20 km north-west of Pultusk (Bodart). In Höpfner the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin made the approach very difficult; the broken ground before Golymin, whose approach the Russian artillery commanded, soon set limits to the French advance, and the fight on the Russian right ran out into skirmishing back and forth across the meadows; Prince Tscherbatow was detached to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn, and two Russian battalions defended the woods; on the Russian night march guns and wagons had sunk in the mud above the axles. Marshal Davout wrote that the ground on the right where General Rapp sought to cross swords was very marshy and that the roads were frightful. General Rapp wrote that the bad weather had made the ground absolutely impracticable, the horses sinking to the breast, that cavalry had never been seen to move over such frightful ground, and that all the country from Nasielsk to Garnowo was nothing but a great marsh. The Grand Duke of Berg found the enemy on Golymin in front of Garnowo, with his left on a wood held by some battalions of infantry and his right on a small village in front of Golymin, Kalenczyn by the editor's note; his postscript says the roads were frightful and the country full of marshes. General Curély recalled the Russians placed on a plain with a wood on their left, filing along the road through Golymin to Makow, the roads being frightful, above all for the French, who had only cross-roads. The editor calls Golymin the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position. In the editor's account of the 7th corps an impracticable marsh stopped General Lefranc's brigade, and General Heudelet found himself entirely in the plain. The report on General Durosnel's brigade found the ground at Pomorze too muddy for any bold stroke, and his postscript the roads dreadful, the horses in mud up to the belly; General Corbineau found the ground so bad that one could go only at a very slow walk.",

      "rationale": "Bodart's location line, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101 and 122-125; Foucart pp. 473, 475, 478-480, 483, 484, 487, 488 and 490-492). The ground and the weather were given, so the claim is tagged inherited; the Russian position was Gallizin's choice (claim side-b-command). Höpfner's Kalęczyn is Foucart's Kalenczyn (our reading). Höpfner's plan of the area of Golymin, to which his note refers, was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '1806 26/12. Engagement at Golymin (6.)'; 'victory of the French (27,000 men) under Marshal Davoust over the Russians (22,000 men) under Lieutenant General Prince Gallitzin'; '(market town in Russian Poland, 20 km north-west of Pultusk)'; Höpfner, 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); 'so the combat on the Russians' right wing gradually ran out into a skirmishing fight, back and forth across the meadows, until dark'; 'Prince Gallizin detached General Prince Tscherbatow with the Kostroma Musketeer Regiment and 4 light guns to occupy the bushes in front and the ground toward Kalęczyn,' (p. 123); '« The Russians had 8 or 10 pieces in battery, the whole placed on a plain, and on their left a wood'; 'the Russian army, which came from Pultusk, was filing along the road that crosses Golymin to go to Makow; the roads were frightful, mainly for the French army, which had only cross-roads...'; the editor, 'one understands from this that the combat was fierce at Golymin, the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position in this affair'; 'here are the movements of the 7th corps, according to General Desjardins's report and the journal of march of the 3rd [so printed] army corps:'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements';       "id": "side-a-logistics",
      "dimension": "logistics",
      "value": "Side A's means. In Höpfner Marshal Augereau could bring up his troops on the bad roads only little by little, apparently without artillery yet, and the first brigade of his corps, attacking, had nothing to oppose to the Russian canister. Marshal Davout reported that the 2nd division and 4 pieces of artillery of the 1st division could arrive only at nightfall, that the roads were frightful and it would take all night to bring up the guns of the other divisions, and that the night was being used to bring up the artillery and replace the cartridges, of which the 1st division was short at the end of the day; the 3rd corps's journal says that the 1st division had fought without artillery, which had not been able to follow because of the bad roads. General Rapp wrote that they had met the French artillery stuck in the mud everywhere, and that he had just learned that the bread wagons had had to be unloaded at Nasielsk because they could not continue. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that the heavy cavalry division arrived at nightfall and could take no part, that almost all the artillery had stayed on the bad roads, and that he had come back to Garnowo to feed the cavalry's horses. General Curély recalled that the brigade Lasalle waited 3 hours for the Grand Duke's troops, who arrived slowly, and that a single cannon, which managed to reach the line, fired toward the enemy without reaching him. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the corps had neither artillery nor cavalry; the editor also writes that the reserve cavalry's other troops certainly did not set off before half past 10 and came into line only about one in the afternoon.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Read from the page images (Höpfner p. 124; Foucart pp. 473, 475, 476, 478, 480, 482-484, 487 and 488). The roads and the weather were given, while the order of march and the choice to engage before the guns came up were commanders' decisions, so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'Marshal Augereau, who on the bad roads could bring up his troops only little by little, but, as it seems, no artillery yet, went forward beyond Ruskowo with the first brigade of the division Desjardins, while he held back the second brigade at the village when he had become aware of his opponent'; 'meanwhile the first brigade of Augereau's corps had gone forward to the attack'; 'when the French continued the attack, they came into the musket and canister fire of the Russians, to the latter of which they had nothing to oppose, and were repulsed'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'the 2nd division could arrive only at nightfall¹, as could 4 pieces of artillery of the 1st division'; 'the roads are frightful; it will take all night to bring up the pieces of the other divisions'; 'we are using this night to bring up the artillery and replace the cartridges'; 'at the end of the day the 1st division was short of them¹'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'the dragoons were placed in reserve behind the 1st division'; 'this division had fought without artillery (it had not been able to follow because of the bad roads) against an infantry ten times stronger and 12 to 15 pieces of cannon....'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'everywhere we met our artillery stuck in the mud'; 'I have just learned that the wagons loaded with bread had to be unloaded at Nasielsk because they could not continue on their way...'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'the heavy cavalry division arrived at nightfall and could take no part in the action; almost all the artillery had stayed in the bad roads'; 'P.S. I have come back here to feed the' (p. 483); 'horses of the cavalry.       "value": "Side B's means, in Höpfner. On the night march from Slubowo the troops, and still more the horses, were completely exhausted, and were allowed some rest already ¾ Meilen from Slubowo; guns and wagons sank in the mud above the axles, and the very bad weather made the march extraordinarily difficult. Prince Gallizin's column reached Golymin at 8 in the morning of the 26th after a march of 13 hours, his troops so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; he decided to stay halted as long as their state urgently required, and sent ahead to Makow to prepare everything for their reception and refreshment. He took the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars back into reserve because they were very exhausted. The two battalions in the woods laid down their packs before going over to the attack. General Count Pahlen had had to leave behind one cannon and two ammunition wagons. In the retreat the artillery set off first.",

      "rationale": "Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102 and 123-126); he names no source for the state of the troops beyond the reports he follows for the combat (claim hoepfner-side-b). The guns, caissons and baggage the Russians abandoned on the roads are in claim side-b-losses-reported. English renderings (ours): 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'already ¾ Meilen from Slubowo the troops were allowed some rest; they, and still more the horses, were completely exhausted'; 'guns and wagons sank in the mud above the axles, and the very bad weather also made the march extraordinarily difficult'; 'at 8 in the morning of the 26th the column, after a march of 13 hours, reached Golymin, 1½ Meilen away'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'with the remaining troops Prince Gallizin posted himself before Golymin: in the first line the Taurian Grenadier and Dnieper Musketeer Regiments and the still available squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier and Pskov Dragoon Regiments; as reserve, east of Golymin, astride the road to Makow, the Little-Russian cuirassiers, the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, which the prince took back as they were very exhausted, and the troops of the 7th Division'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin';       "id": "side-a-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Side A's information. At 6 in the morning the major general wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg that the Emperor, not knowing what was happening at Strzegocin and Golymin, wished to wait for news, above all from Marshal Davout, and that a letter just received from Davout said he had not been able to reach Strzegocin the day before because of frightful roads and would attack the enemy's camp there that morning if it had not been evacuated in the night; at half past 7 he wrote to Davout that the enemy in front of him would surely have retreated on Golymin, and that he must march with caution and keep his corps well together, as there were many scattered and cut-off columns; at 9 he wrote to the Grand Duke that the enemy had left Strzegocin at 2 in the morning for Golymin, that he should not mistake the enemy's direction, and that it was not yet known whether Marshal Lannes had taken Pultusk. Davout reported that a column that appeared very numerous had been seen at Bielice the day before, that he had sent Colonel Exelmans there, who left with 200 horses (the editor's note), and that on his arrival he found the enemy before him. By the editor's note a squadron of dragoons had seen an enemy corps in bivouac with much artillery beyond Smolechowo on the 25th; Captain Scitivaux of the 8th dragoons reported from Smolechowo on 26 December that he was placed there with a squadron by Davout's orders to observe the march of the enemy, who was retreating on Pultusk, Golymin and Sturze (?); and, by the 3rd corps's journal as the note reports it, the marshal sent out parties all night to learn the march of two enemy columns, one seen on the 25th toward Bielice and the other withdrawn a quarter of a league beyond Strzegocin. By another note Davout put off the 2nd division's departure for some hours, for fear that the corps seen toward Bielice would debouch behind his 3rd division, until General Morand had recognised the Russian column on the march. The editor thinks the Grand Duke, told at half past 6 in the morning that Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin, probably sent part of his light cavalry that way for news. The Grand Duke reported that he reconnoitred Augereau's corps and the enemy by his left and later had Golymin reconnoitred, judged by the few fires that the enemy was retreating on Makow, had with the others generally thought the enemy 50,000 men, had no news of Marshal Lannes and no word from Watier's or Durosnel's cavalry, and excused his report as perhaps a little disjointed, being extremely tired. In the editor's account of the 7th corps General Desjardins, seeing many troops on his left and having no cavalry, sent staff officers to reconnoitre: it was the enemy; General Heudelet, surrounded by Cossacks and hussars, forbade firing until the enemy was on the bayonets, the darkness being so great, the position such and the French cavalry so close that firing would have been imprudent; a battalion of the 14th, in reserve to support the 16th light, could not fire for fear of killing French soldiers; the 7th light was separated from the 7th corps from the beginning of the engagement, and at 10 in the evening General Amey, at Watkowo with Generals Corbineau and Durosnel, did not know where his division general was. In the 3rd corps's journal the darkness and the uncertainty of the point of attack made any concert with Augereau's corps impossible. General Corbineau wrote at 10 in the evening that, doubting whether a very great movement of cavalry around the burning village of Kalenczyn was the enemy's, General Durosnel had it reconnoitred and attacked, and was assured it was Russian because a corporal of the attacking picket was wounded by a lance; that the night prevented judging the enemy's strength; that General Durosnel had joined General Amey, of the division Heudelet, who had the 7th light infantry regiment with him and did not know where his division general was; and that the enemy's movement was very undetermined, now toward his right, apparently from Kalenczyn to Makow, now toward his left and the road from Kalenczyn to Golymin.",

The information available followed partly from the ground and the dark and partly from the commanders' own reconnaissance, so the phase is unresolved. 'it is not surprising that the brigade Lasalle was in front of Buskowo at 10 o'clock; for from Kosniewo, where it had spent the night, it was only 8 kilometres away, and the Grand Duke, informed at half past 6 in the morning that Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin, probably sent part of his light cavalry in that direction for news'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'my advance guard made its junction with Marshal Davout's corps at the village of Garnowo at the same time as I was reconnoitring by my left Marshal Augereau's army corps and the enemy on Golymin, in front of Garnowo, resting his left on a wood that he had occupied by some battalions of infantry'; 'then I had Golymin reconnoitred'; 'it seems to me that the enemy is retreating on Makow, to judge by the few fires we see, though we have noticed that a large column had none, which' (p. 482); 'further confirms his retreat' (p. 483); 'Sire, we all generally thought that the enemy had 50,000 men'; 'I have as yet no news of Marshal Lannes, and neither Watier's nor Durosnel's cavalry has communicated with me;'; 'Your Majesty will perhaps find this report a little disjointed, but I beg you to excuse me, for I am extremely tired;';       "value": "Side B's information, in Höpfner. Prince Gallizin waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession on the 25th, and marched with enemy parties accompanying him on both sides; on the march to Golymin he had General Dochtorow informed that the French were advancing from all sides. At Golymin Colonel Kreuz reported the enemy cavalry approaching and threatening to attack, the prince soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, and soon enemy infantry, the head of the division Desjardins, also appeared beyond Ruskowo at the edge of the wood. General Count Pahlen held the crossing at Lopaczyn on the 25th until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off; on the 26th he and General Tschaplitz ran into Durosnel's light cavalry brigade at Pomorze and were probably caused by this to turn off to the left by Paluki. The news of the battle won at Pultusk reached General Buxhöwden's headquarters at Makow on the morning of 27 December.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 101, 102, 122, 123 and 126). He names Gallizin's report, Danielewski and the French reports as his sources for the combat (claim hoepfner-side-b), and his 'wohl' marks the cause of Pahlen's detour as his inference. The information followed from the retreat and from the generals' own observation, so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'the prince kept it with him, as he knew Strzegocin to be already in the enemy's possession'; 'as darkness fell the retreat was begun, and they had to cover themselves by detachments on the right toward Pultusk and on the left toward the Sonna, as enemy parties accompanied the march on both sides'; 'Prince Gallizin, as mentioned, had already on the march to Golymin had the commander of the 7th Division, General Dochtorow, given news of his approach and informed that the French were advancing from all sides'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'soon, however, enemy infantry also appeared beyond Ruskowo at the edge of the wood, the head of the division Desjardins of Augereau's corps'; 'on the 25th General Count Pahlen had held the crossing at Lopaczyn with his rear guard until he had convinced himself that the road to Pultusk was already blocked to him and 2 squadrons of hussars cut off'; 'on the morning of 26 December both generals continued the retreat on Golymin'; 'at 3 in the afternoon Generals Pahlen and Tschaplitz had also joined Prince Gallizin on the Russians' right wing, coming from Ciechanowo'; 'on the march they had run into the light cavalry brigade Durosnel of Augereau's corps at Pomorze, and had probably been caused by this to turn off to the left on Paluki, so as to reach Golymin from there via Obiedzyn';       "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side A's objectives, in the orders given by the Emperor on the morning of the 26th. The major general wrote to Marshal Augereau at 6 in the morning that the Emperor intended him to send off one division at half past 7 to march on Golymin, with the other ready to leave about 9, but, if he heard a very heavy cannonade toward Strzegocin, to direct his corps there without further order to support Marshal Davout; and to order General Durosnel to go with his light cavalry between Ciechanow and Golymin to Pomorze and Gostkowo, to cut the road and gather up all the enemy's baggage. He wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg at the same hour that his cavalry was to wait for orders, and to Davout at half past 7 that he would have followed the enemy to Golymin, for which Augereau was also making, to fall on the enemy's flanks if he stood, but that if the enemy had gone toward Pultusk he should follow him there. At 9 he wrote to the Grand Duke to set out with his cavalry and fall on the enemy's flanks, the roads being bad, so that the artillery and baggage must be his; having arrived at Golymin, he was to send detachments toward Pultusk to communicate with Marshal Lannes and to have Augereau's corps pushed beyond Golymin if possible, while Davout's corps stayed at Golymin with one of its divisions on the high road to Pultusk, to act if necessary, as it was not yet known whether Lannes had taken Pultusk. A dispatch at 9 told Augereau of the enemy's movement on Golymin and the Grand Duke's march, with the order to march some battalions briskly to support the cavalry. In Höpfner the French thus advanced on Golymin from three sides, Augereau's division Desjardins into the right flank of the Russian troops expected there. Davout reported that he had sent General Daultanne the order before noon to join him with the 3rd division, and that the order was repeated. The Grand Duke wrote that at 6 the next morning all his cavalry would be under arms with Augereau's corps at Golymin, to receive battle if the enemy prepared to attack and to pursue him if he was retreating.",

The 9 o'clock dispatch to Augereau is printed as a summary, not as the letter's text (our reading). The 3rd division of Davout's corps fought at Pultusk (the Pultusk entry, B377d). English renderings (ours): Foucart, 'orders given by the Emperor on the morning of the 26th'; the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Augereau'; 'Lopaczyn, 26 December 1806, 6 in the morning'; 'further order, your army corps to support Marshal Davout, who in that case would have a serious affair there' (p. 459); 'give General Durosnel the order to go with his light cavalry between Ciechanow and Golymin, to the point of Pomorze and Gostkowo, so as to cut the road and gather up all the enemy's baggage;       "value": "Side B's objectives. In Höpfner, General Bennigsen's order reached Prince Gallizin only toward evening on the 25th: to retreat on Golymin. Field Marshal Kaminskoi had announced the decision to accept battle at Pultusk and on the 25th ordered General Count Buxhöwden to set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place. Gallizin asked General Dochtorow to take him in with the 7th Division; Dochtorow, ordered by the field marshal to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk, sent his division off and stayed at Golymin in person to take in the prince. Gallizin decided to stay halted at Golymin as long as the state of the troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow; toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow and he followed about 9. At Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk, which arrived on the morning of 27 December, changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier. The editor writes that at the beginning of the engagement the Russians were filing toward Golymin, presenting their left flank; that another column, the division Panin, marching from Ciechanow on Pultusk, was making for the rendezvous General Buxhœvden had fixed for his army corps; and that on learning of General Panin's arrival the first Russian column made a general movement by its right to join him; Golymin was the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Höpfner and Foucart, read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 101, 102, 122, 123 and 126; Foucart p. 487). Höpfner gives the orders and decisions without naming a document beyond the reports he follows (claim hoepfner-side-b). The halt at Golymin and the retreat to Makow were Gallizin's decisions within his superiors' orders (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created. The editor's 'key of the position' is his judgement, and his division Panin is compared with Höpfner's Pahlen and Tschaplitz in claim foucart-side-b. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'before Prince Gallizin, who had waited in vain for orders from General Bennigsen, the heads of the enemy appeared at Slubowo on the 25th from the direction of Nowemiasto, and attacked a squadron of the Pskov Dragoon Regiment pushed forward'; 'only toward evening did General Bennigsen's order to retreat on Golymin reach [printed 'ereichte'] the prince, and free him from a very painful situation'; 'Field Marshal Kaminskoi, on his return to Pultusk, had announced the decision to accept battle at Pultusk, and on the 25th had ordered that for this General Count Buxhöwden should set the 7th Division marching via Makow to Pultusk and the 5th Division from Makow to the same place;'; 'Prince Gallizin sent ahead to Golymin to inform General Dochtorow of his approach, and to ask him to take him in with the 7th Division, as he [was] from two sides by the enemy' (p. 101); 'threatened' (p. 102); 'General Dochtorow had received this news at the moment when the field marshal's order had arrived' (p. 122); 'to set out with the division via Makow to Pultusk' (p. 123); 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'toward evening the troops of the division Dochtorow began the retreat on Makow; Prince Gallizin followed about 9 o'clock, when the French had already gone to complete rest'; 'at Makow, General Buxhöwden's headquarters, the news of the battle won at Pultusk had indeed arrived on the morning of 27 December, but it changed nothing in the decision to continue the ordered retreat to the Russian frontier'; the editor, 'at the beginning of the engagement the Russians were filing past, heading for Golymin and presenting their left flank'; 'another Russian column, the one that had been repulsed at Sonsk on the 25th by the Grand Duke, was on the march from Ciechanow to Pultusk'; 'this column (division Panin) had about 12 kilometres to cover on a high road to reach the place of rendezvous fixed by General Buxhœvden for his army corps; it was this column that came out about 2 or 3 in the afternoon on the left flank of the 7th corps, while Marshal Augereau was moving on Golymin'; 'as soon as it learned of General Panin's arrival, the 1st Russian column made a general movement by its right to join him'; 'one understands from this that the combat was fierce at Golymin, the head of the road to Makow by Karniewo and the true key of the position in this affair'.",
