      "dimension": "posture",
      "value": "Side A attacked. Bodart has a victory of the French. In Höpfner the Grand Duke of Berg's advance guard, two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle, had pressed Colonel Kreuz and thrown him back on Garnowo when the 3 squadrons of cuirassiers hastened up in support and, after some fluctuating fighting, threw the enemy back toward the wood; the French cavalry deployed opposite the Russian cavalry; the first brigade of Augereau's corps went forward to the attack, and when the French continued the attack they came into the Russians' musket and canister fire and were repulsed; the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success; the division Heudelet went forward to the attack from Watkowo; the head of the division Morand, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, and the French infantry attacked the woods repeatedly; and Marshal Davout sent the brigade d'Honnières with the cavalry under General Rapp toward Zawady to threaten the Russian retreat. Davout reported that General Morand had the wood attacked and carried it, and that the enemy infantry, coming forward to retake it, was repulsed after a very lively engagement; in the 3rd corps's journal Morand directed the columns of the 1st brigade to attack the woods of Golymin about half past 3, and General Rapp moved to the right with his dragoons. Rapp wrote that he was wounded as he intended to charge the Russian infantry and cavalry retreating before Davout's right, and that the enemy at once retreated without the French being able to reach him. The Grand Duke reported that the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud, formed in two lines, engaged the enemy while the advance guard of the division Morand drove the Russian infantry out of the wood; that he then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and that as Nansouty set about it the enemy faced about and the brigades Lasalle and Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown; that the brigade Milhaud, on the right, charged the enemy in flank while the head of the division Klein charged him in front; that Augereau, pushing a large enemy corps before him, himself directed his march on Golymin; and that the division Desjardins, manoeuvring by its right, occupied the small village in front of Golymin, which the enemy had burnt on abandoning it, while Augereau's 2nd division marched straight on the village of Golymin, pushing the enemy before it. General Curély recalled that Augereau drew up almost all his infantry in square and in mass in the middle of the plain, within cannon range of the road on which the Russians were filing; that the attack was ordered about 2 in the afternoon; that the brigade Lasalle, on the extreme left, was to charge the Russian artillery but had gone barely twenty paces when a cry of 'Halt! Halt!' was heard and repeated in both regiments, and that, though the enemy did not fire a cannon shot, the two regiments broke and retreated, with neither horseman nor foot soldier in front of the brigade; and that the cavalry of the right was not stopped in its charge and overthrew the enemy, who was charging too; the editor calls it the panic of the brigade Lasalle. In the editor's account of the 7th corps the marshal halted the 2nd brigade in the plain so as not to be outflanked, about 2 o'clock by the editor's note; General Amey's brigade took Watkowo; General Sarrut's brigade, sent between Watkowo and Golymin, was approaching the enemy when some Russian cavalry appeared on its flank while 3 pieces of cannon battered it in front; General Heudelet ordered a square, whose file fire dispersed a charge on its right; and General Lefranc's brigade, ordered to carry the three pieces, went to the attack and was covered with canister at 50 paces, and a terrible fusillade began on both sides, but an impracticable marsh prevented the infantry from going further; it was night. The 3rd corps's journal has Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy, nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps, an hour after nightfall. Side B halted and stood: in Höpfner Prince Gallizin's troops, on reaching Golymin at 8 in the morning, were too exhausted to march on; when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, reported the enemy cavalry approaching and threatening to attack him, the prince sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment to hold up the enemy and, though he soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces, decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required and then to continue the retreat to Makow. The two battalions he sent forward defended the woods and went over to the attack themselves after laying down their packs; once Gallizin had taken them in, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire; the troops kept in reserve, General Dochtorow's in particular, intervened decisively; and the cavalry went to meet General Rapp: in the cavalry fight that followed, without decisive result, when the Russian cavalry was once forced back behind its infantry, the French pursuing it came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery and had to return with great loss.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Coded A_attacked: side A's corps attacked side B's detachment, which had halted before Golymin because its troops were too exhausted to march on; side B's cavalry charges and the battalions' attack in the woods were made in the fight for its position before Golymin and do not, by the brief, make the defender an attacker (our reading). The times are kept as printed: the attack ordered about 2 in the afternoon (Curély), the halt of Augereau's 2nd brigade about 2 (the editor's note), Morand's attack about half past 3 (the 3rd corps's journal) and Augereau's corps at grips with the enemy an hour after nightfall (the same journal). Where the passages name who ordered an attack, it was a marshal or general on the field (claim side-a-decisions), so the claim is tagged commander_created; whether anyone directed side A as a whole is disputed (claim side-a-command). Höpfner's 'der Fürst' and 'Er' on p. 123 are Prince Gallizin, named in the sentence on Dochtorow before them; the 'maréchal' of the editor's account of the 7th corps is Augereau; and the brigade that the Russian cavalry and the 3 pieces met is General Sarrut's, named in the sentence before (our reading). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'the Russian general therefore had his division march off at once and stayed behind at Golymin only in person, with the Moscow Musketeer and the Moscow Dragoon Regiments, to take in Prince Gallizin'; 'when the prince arrived at Golymin at 8 in the morning, his troops were so exhausted that a further march was not to be thought of for the moment; they had to be allowed some rest'; 'scarcely, however, had the detachment assembled and to some extent sorted itself out when Colonel Kreuz, who had formed the rear guard with the 2 squadrons of Sumy hussars, sent the report that the enemy cavalry was approaching and threatening to attack him'; 'the prince at once sent forward 3 squadrons of the St. George Cuirassier Regiment in support to hold up the enemy, but soon convinced himself that he would have to deal with very considerable enemy forces'; 'he decided nevertheless to stay halted as long as the state of the troops urgently required, and then to continue the retreat to Makow, to which word was sent ahead at once to prepare everything for the reception and refreshment of the troops'; 'it was the advance guard of the Grand Duke of Berg, two regiments of hussars under General Lasalle, which had pressed Colonel Kreuz and thrown him back on Garnowo, when the 3 squadrons of cuirassiers hurried up in support and, after some fighting to and fro, threw the enemy back to the wood'; 'the French cavalry deployed opposite the Russian cavalry'; 'meanwhile the first brigade of Augereau's corps had gone forward to the attack'; 'when the French continued the attack, they came into the musket and canister fire of the Russians, to the latter of which they had nothing to oppose, and were repulsed'; 'the advance of the second brigade of the division Desjardins seems to have had no better success, as the dissolved ground and the wet meadows before Golymin' (p. 124); 'made the approach difficult in a high degree; and even when the division Heudelet had arrived and went forward to the attack from Watkowo, it was held up for a time by Russian cavalry thrown against it, and when this withdrew, the French soon found limits set to their advance over the broken ground before Golymin, the approach to which was commanded by the Russian artillery' (p. 125); 'when the Russian cavalry at Garnowo saw a superior enemy cavalry deploying opposite it, it withdrew on Golymin; and when the head of the division Morand of Davout's corps also arrived and, advancing, threatened Prince Tscherbatow's left flank, Prince Gallizin sent forward the 2nd battalion of the Taurian Grenadier and 1 battalion of the Dnieper Musketeer Regiments as well to occupy the bushes in front, supported by the 2 squadrons of Pskov dragoons that had not yet been in action'; 'both battalions defended the woods with great bravery against repeated attacks of the French infantry; indeed, after laying down their packs, they themselves went over to the attack, in which, however, they were overwhelmed by great superiority and thrown back on Golymin'; 'as soon as Prince Gallizin had taken in the broken battalions, he repulsed the following French with loss in all further attacks by artillery fire'; 'Marshal Davout now sent the brigade d'Honnières, with the cavalry under General Rapp, forward in the direction of Zawady, so as to threaten the Russians' retreat; but now the troops that had remained in reserve, and in particular General Dochtorow's, also intervened decisively'; 'the cavalry went to meet General Rapp'; 'the cavalry fight that then developed, in which the Moscow Dragoon Regiment particularly distinguished itself by several successful attacks, had no decisive result, and when the Russian cavalry was nevertheless' (p. 125); 'once forced to go back behind its infantry, the French in pursuing came under the fire of the infantry and the Russian artillery in such a way that they had to return with great loss and General Rapp was severely wounded' (p. 126); Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Morand had the wood attacked that was' (p. 474); 'on the right of the plain occupied by Prince Joachim's cavalry, and carried it' (p. 475); 'the enemy infantry moved forward to retake this wood'; 'after a very lively engagement it was repulsed'; the journal, 'extract from the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps'; 'about half past 3, the 1st brigade being formed, General Morand directed its columns to attack the woods of Golymin'; 'General Rapp moved to the right with his dragoons....'; Rapp, 'General Rapp to the Emperor'; 'Strzegocin, 27 December 1806'; 'I received my wound at the head of the 5th and 9th dragoon regiments at the moment when I intended to charge the Russian infantry and cavalry that were retreating before Marshal Davout's right'; 'the enemy at once made his retreat without our being able to reach him'; the Grand Duke, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor, at Ciechanow'; 'Garnowo, 27 December 1806, 1 in the morning'; 'the brigades Lasalle and Milhaud formed on two lines and engaged the enemy in that order, while the advance guard of the division Morand succeeded' (p. 480); 'in driving the Russian infantry out of the wood' (p. 481); 'I then ordered General Nansouty to charge the enemy cavalry, which was making a retrograde movement, and as he was setting about carrying out this order, the enemy faced about and the brigade Lasalle and that of General Marulaz were vigorously charged and overthrown'; 'the brigade Milhaud, which was on the right, charged the enemy in flank, while the head of the division Klein charged him in front'; 'all this was going on in front of Golymin, while Marshal Augereau, who was pushing a large enemy corps before him, was himself directing his march on Golymin'; 'the enemy, who constantly outflanked it by its left, which it refused;' (p. 482); Curély, 'General Curély, then a sub-lieutenant in the elite company of the 7th hussars, brigade Lasalle, tells of the combat of Golymin in these terms in the itinerary of his campaigns:'; It might have been about 2 o'clock'; 'the 2nd division, General Heudelet, was hastening its march; as soon as the 1st brigade of that division, 7th light, General Amey, was formed, it made for Watkowo, which it took'; 'General Heudelet was forming the 2nd brigade, General Sarrut, as it arrived, so as to have it support the 1st division; but the marshal had its direction changed, ordering it to move between Watkowo and Golymin'; 'it was approaching the enemy when some Russian cavalry appeared on its flank, while 3 pieces of cannon battered it in front'; 'General Heudelet, judging rightly that, being entirely in the plain and having a long line of cavalry before him, he would soon be charged, at once ordered the formation of a single square'; 'scarcely had this manoeuvre been carried out when a charge came on its right, but it wavered at the sight of the square's good bearing, and the file fire directed at it dispersed it in an instant'; 'the marshal at once ordered General Lefranc to carry, with his brigade, the three pieces that were hampering our movements'; 'the brigade went to the attack: at 50 paces the enemy covered it with grapeshot; a terrible musketry began on both sides; but an impracticable marsh prevented our infantry from getting further; it was night'; the journal, 'an hour after nightfall Marshal Augereau's corps was at grips with the enemy nearly a league to the left of the 3rd corps'.",

### B378b: BELAGERUNG und EINNAHME von Breslau (6./12. bis 1807 6./1. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p378, as printed:

```text
1806 6./12. bis 1807 6./1. BELAGERUNG und EINNAHME von Breslau
(Hauptstadt von Preußisch-Schlesien).
Die Franzosen, Bayern und Württemberger (zus. 27.000 M. mit 52 Feld- und Belagerungsgeschützen) unter Pz. Jerôme Bonaparte nötigen die preußische Besatzung (6.000 M. mit 272 Geschützen) unter Gen.-Lt. v. Thiele zur Übergabe des Platzes. Die Garnison durfte mit allen militärischen Ehren ausmarschieren, mußte jedoch die Waffen niederlegen und geriet in Kriegsgefangenschaft. Die Offiziere (135) wurden gegen ehrenwörtliche Verpflichtung, in diesem Kriege nicht mehr gegen Frankreich oder dessen Bundesgenossen zu dienen, auf freien Fuß gesetzt.
```

      "value": "Bodart gives side A as the French, Bavarians and Württembergers, together 27,000 men with 52 field and siege guns, under Prince Jérôme Bonaparte, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 6,000 men with 272 guns under Lieutenant General v. Thiele, which side A compelled to surrender the place; the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war, and the officers, 135, were set free on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.",
      "status": "supported",

      "rationale": "Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's returns (claim side-b-strength), the Emperor's letter of 3 December another view of it (claim side-b-strength-other), and Höpfner, Jérôme's letter and the Emperor's letters side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 6,000 men are Höpfner's reckoning of 6000 at the beginning of the second investment, and his 135 officers are the officers of Höpfner's return of 1 January, while Höpfner has 116 officers and 5270 non-commissioned officers and men march out (claim side-b-losses) (our comparison). His 272 guns are not a figure in the passages read: Höpfner has 208 pieces on the walls and 46 in reserve or unusable, which make 254, and 240 guns handed over (our arithmetic and comparison). No passage read gives side A 27,000 men or 52 guns: by the assurance of Jérôme's adjutant on 18 December the siege corps was to reach 22,000 with Deroy's division, and the Emperor reckoned Jérôme's corps on 7 January at more than 30,000 with two units arriving (our comparison). His dates, 6 December 1806 to 6 January 1807, are the day Höpfner has side A's cavalry appear before Breslau for the second time and the evening he has the Nikolai and Oder gates handed over to side A; Foucart has the capitulation signed on 3 January and Höpfner on 5 January (claims posture and capitulation; our comparison). Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 6/12 to 1807 6/1. Siege and capture of Breslau'; 'the French, Bavarians and Württembergers (together 27,000 men with 52 field and siege guns) under Prince Jerôme Bonaparte compel the Prussian garrison (6,000 men with 272 guns) under Lieutenant General v. Thiele to surrender the place'; 'the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours, but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war'; 'the officers (135) were set free against an undertaking on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies'.",

      "value": "Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: at the beginning of the arming works the garrison consisted of the infantry regiment Thile, the 3rd musketeer battalions von Hohenlohe and Treuenfels and the fusilier depot Greifenberg, 68 officers and 3046 men; men of several cavalry depots, 4 officers and 118 men; and artillery, 24 officers and 690 men; together 96 officers and 3854 men. Reinforced by men returning from leave, Ranzionirte, Jäger called in and several invalid companies, on 1 January it still counted infantry, 89 officers and 3909 men; Jäger, 1 and 74; invalids, 10 and 363; artillery, 26 and 854; cavalry, 9 and 641, with 240 horses; together 135 officers, 5841 men and 240 horses; so that, counting the loss in dead, wounded and deserters, the garrison at the beginning of the second investment may be reckoned at 6000 men. Assuming that only part of the invalids was fit for duty on the walls, that about 400 men served as helpers to the artillery and in the laboratories and that about 450 lay in hospital, Höpfner regards only 5000 men as real defenders of the walls, while the arming plan of 1805 required 10,320 men to garrison all the works; and the men of the regiment Thile, mostly Poles, could not be particularly counted on. The government had about 2000 recruits who had come back from the march to Graudenz removed from the town instead of enrolling them, by its statement because it saw no means of arming them.       "id": "side-a-strength",
      "dimension": "strength",
      "value": "Side A (the Silesian corps of Bavarian and Württemberg troops under Prince Jérôme, with French generals, sappers and artillerymen). Höpfner's formation of the corps at the beginning of operations: the first Bavarian division, Lieutenant General Deroy, 8185 men; the second, Lieutenant General Wrede, 5830 men, together 14,015 Bavarians; the Württemberg division, Lieutenant General Seckendorf, 8642 men; the corps 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men of infantry, 3241 of cavalry and 1055 of artillery, or 22,946 men; the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments, the 5th light battalion La Motte and apparently several batteries arrived only later. For Breslau the Emperor wrote on 3 December that Jérôme was to go there with Wrede's division and Vandamme with the Württembergers, Deroy's division staying where it was with half the cavalry, and the major general that Vandamme was to leave 1,000 men at Glogau. Höpfner: Montbrun set out with the Württemberg cavalry on 4 December and Vandamme followed with the Württemberg infantry, and Jérôme left Kalisch on the 5th with Wrede's division and Lefebvre's cavalry, Deroy's division and Mezzanelli's cavalry brigade staying at Kalisch; Vandamme reached Lissa on the 6th with the advance guard of the Württemberg infantry; on 9 December the Bavarian infantry crossed to the left bank at Kosel, the two light battalions and Lefebvre's cavalry brigade with 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers staying on the right bank. Foucart: Montbrun formed the investment on the left bank on the 7th with the 1st and 2nd regiments of chevau-légers and the chasseurs à pied, and Vandamme arrived before Breslau on the 8th; Jérôme wrote on 8 December that the 2nd division, 4,700 men strong, would be before Breslau on the right bank that evening. Höpfner: on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners of 66 men each arrived, and on the 17th the artillery was reinforced by 1½ companies of French. In the middle of December the Württembergers, supported by Wrede's division, most of the sappers, miners and artillery and part of Montbrun's cavalry brigade were employed in the siege on the left bank, with 2 squadrons and half a light battalion at Gnichwitz and 1 squadron at Neumarkt; the two battalions of Württemberg Jäger and Lefebvre's brigade were on the right bank; and Deroy's division and Mezzanelli's brigade were at Polnisch Wartenberg, 2 days' marches away, until Jérôme called them up on the 16th, the besieging troops already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength. By the assurance of Jérôme's adjutant on 18 December, Deroy's division, 10,000 men strong, was to arrive that day and bring the siege corps to 22,000 men; the division arrived and took post partly on the left bank and partly on the right. Foucart has Deroy's division only then arriving on the right bank, and 2 infantry regiments and 2 light infantry battalions of Minucci's division crossing to the left bank, when Jérôme left on the 20th. By the disposition for the storm (claim side-a-command), it was to be made by a column of 2 Württemberg battalions, General Minucci at the head of 3 Bavarian infantry regiments followed by the Württemberg infantry, 2 Bavarian companies, a detachment of 150 Bavarian volunteers and another detachment. After the capitulation General Minucci remained in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries. The Emperor wrote on 7 January that Jérôme's corps must now be more than 30,000 men strong, with the arrival of the 5th light infantry battalion and the 14th Bavarian infantry regiment. No passage read gives a return of side A at the capitulation.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Höpfner, the French letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The troops before Breslau changed with the Emperor's and Jérôme's orders, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's formation table, of the beginning of operations, was read for the Glogau entry; as recorded there, his corps figures make 21,946, not the printed 22,946, his three division totals make 22,657, and the rows of the second Bavarian division and of the Württemberg division make 7018 and 8652, not the printed 5830 and 8642 (our arithmetic). Jérôme's 2nd division is read as Wrede's, which Höpfner has marching with him from Kalisch (our reading); its 4,700 compare with Wrede's printed 5830 at the beginning of operations, and the adjutant's 10,000 for Deroy's division with its 8185 (our comparison). The adjutant's 22,000 is an assurance given to the enemy, and the Emperor's 'more than 30,000', which counts two units still arriving, a reckoning from Warsaw; neither is a return (our reading). Höpfner has Vandamme reach Lissa with the advance guard on the 6th and Deroy's division arrive about the 18th, Foucart has Vandamme arrive before Breslau on the 8th and Deroy's division only on the 20th (our comparison). The 1,000 men to be left at Glogau and the troops named for the storm are an order and a disposition, not counts. Bodart's 27,000 with 52 guns are in claim bodart-strength; no passage read totals side A's guns before Breslau, and the guns Höpfner names in the batteries are in claim means-and-supply. English renderings (ours): 'First Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Deroy'; '[total] 8185 men' (the division's total, at the foot of its table); 'Second Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Wrede'; '[total] 5830 men. Together 14,015 men Bavarians.1)' (the second division's total and the two divisions' sum, at the foot of the table continued from p. 15); 'Württemberg Division. Lieutenant General Seckendorf'; 'together 8642 men Württembergers'; 'the Silesian corps thus consisted at the time of 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men' (the sentence continues on p. 17); 'infantry, 3241 men cavalry and 1055 men artillery, or 22,946 men' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 16); '1) there arrived only later the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments and the 5th light battalion La Motte and, as it seems, also several batteries'; 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... General Vandamme is to leave 1,000 men at Glogau'; 'as early as 4 December, after the garrison of Glogau had laid down its arms, General Montbrun set out with the Württemberg cavalry; General Vandamme followed with the Württemberg infantry on the left bank of the Oder against Breslau, and on 5 December Jerome set out from Kalisch with the division Wrede and General Lefebvre's cavalry, likewise to move before Breslau. At Kalisch there remained only the division Deroy and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, from which the 1st Chevauxlegers Regiment Kronprinz marched off to the great French army.1)'; 'General Vandamme still reached Lissa on the 6th with the advance guard of the Württemberg infantry'; 'on 9 December the Bavarian infantry that had arrived crossed to the left bank of the Oder at Kosel; only the two light battalions and the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, with 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers, remained behind on the right bank. Jerome moved his headquarters to Lissa'; 'the next day, the 7th, the general formed the investment of Breslau on the left bank; he placed the 2nd regiment of chevau-légers at Gross-Möchbern, the chasseurs à pied at Neukirch and Höflchen (headquarters), the 1st of chevau-légers, 2 squadrons at Klein-Möchbern and the two others at Kleinburg, with a reconnaissance of 25 horse toward Schweibnitz and a post of the same strength at Roth-Kretschen'; 'General Vandamme, having left Glogau on the 5th, arrived before Breslau on the 8th. The detachment at Gnichwitz having been attacked in the night of the 7th to the 8th and forced to fall back, General Montbrun sent 2 squadrons and half a battalion of light infantry to that point, and himself moved his quarters to Kriethern to watch the Schweibnitz road better'; 'Prince Jérôme to General Vandamme. Oëls, 8 December 1806'; '(he arrived at Oëls on the 7th and will be at Hundsfeld on the 8th at midday)' (Foucart's summary); 'this evening the 2nd division, 4,700 men strong, will be before Breslau on the right bank. I mean to attack only tomorrow'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'accordingly the corps employed in Silesia had in the middle of December the following positions: headquarters at Lissa; the Württembergers, supported by the division Wrede, the greater part of the sappers, miners and artillery, the last reinforced on the 17th by 1½ companies of French, and a part of the cavalry brigade Montbrun on the left bank of the Oder, employed directly in the siege. At Gnichwitz on the Schwarzwasser, halfway to Schweidnitz, 2 squadrons and ½ a light battalion, to watch the roads from Schweidnitz to Breslau and to Glogau. At Neumarkt 1 squadron. A part of the cavalry brigade Montbrun roaming in the neighbourhood of Breslau. On the right bank of the Oder the two battalions of Württemberg Jäger, behind them the cavalry brigade Lefebvre; at Polnisch Wartenberg, 7 Meilen (German miles) from Breslau, the division Deroy and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, thus 2 days' marches away'; 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'on 18 December Captain Ducaudras, Jerome's adjutant, presented himself and demanded the release of all the Prussian officers who were prisoners of war released on their word of honour and were staying in Breslau without' (the sentence continues on p. 60); 'taking part in the defence. By the adjutant's assurance the Bavarian division Deroy, 10,000 men strong, was to arrive on that day and reinforce the siege corps to 22,000 men. Indeed considerable movements in the enemy's positions were observed soon afterwards' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 59); 'the division had arrived, and the siege corps now took the following positions: General Vandamme on the left bank of the Oder, with the Württembergers on the right wing, the division Wrede in the centre and part of the division Deroy on the left wing at Pöpelwitz on the Oder, from where these last troops occupied the parallels on the Oder; further General Deroy on the right bank with the rest of his infantry, of which 3 companies of the light battalion Taxis were detached to Steinersdorf - south-east of Breslau - toward Brieg, and the cavalry brigade Mezzanelli, which was to reconnoitre the neighbourhood and especially watch Brieg, where the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was believed to be assembling the relief corps; further the cavalry brigade Lefebvre, reinforced by the light battalion Zoller, in front of Lissa toward Neumarkt, to cover headquarters and secure the transports from the lower part of Silesia; finally the cavalry brigade Montbrun in front of Krietern, which in connection with the brigade Lefebvre was to watch all the roads to Breslau on the left bank of the Oder by pickets and patrols pushed forward, so as to be able to report the approach of the relief troops early. The dragoon regiment Taxis had been detached to Liegnitz'; 'the prince left Lissa on the 20th with General Lefebvre and the 2nd regiment of Bavarian chevau-légers. Deroy's division was only then arriving on the right bank before Breslau, and 2 infantry regiments and 2 battalions of light infantry of Minucci's division were crossing to the left bank'; 'the disposition for the attack laid down the following: a column of 2 Württemberg battalions was to climb the unrevetted walls on the bridges to be thrown, advance against the Ohlau gate, seize it, and make the entry into the town easier for General Minucci at the head of 3 Bavarian infantry regiments, followed by the Württemberg infantry. 2 Bavarian companies were at the same time to attack the tambour before the bridge of the outer ditch at the Ohlau gate; finally a detachment of 150 Bavarian volunteers was to advance along the Ohlau and another against the Schweidnitz gate, and all the batteries were to keep up their fire briskly, to divide the attention of the besieged during the storm'; 'the besiegers, at their head Jerome, who had arrived again, filed through Breslau and marched out again by the Schweidnitz gate. General Minucci remained behind in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries'; 'the Emperor to the major general.     {
      "id": "bodart-commanders",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Bodart names Prince Jérôme Bonaparte as side A's commander and Lieutenant General v. Thiele as side B's. Höpfner: the governor of Breslau was Lieutenant General Thile, the commandant Major General Kraft and the engineer officer of the place Lieutenant Poblotzky, while General Lindener, engineer general and brigadier of the Silesian fortresses, who had let himself be enclosed on 6 December despite Count Götzen's instruction to leave Breslau, gained a weighty voice in the arrangements for the defence. The Emperor wrote on 3 December that he wished Jérôme to have the honour of taking Breslau in person, and the major general that Jérôme would take command of the siege. On 17 December the Emperor told the major general to send Jérôme the order to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to reach Warsaw with all speed; Jérôme left on the 20th. Höpfner says that, so as not to leave Vandamme the supreme command in Silesia, Jérôme continued to regard himself as commander of the Silesian corps and gave the conduct of business to the chief of the general staff, General of Division Hédouville, a measure he holds the more justified as the troops of the Confederation of the Rhine, especially the Bavarians, had given continual cause for complaints of indiscipline, levying contributions and ill-treating the inhabitants, in the higher ranks too; and that Vandamme's new batteries and his bombardment and summons of 25 December were undertaken without Hédouville's knowledge. Vandamme's general staff officer, Colonel Duveyrier, carried the summons of 25 December and the negotiations that ended in the capitulation, signed on 5 January by Höpfner. Jérôme came back for the end: Höpfner has the besiegers, Jérôme at their head, file through Breslau after the garrison marched out, and Foucart has him arrive at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison file past him on the 8th.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner, the Emperor's and the major general's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images. Side A's command passed during the siege, on the Emperor's order, from Jérôme in person to others, while side B's commanders were in post before the investment; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Bodart's Thiele is Höpfner's governor Thile (our comparison); Höpfner prints the commandant's name 'Kraft' on p. 51 and 'Krafft' on pp. 87 and 110 (claim side-b-command). Bodart's Jérôme commanded before Breslau until 20 December; by the Emperor's letter of 17 December the command of the siege was then to pass to Vandamme, while by Höpfner the conduct of business passed to Hédouville and Vandamme acted on his own; the order and Höpfner's account may concern different commands, of the siege and of the corps, and who commanded from the 20th is left open (our comparison and reading). The capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. The credit is not assigned here to any one commander. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'governor of Breslau was Lieutenant General Thile, a generally respected, strict and brave officer,' (the sentence continues on p. 51); 'commandant Major General Kraft, engineer officer of the place Lieutenant Poblotzky. From a government so composed a capable defence could be expected despite the unfavourable circumstances, but unfortunately General Lindener, who despite Count Götzen's instruction to leave Breslau had nevertheless let himself be enclosed on 6 December, gained as engineer general and brigadier of the Silesian fortresses a weighty voice in the arrangements for the defence and a sure influence on the government's views of the tenability of the place' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 50); 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... you will have a bridge thrown over the Oder to establish your communications with General Vandamme; you will take command of the siege...'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Kutno, 17 December 1806'; 'send a Pole to the camp before Breslau with the order to Prince Jérôme to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to set out in person with all speed, so as to reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd. He will order General Deroy to march with his division from Wartenberg, where it must be, on Lowicz'; 'on the 20th Jerome left the troops before Breslau to go to the great army in Poland, whither Napoleon had called him on his repeated request. So as not to leave General Vandamme, with all recognition of his brilliant military qualities, the supreme command in Silesia, a province in which Napoleon had most strictly ordered the maintenance of order, Jerome continued to regard himself as commander of the Silesian corps and gave the conduct of business to the chief of the general staff, General of Division Hédouville'; 'this measure was all the more justified as the troops of the Confederation of the Rhine, but especially the Bavarians, had since entering Prussian soil continually given cause for complaints of a lack of discipline, of a taste for levying contributions under threat of fire, of ill-treatment of the inhabitants, etc., complaints that did not concern the common man only but were well founded in the higher ranks too.1)'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. The bombardment still went on even now.       "id": "side-a-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: on 7 December Vandamme, with the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack; the troops disposable for the siege being too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, they kept to the lower Oder and decided on two parallels and two mortar batteries right and left of the Nikolai suburb, chosen as the point of attack because Blein hoped to find an earthen batardeau there. The siege works began in the night to the 8th with few workers; batteries were built from the night to the 9th, guns were brought into them in the night to the 10th, and the bombardment of the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom began on the 10th at 6 in the morning, the fire being directed more at the town than at the walls. After 1 o'clock Jérôme's adjutant, Captain Desterno, summoned the place, announcing the fall of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the French entry into Warsaw. The parallels were extended and second parallels begun from the night to the 12th; the fire was slow on the 12th while side A awaited munition and replacement guns from Glogau; French sappers and miners arriving on the 13th dug cuts and built batteries; an approach trench from the left second parallel struck an arm of the Oder in the night to the 14th; and the batteries were armed in the night to the 15th. On the 15th the bombardment lasted from 6 in the morning to 1 in the afternoon, and at 2 Jérôme had Lefebvre summon the fortress again, threatening to turn the town into a heap of ashes and saying that Napoleon had ordered the works razed after the capture; after the refusal the bombardment was renewed at 3. In the night to the 16th side A set fire to the woodpiles before the Ohlau gate, burning 24,000 Klafter of wood. It bombarded again from 5 in the evening of the 16th and on the 17th, when an adjutant of Jérôme's brought back the body of Lieutenant Lehsten; on the 20th from 4 to 9 in the morning, after 24-pounders and 2 heavy mortars had been brought in, the besiegers firing exclusively at the town; and on the 21st and 22nd. On the plan of Blein, who had reconnoitred the works on the left bank on 17, 18 and 19 December for want of a good plan of Breslau, and with Jérôme's approval, side A attempted a storm at the unrevetted wall near the Ohlau gate, where two very wide and deep water ditches had to be crossed: Blein had rafts built of ladders joined in pairs, to be held above the water by empty casks and covered with planks; on the 22nd the means of crossing were gathered by day behind Neudorf, opposite the Schweidnitz gate, to make the garrison expect an attack there; Hédouville, Vandamme, Pernety and Blein went to the Ohlau suburb at 11 at night, and the troops were posted at 4 in the morning of the 23rd, but the carriers asked for to carry the rafts had not come, the inexperienced sappers bound the rafts slowly, a drunken officer hindered them, and a shout and a sapper's leap into the water alerted an artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; under canister and musket fire the attackers retreated with considerable loss. Vandamme, who had ordered 4 new batteries to take a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars arriving from Glogau, resolved on General Minucci's return to set the town seriously on fire and to tell the governor of the relief's defeat and of his means to destroy the town, expecting that a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather, all without Hédouville's knowledge; the bombardment was resumed on the 25th and Duveyrier summoned the town. Vandamme refused an armistice but empowered Duveyrier to conclude a capitulation, and then granted an armistice until 8 in the morning of the 27th, during which side A continued its works and alarmed the Springstern. On 2 January Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer repeated all the reasons for surrender; on the 3rd side A answered the walls' fire with the most violent bombardment of the siege, and at 4 in the afternoon Duveyrier came empowered to negotiate the surrender while the bombardment went on; the governor obtained neither an armistice of 8 days nor leave to send an officer to Kalisch, and 3 days were granted only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison; on 5 January the points of capitulation were signed after 6. Höpfner judges the French siege works very irregular: the whole attack was directed at the town, a siege against the works being thought useless against the defender's superior artillery, and side A counted on frost robbing the fortress of its wet ditches.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Höpfner, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Breslau, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for the reconnaissances, the summonses or the negotiations; his account of the storm's planning gives details from the besieger's side without naming its source on these pages; he cites Blein's report to Napoleon on p. 112 (claim side-b-command) and Blein's confirmation on p. 118 (our reading). In his garrison-side account it became apparent at 6 in the morning that side A was trying to cross the outer ditch by two cask bridges at the ravelin R., which he places before the Ziegel gate, while his account of the attack has the first raft brought into the outer ditch at 5 near the Ohlau gate and an artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin give the alarm; the two are not reconciled here, and Höpfner's Plan XVIII of Breslau, which would show where the works lay, was not inspected (our comparison). Foucart's narrative leaves the operations against the place aside by its own footnote (claim side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): 'likewise on the 7th General Vandamme, accompanied by the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'the siege works began as early as the night to the 8th, with so small a number of workers that they had to be limited to building two short parallels toward the projected batteries; one parallel was to rest on the left on the Oder, the other on the left on the Nikolai suburb'; 'in the night to the 9th the besieger began building the projected batteries, and a third battery was worked at in the prolongation of the street of the Nikolai suburb; on the right bank of the Oder too, at the Elbing and behind the Mönchswiese, gun positions were completed'; 'in the night to the 10th the enemy brought, on the left bank, 2 mortars and 3 howitzers into the battery right of the Nikolai suburb, 3 howitzers into the battery in the prolongation of the Nikolai suburb, 3 mortars, 1 siege howitzer and 3 field howitzers into the battery at the left parallel, and finally the 10 pieces named into the batteries on the right bank of the Oder'; 'on the 10th at 6 in the morning the enemy was able to begin the bombardment against the front at the Nikolai gate and the Dom; the enemy's shells did the burghers' hou-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 55); 'ses considerable damage without setting them on fire. Since in general the enemy's fire was directed more at the town than at the walls, the garrison was far safer on the walls than in its quarters' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 54); 'toward midday the fire fell silent, and after 1 o'clock Captain Desterno, a former Prussian dragoon lieutenant and at the time Jerome's adjutant, appeared as parlementaire and handed over a letter of summons in which the capture of Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin and Glogau and the entry of the French into Warsaw were communicated and the hopelessness of a relief was declared. The parlementaire added that the French had also crossed the Vistula at Thorn and had nowhere seen Russians, that the King had already gone back behind Memel, and that Napoleon had declared he would not make peace before he had humbled Russia and broken the alliance with Prussia'; 'in the night to the 12th the enemy extended the left parallel nearer to the Oder and the right parallel to the capital of the Hunde bastion, and began a second parallel on the left at the Oder and on the right of the suburb. A parallel with a battery was also laid out on the right side of the Oder, 400 paces from the Oder crownwork'; 'on the 12th and in the night to the 13th the town was indeed fired on, but only slowly, since the enemy was still awaiting munition and, in place of the dismounted guns, replacements from Glogau'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'in the nights to the 14th and the 15th the besieger worked at the zigzags connecting the two parallels right of the suburb of St. Nikolai, and in the latter night the batteries built one after another were armed: the 2 batteries of the first parallel right of that suburb, counted from the left wing, with 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers, and with 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers; the batteries of the second parallel with 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and with 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders respectively, these last batteries for firing on the batteries of the place. On the right bank of the Oder 8 field howitzers could be brought into action. Two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet arrived from Glogau'; 'on 15 December at 6 in the morning the bombardment thus began anew and lasted until 1 in the afternoon. The town suffered considerably, especially the convent of the Elisabethines, but the fire was put out everywhere'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'since the evening and the night to the 16th passed quietly against expectation, the garrison believed all the more that it could read this quiet as a sign of the besieger's departure, as he had, without any explicable reason, set fire in the night to the 16th to the woodpiles before the Ohlau gate, whereby 24,000 Klafter of wood burnt'; 'toward 5 in the evening the enemy began the bombardment anew, whereby the first considerable fire broke out in the town; a large house at the Siebenrader mill burnt down, and the one beside it had to be pulled down. The bombardment lasted until 7½ o'clock and was' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); 'continued on 17 December at daybreak, until at 8½ o'clock an adjutant of Jerome's with a detachment brought the body of Lieutenant Lehsten and asked for the exchange of the captured Captain Debruir, which the governor, however, did not grant. With pauses the bombardment lasted into the night. The fire it caused was put out' (the first words end the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'in the night to the 20th the 24-pounders held back until then and 2 heavy mortars that had arrived by water were also brought into the batteries, and from 4 until 9 in the morning of 20 December the town was most violently shelled. The main loss fell on the burghers, since the besiegers directed their fire exclusively at the town'; 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'in the evening at 10 o'clock the fire was repeated, and at midnight to the 22nd it was reported to the governor that the enemy was attacking the Dom. Fire from heavy guns and small arms was opened from all the works, but the enemy kept quiet. On the other hand he bombarded' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'on 23 December at 6 in the morning it became apparent that the enemy, under the protection of the fire and of those demonstrations, was trying to cross the wet outer ditch at the ravelin R. by two cask bridges, so as to storm the fortress from there'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'in consequence of this result Colonel Blein had at once laid before Jerome a plan for the attack on the fortress, whose success was to force the governor to immediate surrender. The plan required several false attacks to divert the garrison's attention from the true point of attack, the unrevetted place near the Ohlau gate, where both ditches were to be crossed before daybreak. Jerome had approved the plan, and all materials for its execution had at once been collected. On the 22nd, after Jerome's departure, Colonel Blein had reported to General Hédouville that all was ready for execution'; 'the task was to cross two very wide and deep water ditches and to make oneself master of a double rampart. To that end Colonel Blein had had rafts built of ladders joined 2 and 2, which were to be held above the water by empty casks and covered with planks'; 'since it was not thought possible to hide the preparations for these works from the garrison, all the means of crossing had been brought together by day on the 22nd behind Neudorf, opposite the Schweidnitz gate, to make the garrison believe that an attack on this point was intended, and to mislead it still more all the vessels on the Ohlau had also been moved to the same area'; 'at 11 o'clock in the night General Hédouville, with Generals Vandamme and Pernety and Colonel Blein, had also gone to the Ohlau suburb to make the arrangements still needed on the spot'; 'at 4 in the morning of the 23rd the troops ordered had been posted in the Ohlau suburb. Earlier the attack could not have begun because of the moonlight. Special workers had been asked for to carry the rafts; but they had not arrived, and the attacking troops had now had to be used to carry the rafts as well'; 'only at 5 o'clock could the first raft be brought into the outer ditch; it was 30 feet long, and 3 others of 12-15 feet had to be brought in to reach the far bank. The sappers, inexperienced in such work, had been able to bind the rafts together only slowly; a drunken officer had come onto the rafts and also greatly hindered the workers; and finally a thoughtless shout, and the leap of a French sapper non-commissioned officer into the water to fasten the rafts to the palisades of the enveloppe under attack, had drawn the attention of an' (the sentence continues on p. 65); 'artilleryman on the Ohlau ravelin; he had fired a round of canister at the place of the noise, and at once the guns of the Bernhard and Taschen bastions, which commanded the enveloppe, and the infantry garrison of the adjacent walls had joined in this fire. Two enemy soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the very beginning of the fire, the other carriers ran away, and the enemy saw himself forced to retreat with considerable loss. A French officer who was on the rafts had to surrender with some privates' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 64); 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'the bombardment was therefore, on the 25th after 1 o'clock, o-' (the sentence continues on p. 80: 'opened again'); 'pened again and lasted until 3 o'clock. At that time Colonel Duveyrier, general staff officer of General Vandamme, appeared with the summons to surrender, with the most boastful statements about the advantages won against the Prince of Pless as well as in Poland and Prussia. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'soon afterwards, at 10½, Colonel Duveyrier appeared again; General Vandamme had not granted the armistice, but had given the parlementaire full power to conclude a capitulation. The governor kept to his demand and regarded the negotiation as broken off'; 'on 26 December at 3 in the morning Colonel Duveyrier came back again and brought the enemy general's consent to the armistice, which was to last until 8 in the morning of the 27th'; 'in view of this favourable mood of the burghers, and because the enemy continued the works against the fortress during the armistice and also alarmed the Springstern, the governor ended the armistice as early as 10 o'clock on the 26th, so that in the afternoon the fire from the walls began anew'; 'on 2 January at 11 o'clock Colonel Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer were let in. Their business consisted in the request for the release of several persons, mostly of the female sex, and besides in the enumeration, repeated to weariness, of all the reasons that were to make the sur-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 110); 'render of the fortress necessary. Both officers were dismissed with expressions of courtesy, and at 3 o'clock the garrison's fire began again, at 5 o'clock a 2-hour bombardment by the enemy' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 109); 'toward 11 o'clock Captain Hammerer appeared again as parlementaire and took with him a letter of the governor with the request to send Colonel Duveyrier into the town to open negotiations. Nevertheless the fire from the walls was kept up, and was answered by a bombardment beginning at 1¼ in the afternoon, the most violent of the whole siege'; 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'as for the siege works of the French, they were conducted very irregularly and could probably lead to the goal only under such peculiar circumstances'; 'as already mentioned, and as the engineer Colonel Blein also confirms, the whole attack was directed exclusively at the town. A siege advancing against the works was held to be useless, because all the advantages were on the defender's side owing to his superior artillery, and it was counted on that when frost set in, robbing the fortress of its only means of protection, the wet ditches, the capitulation must follow'.",
      "citations": [
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p52-figures-v1",
          "section": "p52",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Ebenfalls am 7. rekognoszirte der General Vandamme, begleitet vom Artillerie-General Pernety und vom Ingenieur-Obersten Blein, den Platz, um den Angriffspunkt zu ermitteln."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p52-figures-v1",
          "section": "p52",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 52 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Die zur Belagerung disponiblen Truppen waren zu schwach, um sich an der obern Oder aufzustellen, wo man den Beunruhigungen der preußischen Parteien aus den übrigen Festungen zu sehr ausgesetzt schien; man beschränkte sich daher vorläufig auf das Terrain an der untern Oder und wollte sich rechts bis gegen die Ohlauer Vorstadt ausdehnen. Der Bau zweier Parallelen und zweier Wurfbatterien, rechts und links der Nikolai-Vorstadt, wurde beschlossen, und zwar um so mehr diese Vorstadt zum Angriffspunkt bestimmt, als der Oberst Blein die Hoffnung hegte, daß er daselbst auf ein Batardeau in Erde treffen würde, das den Uebergang über den Graben erleichtern könne."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p53-figures-v1",
          "section": "p53",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 53 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Die Angriffs-Arbeiten begannen bereits in der Nacht zum 8. mit einer so geringen Zahl von Arbeitern, daß man sich darauf beschränken mußte, zwei kurze Parallelen nach den projektirten Batterien zu erbauen; die eine Parallele sollte sich links an die Oder, die andere links an die Nikolai-Vorstadt lehnen."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p54-figures-v1",
          "section": "p54",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "In der Nacht zum 9. wurde von Seiten des Belagerers der Bau der projektirten Batterien begonnen, und eine dritte Batterie in der Verlängerung der Straße der Nikolai-Vorstadt gearbeitet; auch auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer beim Elbing und hinter der Mönchswiese wurden Geschütz-Aufstellungen zu Stande gebracht."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p54-figures-v1",
          "section": "p54",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "In der Nacht zum 10. führte der Feind auf dem linken Ufer in die Batterie rechts der Nikolai-Vorstadt 2 Mörser und 3 Haubitzen, in die Batterie in der Verlängerung der Nikolai-Vorstadt 3 Haubitzen, in die Batterie bei der Parallele links 3 Mörser, 1 Belagerungs- und 3 Feldhaubitzen, und endlich in die Batterien auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer die bezeichneten 10 Geschütze."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p54-figures-v1",
          "section": "p54",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 54 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 10. Morgens 6 Uhr war der Feind im Stande, das Bombardement gegen die Front am Nikolai-Thor und den Dom zu beginnen; die feindlichen Wurfgeschosse fügten den Bürgerhäu-"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p55-figures-v1",
          "section": "p55",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "sern erheblichen Schaden zu, ohne zu zünden. Da im Allgemeinen das feindliche Feuer sich mehr auf die Stadt als auf die Wälle richtete, so befand sich die Besatzung auf diesen weit sicherer als in ihren Quartieren."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1851-bd4-p55-figures-v1",
          "section": "p55",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 55 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Gegen Mittag schwieg das Feuer, und nach 1 Uhr erschien der Kapitain Desterno, ehemaliger preußischer Dragoner-Lieutenant und zur Zeit Adjutant Jerome's, als Parlamentair und überreichte ein Aufforderungsschreiben, in welchem die Einnahme von Magdeburg, Stettin, Küstrin und Glogau, der Einzug der Franzosen in Warschau mitgetheilt und die Hoffnungslosigkeit für einen Entsatz ausgesprochen wurde. Der Parlamentair fügte hinzu, daß die Franzosen auch bei Thorn die Weichsel überschritten und nirgends Russen gesehen hätten, daß der König bereits bis hinter Memel zurückgegangen sei und Napoleon erklärt habe, nicht früher Frieden zu machen, als bis er Rußland gedemüthigt und das Bündniß mit Preußen gesprengt habe."

          "quote": "In der Nacht zum 12. verlängerte der Feind die Parallele links näher gegen die Oder, und die Parallele rechts bis zur Kapitale des Hundebastions, und begann eine zweite Parallele links an der Oder und rechts von der Vorstadt. Auch wurde eine Parallele mit einer Batterie auf der rechten Oder-Seite, 400 Schritt vom Oder-Kronwerk, angelegt."

          "quote": "Am 12. und in der Nacht zum 13. wurde die Stadt zwar beschossen, aber nur langsam, da der Feind erst Munition und an Stelle der demontirten Geschütze Ersatz aus Glogau erwartete."

        {

          "quote": "Aus der zweiten Parallele links sollte ein Laufgraben mit einem kleinen Waffenplatz vorgeschoben werden, um aus demselben durch die württembergischen Jäger die preußischen Kanoniere auf dem Bürgerwerder zu beunruhigen; man stieß indessen in der Nacht zum 14. sehr unerwartet auf den Oderarm, der den Feind von den Werken des Bürgerwerders trennte."

        {

Auf dem rechten Oder-Ufer konnten 8 Feldhaubitzen in Thätigkeit gesetzt werden. Zwei 24pfünder und ein schwerer Mörser waren noch nicht von Glogau eingetroffen."
        },
        {

          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 56 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 15. Dezember Morgens 6 Uhr begann das Bombardement somit aufs Neue und dauerte bis 1 Uhr Nachmittags. Die Stadt litt bedeutend, besonders das Kloster der Elisabethinerin, doch wurde das Feuer überall gelöscht."

          "quote": "Um 2 Uhr Nachmittags ließ Jerome die Festung abermals durch den General Lefebvre auffordern. Derselbe wurde mit unverbundenen Augen zum Gouverneur geführt, dem er viel Schmeichelhaftes über die"

        {

          "section": "p57",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 57 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "bisherige Vertheidigung sagen und erklären mußte, daß, wenn die Besatzung die angebotene ehrenvolle Kapitulation nicht annähme, die Stadt in einen Aschenhaufen verwandelt werden würde, wozu alle Mittel vorhanden wären. Auch fügte der General hinzu, daß Breslau zum Letztenmale belagert würde, indem Napoleon befohlen habe, gleich nach der Einnahme die Festungswerke zu schleifen.           "quote": "Da der Abend und die Nacht zum 16. wider Erwarten ruhig verliefen, so glaubte die Besatzung um so mehr, diese Ruhe auf einen Abmarsch des Belagerers deuten zu können, als derselbe ohne allen erklärbaren Grund in der Nacht zum 16. die Holzstöße vor dem Ohlauer-Thor anzündete, wodurch 24,000 Klafter Holz verbrannten."

          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 4 (1851), p. 63 (transcribed from the page image)",

Jerome hatte den Plan genehmigt, und sofort waren alle Materialien zur Ausführung beigetrieben worden.       "value": "Höpfner: when the arming of Breslau began on 19 October at General Lindener's instance, the government had the guns taken to the outworks and ordered their palisading, and divided the fortress into 4 main fronts, each under an infantry staff officer and an older artillery officer; it meant to hold all the outworks, but when Lindener arrived on 6 November he had the defence restricted to the main wall, keeping only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork, the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. occupied, the Dom and the Springstern being drawn in later. The suburbs were not cleared. On 7 December the government sent Lieutenant Fiebig with half the horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to destroy the bridges over the old Oder and demolish the casemates at the Paßschleuse, which succeeded, and Captain Debruir was taken prisoner; the garrison set fire to the Nikolai suburb at 6 in the evening, by the order of the narrative on the 7th, to the nearest houses of the Oder suburb on the 8th and in the night to the 9th, to the Hinter-Dom suburb, and to the Ohlau suburb on the evening of the 11th; Fiebig was ordered with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder, later held also by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry as an outpost. The governor decidedly rejected the summons of 10 December and did not stop firing during the parley, and rejected Lefebvre's summons of the 15th. On the 11th side A bombarded only from the left bank, the artillery Lieutenant Zimmermann on the Springstern, shot soon afterwards, having silenced its fire on the right, and on the left bank too the defender's fire at last gained the upper hand. On 16 December, on a report that side A had withdrawn its guns, the governor sent out a sortie of 2 officers, 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers from the Nikolai gate, without naming a leader; it was driven back. The garrison of the Bürgerwerder resisted its officers by force on the 16th; it was relieved and the two most involved were shot two days later. On the 17th the governor refused to exchange Captain Debruir; a deputation of burghers asking that the town be spared was sent away reassured, and another on the 21st without hope of relief. On 25 December the governor refused Duveyrier's summons; during the parley a petition of the magistracy and the merchants, followed by a deputation of 6 burghers, asked him to end the town's sufferings if possible, and he put the burghers' requests to the generals and staff officers, of whom only Major Lepel of the regiment Thile was unconditionally against regard for the town, and at 9 o'clock asked Vandamme for an armistice; offered a capitulation instead at 10½, he kept to his demand and regarded the negotiation as broken off. He accepted the armistice brought at 3 in the morning of the 26th, but after a second deputation at 8½ protested that the burghers would rather be killed than vote for surrender, he answered the petition that, being now convinced that by far the greatest part of the inhabitants dreaded any surrender, he could take no further account of it, and, because side A went on with its works and alarmed the Springstern, he ended the armistice at 10 o'clock. On 30 December, when firing and the burning of Dürgoy were reported from 6 in the morning, the governor answered that side A was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out; Lindener saw only some cavalry at Dürgoy, the commandant General Krafft rebuffed those who tried to persuade him that side A was not manoeuvring, and the garrison was assembled at 11 for a sortie only in case side A should be beaten, but the fire receded and the relief had been beaten; from then on the mood of the burghers and the troops turned very bad against the government, everyone ascribing the omission of a sortie to the most impure motives. When frost set in, measures were taken to break the ice of the Oder and the ditches. On 3 January, after a petition signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers and one of the magistracy, the governor asked for Duveyrier, consulted Krafft and Lindener, and resolved to capitulate; he could obtain neither an armistice of 8 days, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new relief, nor leave to send an officer to Kalisch, but only 3 days to arrange the affairs of the town and the garrison. Höpfner says the artillery had especially distinguished itself everywhere in the short siege and, with the Land reserves, alone kept the old Prussian discipline at the end, and cites Colonel Blein's report to Napoleon that the artillery of Breslau had shown it came from a good school, had adorned the French trenches and made many embrasure shots. Items 3-6 of a numbered list of the government's faults are the lack of attention to provisioning, the omission of the sortie on 30 December, the failure to open communication with the Prince of Pless by scouts, for which Lindener is said to have borne the particular blame, and the conclusion of a capitulation without the council of war prescribed by the regulations; Höpfner judges the abandonment of the outworks a fault to be ascribed solely to Lindener, against the engineer of the place. 'because of the extent of the works and their partly difficult connection with one another, the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts, and each was entrusted to a staff officer of the infantry as divisional commander and an older artillery officer, for the complete equipment of the works and their eventual defence'; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47;
