'in view of this favourable mood of the burghers, and because the enemy continued the works against the fortress during the armistice and also alarmed the Springstern, the governor ended the armistice as early as 10 o'clock on the 26th, so that in the afternoon the fire from the walls began anew'; 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'the governor gave for answer: \"that the enemy was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out of the town\"'; 'General Lindener would hear no firing on the Ohlau gate, but saw only some troops of cavalry at Dürgoy, at which he had 2 24-pounders aimed'; 'the commandant present, General Krafft, had been made aware of it, and an attempt had been made to dissuade him from the opinion that the enemy was manoeuvring; but he had spoken harshly to everyone and finally dismissed them with the words: \"that was nobody's business, he himself possessed sufficient judgement, etc.\"'; 'at 11 o'clock the garrison was assembled to make a sortie in case the enemy should be beaten. The fog now grew thicker; one could observe no further, but only heard that the fire moved further and further away in the direction of the Zobtenberg until toward 3 o'clock, so that the relief had been beaten'; 'from this moment the mood of the burghers and the troops turned very bad against the government; for everyone was convinced of the necessity of a sortie and ascribed its omission to the most impure motives'; 'at 3 in the afternoon the sky cleared and it began to freeze. That was the most unfavourable thing that could befall the garrison; for only by open water was the fortress, given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, secured against a coup de main. The necessary measures were taken for breaking the ice of the Oder and the fortress ditches'; 'on the morning of the 3rd it lay out for signature at the town hall, where the opposition of a numerous counter-party made itself known. Nevertheless this request, signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers of all the guilds and trades, was handed to the governor together with a petition of the magistracy on the same matter, and a special list was attached by which only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, were said to be left in the town, and a shortage of wood threatened bakers and brewers' ('it' is the circular petition named in the preceding sentence); 'toward 11 o'clock Captain Hammerer appeared again as parlementaire and took with him a letter of the governor with the request to send Colonel Duveyrier into the town to open negotiations. Nevertheless the fire from the walls was kept up, and was answered by a bombardment beginning at 1¼ in the afternoon, the most violent of the whole siege'; 'the governor summoned the commandant, Major General Krafft, and General Lindener, laid before them the report of the chief commissariat office and the burghers' peti-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 111); 'tions, and asked their opinion. The result of the deliberation was that they resolved to enter into a capitulation' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 110); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'only the artillery and the Land reserves kept the old Prussian discipline, as indeed the artillery had especially distinguished itself everywhere in this sho-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 112); 'rt siege.1)' (the end of the word and sentence begun on p. 111); '1) Colonel Blein says in his report to Napoleon: \"the artillery of Breslau has proved that it came from a good school; it has adorned our trenches and made many embrasure shots\"'; 'the abandonment of the outworks must therefore be regarded as a fault that, as we have seen, is to be ascribed solely to General Lindener, in contradiction with the engineer of the place. The enemy, when he found the outworks abandoned, at once took on another air; he recognised from it the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government, which wished only to secure itself against a coup de main and to secure a good capitulation'; '3) lack of attention to the provisioning of the place, on the part of the garrison as well as of the burghers. For the supply of baking wood too it would only have been necessary to have the thousands of Klafter of firewood before the Ziegel gate carried into the town by the many Oder boats'; '4) the omission of the sortie on 30 December, of which we have already spoken in detail above'; '5) the omission to open communications with the Prince of Pless by scouts. General Lindener is said to have borne the particular blame for this'; '6) that a capitulation was concluded without first having called the council of war prescribed by the regulations'; 'not to accuse the government of a particular omission, but to point out in general that in single cases, where the commandant sees the impossibility of holding the fortress longer, the possibility still remains of cutting through with the garrison to the field army or to fortresses nearby, we mention such a possibility at Breslau too. For a definite judgement on this, more adequate materials would have to be available'; 'if one reckons that about 1000 men, excluding the sick, remained behind in the town to conclude a capitulation for the protection of the inhabitants the next morning, and that about 150 men remained behind at the lower Ohlau bridges to prevent the enemy from restoring them quickly, then still 4000 men, including 230 mounted cavalrymen, could have left the fortress and joined the Prince of Pless'.",

      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the siege and capture of Breslau from 6 December 1806 to 6 January 1807: the French, Bavarians and Württembergers under Prince Jérôme compelled the Prussian garrison under Lieutenant General v. Thiele to surrender the place; the garrison was allowed to march out with all military honours but had to lay down its arms and fell into captivity as prisoners of war, and the officers, 135, were set free on their word of honour not to serve again in this war against France or its allies. Höpfner: on the 3rd, after a petition of the burghers and the magistracy, the governor, Krafft and Lindener resolved to capitulate; at 4 in the afternoon Duveyrier came empowered to negotiate, and 3 days were granted only to arrange the affairs of the town and the garrison; on 5 January the points of capitulation were signed by both sides after 6 o'clock, not without disputes. That day insubordination broke out among the troops, with gross defiance of superiors and the destruction and sale of royal property and war stores, and on the 6th the excesses of soldiers and town rabble grew until the Nikolai and Oder gates had to be handed over to side A that evening. On 7 January the garrison marched out toward 10 in the morning and laid down its arms, the worse part smashing many muskets and drums; the besiegers, with Jérôme at their head, filed through Breslau and out by the Schweidnitz gate, and General Minucci remained in Breslau with 9 battalions, 1 squadron and some batteries. The officers were released on their word of honour, the foresters and Jäger called in for fortress service returned to their former service and the invalids and married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families, and the rest of the men were escorted into captivity by the Bavarian 13th Infantry Regiment. Foucart's narrative: Breslau capitulated only on 3 January; the governor at once resumed the negotiations he had broken off, the capitulation was signed on 3 January at 9 in the evening, and Jérôme, who had left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th. The Emperor wrote from Warsaw on 7 January, 'Breslau having surrendered', ordering the investment of Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz.",

      "rationale": "The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's, Foucart's and the Emperor's accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The capitulation's text was not seen; its terms are Höpfner's summary and Bodart's. The dates differ: Foucart has the capitulation signed on 3 January at 9 in the evening, Höpfner the decision and the opening of the negotiation on the 3rd and the signature on the 5th after 6; Bodart's end date, 6 January, is the evening Höpfner has the gates handed over; and Höpfner has the march-out on the 7th, Foucart the garrison filing past Jérôme on the 8th (our comparison). Bodart's honours of war are not in the passages read; Höpfner has the garrison lay down its arms on marching out (our comparison). The garrison's numbers at the end are in claim side-b-losses. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on the morning of the 3rd it lay out for signature at the town hall, where the opposition of a numerous counter-party made itself known. Nevertheless this request, signed by a hundred and some sixty burghers of all the guilds and trades, was handed to the governor together with a petition of the magistracy on the same matter, and a special list was attached by which only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, were said to be left in the town, and a shortage of wood threatened bakers and brewers' ('it' is the circular petition named in the preceding sentence); 'the governor summoned the commandant, Major General Krafft, and General Lindener, laid before them the report of the chief commissariat office and the burghers' peti-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 111); 'tions, and asked their opinion. The result of the deliberation was that they resolved to enter into a capitulation' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 110); 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'on 5 January Colonel Duveyrier appeared again, and the points of capitulation were signed by both sides, not without disputes, representations and counter-representations, after 6 o'clock'; 'already on this day, when the certainty of the capitulation was received, the spirit of insubordination broke out among the troops and showed itself in gross defiance of superiors, destruction of royal property, and sale of the royal effects and war stores'; 'on the 6th these excesses were continued to an increased degree by the military together with the rabble of the town, on the walls as well as in the town, especially at royal buildings, magazines, etc., and neither by the town police nor by cavalry patrols could the debauchery, plundering, shooting in the streets, etc., be stopped, so that they finally saw themselves compelled to have the Nikolai and Oder gates occupied by the enemy as early as the evening of the 6th'; 'on 7 January the garrison marched out toward 10 in the morning and laid down its arms; the worse part of the garrison continued the disorders even here, and a great number of muskets and drums were smashed'; 'the besiegers, at their head Jerome, who had arrived again, filed through Breslau and marched out again by the Schweidnitz gate. Warsaw, 7 January 1807'; '... Breslau having surrendered, you will give Prince Jérôme the order to invest Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz at once, so that only Neisse and Glatz remain, and to keep a reserve corps of infantry, cavalry and artillery at Breslau, where he will stay in person, visiting the three blockades every fortnight, however...'.",

No passage read gives side A's losses in the bombardments, in the covering detachments or from sickness, though Höpfner says the besieging troops were suffering exceedingly from the bad season (claim side-a-strength); Foucart's narrative, which leaves the operations against the place aside, gives none. English renderings (ours): 'in consequence of the news of the return of part of the Bavarian troops from South Prussia against Breslau, the government on 7 December sent Artillery Lieutenant Fiebig with half of the newly raised horse battery, some infantry and 30 horses to the right bank of the Oder, to destroy all the bridges over the old Oder and at the same time to demolish the casemates of the abandoned work at the Paßschleuse, where the old Oder leaves the new above Breslau'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'on the 12th and in the night to the 13th the town was indeed fired on, but only slowly, since the enemy was still awaiting munition and, in place of the dismounted guns, replacements from Glogau'; 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'since Lieutenant Fiebig reported from the Bürgerwerder in the night that the enemy was approaching on the Oder with 12 vessels, to all appearance to land on the Werder, the general alarm was beaten. Two enemy soldiers carrying a raft were shot at the very beginning of the fire, the other carriers ran away, and the enemy saw himself forced to retreat with considerable loss.       "id": "side-b-losses",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Höpfner: the sortie of 16 December was driven back with the loss of 1 officer, Lieutenant Lehsten, and 10 men dead and 7 missing; the two men most involved in the Bürgerwerder mutiny were shot; desertion was increasing very considerably by mid-December and still in the days before 30 December, and was practised ever more boldly at the turn of the year, deserters especially of the regiment Thile betraying the state of the fortress, such as the time and place of the daily relief of the guard, on which side A fired so that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place; by General Lindener's journal the garrison had 13 dead, 24 wounded and 568 sick. There marched out in all 116 officers and 5270 non-commissioned officers and privates, and 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over; the officers were released on their word of honour, the foresters and Jäger returned to their former service and the invalids and married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families, and the rest were escorted into captivity. Foucart's narrative: the garrison that filed past Jérôme on the 8th was 5,500 men strong. Bodart: the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, its officers, 135, set free on their word of honour. The town, separately, by Höpfner: 7 inhabitants were killed and 22 wounded in the bombardment of 21 December; in all, in the houses alone, 35 persons were killed and 88 wounded, 7 houses were burnt and over 1500 damaged, and in the suburbs over 350 properties, excluding Neudorf and Siebenhufen, were burnt down; the magistracy put the town's damage on 3 January at 1 million, a figure later reduced by judicial assessment to 249,145 Thaler.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Separate accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. The journal's 13 dead are not reconciled with the sortie's 1 officer and 10 men dead, the two men shot and Lieutenant Zimmermann's death (claim side-b-command); no passage read counts the deserters. The 116 officers and 5270 men who marched out are 19 officers and 571 men fewer than the return of 1 January (claim side-b-strength), and Höpfner does not say whether the sick or the men sent home are in his count (our arithmetic and reading). Foucart's 5,500 compare with Höpfner's 116 officers and 5270 men, and Bodart's 135 officers with Höpfner's return of 1 January rather than his 116 officers who marched out (our comparison). The 240 guns handed over are compared with the guns on the walls in claim bodart-strength. The town's losses are the inhabitants' and are kept apart from the garrison's. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on 16 December too the enemy kept quiet, and since the governor received the report that the besieger had withdrawn the guns from the batteries, he ordered that a detachment of 2 officers - Lieutenant Lehsten of the infantry regiment Thile and Lieutenant Seelstrang of the cuirassier regiment Henckel - 60 marksmen and 80 horsemen with 300 workers should advance from the Nikolai gate, clear the suburb of the enemy and destroy the enemy's works'; 'toward 1 o'clock at midday the sortie broke out, without a definite leader having been named, but it was met by a lively fire from the ruins of the burnt-down houses in the Nikolai suburb, into which it had incautiously gone, and was driven back with the loss of 1 officer - Lieutenant Lehsten - and 10 men dead and 7 missing. The cavalry brought back 10 prisoners'; 'the garrison of the Bürgerwerder resisted the officers commanding there by force on the 16th; a cavalry detachment had to be sent out to arrest the ringleaders. The garrison was relieved and the two most involved were shot two days later in the Zwinger bastion'; 'desertion was already increasing very considerably in the garrison, although the men were cared for as well as possible; they' (the sentence continues on p. 58); 'had for the most part been provided with greatcoats from the cloth procured for the army by contributions, and each relief of the garrison of the walls received warm beer and brandy, for whose purchase the burghers had made a collection' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 57); 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'desertion was still increasing'; 'complaint came in to the government that desertion was being practised ever more boldly. The locks on the gates of a palisade tambour were found knocked off, and even heaps of earth thrown up against the palisades to climb over them more easily. It was also evident that much about the state of the fortress was betrayed to the enemy by deserters, especially of the infantry regiment Thile; for example, the time and place of the daily relief. At that time the enemy then fired so briskly that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place, and it was found necessary to change the time of the relief more often'; 'the garrison had, by General Lindener's journal, 13 dead, 24 wounded and 568 sick'; 'there marched out in all still: 116 officers, 5270 non-commissioned officers and privates; 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over to the enemy'; 'the foresters and Jäger called in for fortress service returned to their former service, and the invalids and the married non-commissioned officers and soldiers to their families; the officers were released on their word of honour; the rest of the men were escorted into captivity by the Bavarian 13th Infantry Regiment'; 'Prince Jérôme, having left Pultusk on 30 December, arrived at Lissa on the 6th to see the garrison of Breslau, 5,500 men strong, file past him on the 8th'; 'on 21 December the bombardment was renewed from 2½ until' (the sentence continues on p. 62); '5 in the morning. A deputation of burghers again turned to the governor with the request to grant them, amid so many afflictions, the comfort and hope of an early relief. The governor had to dismiss them without such a hope' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 61); 'from the fortress the burning of the market town of Hundsfeld was observed and taken as a sign that the Russians were approaching and the enemy withdrawing and burning the villages of the neighbourhood. But already at 10 o'clock the bombardment began anew, was continued until 1 at midday and did particular damage, since a mass of inhabitants had left their shelters on the strength of that news. 7 inhabitants were killed, 22 wounded'; 'of the burghers, in the houses alone, 35 persons had been killed and 88 wounded; 7 houses had been laid in ashes and over 1500 damaged, and in the suburbs over 350 properties - excluding Neudorf and Siebenhufen - had been burnt down'; 'the damage to the town given by the magistracy on 3 January was said to amount to 1 million; a statement that was later reduced by judicial assessment to 249,145 Thaler'.",

'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town.       "value": "Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: 208 pieces of various calibres stood on the walls and 46 guns were partly in reserve and partly unusable in the arsenal; there were very considerable stores of finished munition, loose powder and iron munition, mostly in a single magazine under the cavalier of the Taschen bastion, whose weak vaults a bomb could have blown up with much of the town. Food had been laid in for only 5-6 weeks, except some articles: the provincial authority had at first called for provisioning for 4 weeks, the government took no energetic measures after the first investment in mid-November, and the burghers' provisioning for 6 months was ordered only on 17 November. Time was too short to restore the works fully, the fortress had only two engineer officers, and the garrison was too weak to help much with the works. Most of the men had greatcoats from cloth bought by contributions, and each relief on the walls got warm beer and brandy paid for by a collection among the burghers. The chief commissariat office reported that wood for baking bread was beginning to run short, and the list attached to the petition of the 3rd gave only about 20,000 pounds of meat, mostly salted, left in the town, with bakers and brewers threatened by a shortage of wood; Höpfner reckons from the commissariat's figures, 40 Klafter used in 10 weeks and 12 handed over, a 3-week supply of baking wood left, and says that thousands of Klafter of firewood before the Ziegel gate could have been brought in by the Oder boats. At the capitulation 240 guns and 3640 Centner of powder were handed over; the fortress is said to have fired about 50,000 rounds. Side A: the capture of Glogau put a considerable mass of heavy guns and great stores of munition into Vandamme's hands; the Emperor wrote on 3 December that the mortars would follow, and the major general that Jérôme was to have a bridge thrown over the Oder to communicate with Vandamme. Höpfner: the vessels of the boat bridge below Glogau were brought up the Oder, a large raft at Kosel serving until they came; in the night to the 10th 2 mortars and 3 howitzers, 3 howitzers, and 3 mortars, 1 siege howitzer and 3 field howitzers were brought into the batteries on the left bank and the 10 pieces named into those on the right bank, where 4 12-pounders and 6 field howitzers had stayed with Lefebvre's brigade; on the 12th side A awaited munition and replacements for its dismounted guns from Glogau; in the night to the 15th the first parallel's batteries received 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers and 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers, and the second parallel's 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders, and 8 field howitzers were in action on the right bank, while two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet come from Glogau; Deroy had a furnace for heated shot built so as to fire on the town from the right bank with 6 howitzers and 2 12-pounders; the 24-pounders held back and 2 heavy mortars arrived by water were brought in during the night to the 20th; and Vandamme ordered 4 new batteries for 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars arriving from Glogau.       "id": "side-a-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Side A: the Emperor wrote on 3 December that intercepted letters showed Breslau had only a fifth of the garrison necessary for its defence and that its general declared he would have to surrender if blockaded for several days by infantry, that a hundred or so bombs would force the town to surrender, and that he did not doubt it would fall into Jérôme's hands in four days; the captured Captain Debruir stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jérôme, and Berthier Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days. Foucart: on the 6th Montbrun sent a party to the right bank for news of the Bavarian troops, which learned nothing at Auras, and sent a trusted man to Schweidnitz to report within two days on the composition of its garrison. Höpfner: on 7 December Vandamme, Pernety and Blein reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack, Blein hoping to find an earthen batardeau before the Nikolai suburb; the approach trench pushed from the left second parallel struck unexpectedly on an arm of the Oder in the night to the 14th; for want of a good plan of Breslau Blein reconnoitred the works on the left bank on 17, 18 and 19 December and found the main wall unrevetted at two places and the enveloppe occupied only before the Nikolai front; Jérôme received from all sides news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling 15-16,000 men in Upper Silesia to relieve Breslau and that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to count 6000 infantry and 400 horse; Vandamme expected that a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to the works; and deserters, especially of the regiment Thile, betrayed much about the state of the fortress, such as the time and place of the daily relief, on which side A then fired. Foucart: Vandamme received the news that the Prince of Pless was gathering troops behind the Neisse and sent Montbrun toward Ohlau on the 28th. Höpfner judges that side A, finding the outworks abandoned, recognised the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "Side A's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The intercepted letters and Jérôme's and Blein's reports were not seen; Debruir's statement is the prisoner's, as Höpfner gives it. The passages read do not show what side A knew of the garrison's true strength; the Emperor's 'fifth of the garrison necessary' and the expectation of four or five days stand against a siege of about a month (our comparison). Blein's findings and Vandamme's expectation are Höpfner's account. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'it appears from intercepted letters that Breslau has only a fifth of the garrison necessary for the defence of the place, and that the general commanding there declares that he will be obliged to surrender if he is blockaded for several days in succession by infantry. A hundred or so bombs thrown into this large and beautiful town will force it to surrender'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'both undertakings succeeded completely, and on the way the French Captain Debruir was taken prisoner, whom General Vandamme had sent from Lissa to Jerome to bring him the news of the capture of Glogau: from the dispatch, torn to pieces, it was learned that the enemy meant to throw a bridge over the Oder at Kosel, below Breslau, and the prisoner himself stated that Napoleon had most earnestly assured Jerome, and Marshal Berthier General Vandamme, that Breslau was an altogether untenable place that could not hold out 5 days'; 'General Montbrun, preceding the Württemberg division, moved before Breslau by the left bank of the Oder. On the morning of the 6th he was a league from the town, at Höflchen, where he took position; he at once sent a party over to the right bank of the Oder to gather information on the arrival of the Bavarian troops, sent a detachment of 25 men and an officer to take post at Gnichwitz, 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweibnitz, and dispatched to Schweibnitz a trusted man he had with him, with the task of reporting to him within two days the composition of the garrison of that place'; 'the party sent to the right bank had spent the night of the 6th to the 7th at Auras without having learned any news of the arrival of Prince Jérôme's troops, which is not at all surprising, since the Bavarians were coming from Kalisch'; 'likewise on the 7th General Vandamme, accompanied by the artillery General Pernety and the engineer Colonel Blein, reconnoitred the place to determine the point of attack'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'complaint came in to the government that desertion was being practised ever more boldly. The locks on the gates of a palisade tambour were found knocked off, and even heaps of earth thrown up against the palisades to climb over them more easily. It was also evident that much about the state of the fortress was betrayed to the enemy by deserters, especially of the infantry regiment Thile; for example, the time and place of the daily relief. At that time the enemy then fired so briskly that several men were killed and wounded at the assembly place, and it was found necessary to change the time of the relief more often'; 'on the 25th the governor of Breslau, on the news of the unfortunate combat of Strehlen, entered into talks for the surrender of the place. But having learned the next day that the Prince of Pless was gathering behind the Neisse the remains of his first column and other troops, he broke off the negotiations'; 'the same information had reached General Vandamme, who on the 28th directed General Montbrun with his cavalry and two Bavarian battalions on Ohlau and had him supported by General Minucci'; 'the abandonment of the outworks must therefore be regarded as a fault that, as we have seen, is to be ascribed solely to General Lindener, in contradiction with the engineer of the place. The enemy, when he found the outworks abandoned, at once took on another air; he recognised from it the weakness of the garrison and the faint-heartedness of the government, which wished only to secure itself against a coup de main and to secure a good capitulation'.",

On 16 December the governor sent out the sortie on a report that side A had withdrawn its guns from the batteries. On 18 December Jérôme's adjutant Ducaudras assured the governor that Deroy's division, 10,000 strong, would arrive that day and bring the siege corps to 22,000, and considerable movements were indeed soon seen. On 25 December Duveyrier summoned the town with the most boastful statements about side A's successes against the Prince of Pless and in Poland and Prussia. On 30 December the governor took the firing and the burning of Dürgoy, reported from 6 in the morning, for a manoeuvre to lure the garrison out: the engineer of the place made the same report at 7, but the governor first asked for Lindener's opinion, and Lindener, who went to the Ohlau gate only at 8, heard no firing there and saw only some cavalry at Dürgoy; Lieutenant Schorlemmer reported toward 9 that side A was hurrying with its light guns and many troops out of the trenches toward the Schweidnitz road and that the fire was coming nearer, and again between 9 and 10 that side A was not manoeuvring and the relief troops could clearly be made out; the governor kept to his preconceived opinion, which Lindener seems not to have taken from him, and Krafft would not be persuaded otherwise, though from the cavalier of the Taschen bastion shells exchanged by the opposing troops were seen bursting and others saw side A's infantry leave the trenches for the fight; only after the parole did the governor and Lindener, from the loft of the Hatzfeld palace, make out troops and gunfire between Oltaschin and Dürjentsch, and the fog then hid the fight. But already at 10 o'clock the bombardment began anew, was continued until 1 at midday and did particular damage, since a mass of inhabitants had left their shelters on the strength of that news. 7 inhabitants were killed, 22 wounded'; 'on 22 December from 3 in the morning with pauses until the evening, and the fire raged most violently in the night to the 23rd, when fires broke out in several places' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); 'since Lieutenant Fiebig reported from the Bürgerwerder in the night that the enemy was approaching on the Oder with 12 vessels, to all appearance to land on the Werder, the general alarm was beaten. The governor gave a refusal' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 79); 'on 30 December at 6 in the morning it was reported from the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates that firing of heavy guns and small arms could be heard and that the village of Dürgoy was burning'; 'at 7 o'clock the engineer of the place made the same report to the governor. The governor, however, first asked for the opinion of General Lindener, who only at 8 o'clock went with the engineer of the place to the Ohlau gate to see for himself what was happening'; 'toward 9 o'clock a new report came to the governor from Lieutenant Schorlemmer that the enemy was hurrying with his light guns and many troops out of the trenches toward the Schweidnitz road, and that the fire was coming nearer and nearer to the fortress'; 'the governor gave for answer: \"that the enemy was manoeuvring to lure the garrison out of the town\"'; 'General Lindener would hear no firing on the Ohlau gate, but saw only some troops of cavalry at Dürgoy, at which he had 2 24-pounders aimed'; 'only between 9 and 10 o'clock did he go to the governor, where Lieutenant Schorlemmer again had it reported: \"the enemy is not manoeuvring, one can clearly make out the relief troops\"'; 'the governor kept to his preconceived opinion, which General Lindener' (the sentence continues on p. 87); 'seems not to have taken from him' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 86); 'from the cavalier of the Taschen bastion it had been clearly seen how the shells that the opposing troops exchanged burst in the air'; 'the commandant present, General Krafft, had been made aware of it, and an attempt had been made to dissuade him from the opinion that the enemy was manoeuvring; but he had spoken harshly to everyone and finally dismissed them with the words: \"that was nobody's business, he himself possessed sufficient judgement, etc.\"'; 'others had seen the enemy's infantrymen running singly out of the trenches in the direction of the fight, so that they had become convinced that the trenches had been abandoned by the enemy at least for the greatest part, and that a sortie was therefore not only justified but required'; 'only after the parole did the governor go with General Lindener to the loft of the Hatzfeld palace to see for himself.     {
      "id": "side-a-objectives",
      "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side A: the Emperor wrote to Jérôme from Posen on 3 December that he wished him to have the honour of taking Breslau in person, going there with Wrede's division while Vandamme went with the Württembergers and the mortars followed, and that he did not doubt it would fall in four days; Deroy's division was to stay where it was with half the cavalry, so that if Breslau was taken and the Emperor had an action in front of Warsaw, Jérôme could be there with it; and once Breslau was taken, Vandamme was to invest Brieg at once, without the Württembergers entering Breslau. The major general's letter of the same day, as Foucart summarises it, gave the Emperor's instructions: Jérôme was to have a bridge thrown over the Oder to communicate with Vandamme and take command of the siege, and Vandamme was to leave 1,000 men at Glogau. Höpfner: the point of attack was chosen at the Nikolai suburb; Napoleon had expected the quick surrender of Breslau, but on Jérôme's report of serious resistance he had Deroy's division, already directed from Kalisch on Petrikau, turned back to Polnisch Wartenberg to be ready to reinforce the troops before Breslau, and Jérôme, hearing of the relief force gathering under the Prince of Pless and in view of the governor's obstinacy, called Deroy's troops up on the 16th. Foucart's narrative: the inexperience of the allied troops did not allow the siege to be pressed as vigorously as the French generals wished, and the delays gave the Prince of Pless time to gather part of the garrisons of the other fortresses, so that it became indispensable to cover the siege troops very seriously; from 15 December two squadrons watched the roads from Brieg level with Ohlau. On 17 December the Emperor told the major general to send Jérôme the order to leave the command of the siege to Vandamme and reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd, Jérôme to order Deroy's division from Wartenberg on Lowicz. Höpfner: Lefebvre's summons of the 15th said Napoleon had ordered the works razed immediately after the capture; Blein's plan of attack was meant to force the governor to immediate surrender, and Jérôme approved it; Vandamme meant to set the town seriously on fire and tell the governor of the relief's defeat and of his means to destroy the town; and the whole attack was directed at the town, side A counting on the capitulation once frost robbed the fortress of its wet ditches. The Emperor wrote on 7 January that, Breslau having surrendered, Jérôme was to have Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz invested at once, leaving only Neisse and Glatz, and keep a reserve at Breslau.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "unresolved",
      "rationale": "The Emperor's and the major general's letters and Foucart's narrative, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The aims moved from a quick capture by Jérôme in person (3 December), through a siege covered against relief, to Jérôme's departure with the command of the siege left to Vandamme (17 December), a storm (23 December) and the bombardment of the town to force surrender; they came from the Emperor and from the commanders, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's statements on Napoleon's expectation and on the order to Deroy cite no document. The passages read do not show what became of the order of 17 December sending Deroy's division on Lowicz; Höpfner and Foucart both have the division arrive before Breslau (our comparison). Foucart's narrative leaves the operations against the place aside by its own footnote and gives those that protected the investment. Lefebvre's statement on razing the works is part of a summons, as Höpfner reports it. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'I wish you to have the honour of taking it in person. You will receive through the staff the order to go there with Wrede's division. General Vandamme, with the Württembergers, is going there for his part. The mortars will follow. The major general is sending you instructions on the conduct of the siege. I do not doubt that in four days it will fall into your hands. Deroy's division stays where it is, with half the cavalry'; 'in this way, if Breslau is taken and I have an action in front' (the sentence continues on p. 94); 'of Warsaw, you will be able to be there with Deroy's division. Meanwhile this division will rest' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 93); 'once Breslau is taken, General Vandamme must be sent to invest Brieg at once, without the Württembergers entering Breslau. It will be quite sufficient for you to enter with the Bavarian corps'; 'the major general to Prince Jérôme. Posen, 3 December 1806'; '(the major general informs the prince of the Emperor's instructions)' (Foucart's summary); '.... you will have a bridge thrown over the Oder to establish your communications with General Vandamme; you will take command of the siege...'; '.... General Vandamme is to leave 1,000 men at Glogau'; 'the troops disposable for the siege were too weak to deploy on the upper Oder, where they seemed too exposed to harassment by the Prussian parties from the other fortresses; they therefore restricted themselves for the time being to the ground on the lower Oder and meant to extend on the right up to the Ohlau suburb. The building of two parallels and two mortar batteries, right and left of the Nikolai suburb, was decided, and this suburb was chosen as the point of attack all the more because Colonel Blein hoped to find there an earthen batardeau that could ease the crossing of the ditch'; 'Napoleon had expected the quick surrender of Breslau, but when he had received from his brother the report that he had met serious resistance, he had at once had the order given to the Bavarian division Deroy, which had already been directed from Kalisch on Petrikau, to return as far as Polnisch Wartenberg, so as to be ready to reinforce the troops before Breslau'; 'when Jerome now received from all sides the news that the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was assembling in Upper Silesia a force of 15-16,000 men to relieve Breslau as soon as possible, that line troops were being drawn for it from all the fortified places to form the core of a force that was to be reinforced by recruits and volunteers called to the colours by a proclamation of the aide-de-camp Count Götzen, and when he further learned that the garrison of Schweidnitz was said to have been reinforced by 3000 recruits, so that it now counted 6000 men of infantry and 400 horse, he had, in view of the obstinacy of the governor of Breslau, the troops available at Polnisch Wartenberg ordered up on the 16th, so as to be equal to every possible event. The besieging troops were already suffering exceedingly from the bad season and their comparatively small strength'; 'the inexperience of the allied troops did not allow the siege of Breslau to be pressed as vigorously as the French general officers would have wished. These delays were all the more unfortunate as they left the Prince of Pless, commanding in Silesia, time to gather part of the garrisons of Schweibnitz, Brieg, Neiss and Kosel to come to the place's help'; 'it therefore became indispensable to cover the siege troops very seriously1'; '1. The operations directed against the place do not come within the frame of this work; I shall leave them aside; but it is not the same with those whose aim was to protect the investment'; 'on 15 December two squadrons went up the Oder, one by the right bank, the other by the left, and stayed in observation level with Ohlau on the two roads leading from Brieg to Breslau'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Kutno, 17 December 1806'; 'send a Pole to the camp before Breslau with the order to Prince Jérôme to leave the command of the siege to General Vandamme and to set out in person with all speed, so as to reach Warsaw on the 21st or 22nd. He will order General Deroy to march with his division from Wartenberg, where it must be, on Lowicz'; 'at 2 in the afternoon Jerome had the fortress summoned again by General Lefebvre. He was led with unbandaged eyes to the governor, to whom he had to say much that was flattering about the' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'defence so far and declare that, if the garrison did not accept the honourable capitulation offered, the town would be turned into a heap of ashes, for which all the means were at hand. The general also added that Breslau was being besieged for the last time, since Napoleon had ordered the fortifications to be razed immediately after the capture. The proposal was rejected, whereupon at 3 o'clock the bombardment was renewed, though not with the violence of the morning, and toward evening it gradually fell silent' (the first words end the sentence begun on p. 56); 'in consequence of this result Colonel Blein had at once laid before Jerome a plan for the attack on the fortress, whose success was to force the governor to immediate surrender. The plan required several false attacks to divert the garrison's attention from the true point of attack, the unrevetted place near the Ohlau gate, where both ditches were to be crossed before daybreak. Jerome had approved the plan, and all materials for its execution had at once been collected. On the 22nd, after Jerome's departure, Colonel Blein had reported to General Hédouville that all was ready for execution'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'as already mentioned, and as the engineer Colonel Blein also confirms, the whole attack was directed exclusively at the town. A siege advancing against the works was held to be useless, because all the advantages were on the defender's side owing to his superior artillery, and it was counted on that when frost set in, robbing the fortress of its only means of protection, the wet ditches, the capitulation must follow'; 'the Emperor to the major general. Warsaw, 7 January 1807'; '... Breslau having surrendered, you will give Prince Jérôme the order to invest Brieg, Kosel and Schweidnitz at once, so that only Neisse and Glatz remain, and to keep a reserve corps of infantry, cavalry and artillery at Breslau, where he will stay in person, visiting the three blockades every fortnight, however...'.",

      "dimension": "objectives",
      "value": "Side B (Prussian): under 22 November the King communicated to the commandants' offices the appointments of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless and of Count Götzen and charged them again, in case of an enemy attack, to defend the fortress entrusted to them most obstinately on their honour and duty until relieved with the help of the Russian operations, and on pain of their heads so to use all their means that they need not surrender it or, after a misfortune, could submit to the strictest court-martial when peace was restored. Höpfner: the government at first meant to hold and defend all the outworks; the suburbs were not cleared, partly in hope of relief by the Russian operations and partly from fear of the burghers' mood. The arrival of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was delayed until 18 December; a formal relief being no longer possible, it still seemed possible by a surprise attack to communicate with Breslau long enough to throw in 1 or 2 battalions of good troops and supplies and bring out the cash, the horse artillery and the muskets handed in by the burghers. On the 3rd the governor asked in vain for an armistice of 8 days to give the Prince of Pless time for a new relief. The governor gave as reasons for the capitulation the weakness of the garrison and its bad quality, shown in insubordination and heavy desertion; the lack of meat and baking wood; the burning of the town to be expected, since the mortar batteries behind the ruins of the suburbs could not be destroyed; the nearness of the large suburbs; and the frost, since the complete freezing of the Oder and the ditches made a general storm to be feared and the weak garrison could not keep the ice broken. Höpfner answers that insubordination on a larger scale showed itself only 2 days before the surrender, that by the commissariat's figures a 3-week supply of baking wood remained, so that only the lack of meat would remain as a reason, the governor fearing to impose privations on a garrison inclined to desert that no longer counted on relief and fearing that at the moment of a storm it would think more of excesses than of resistance, with the plundering of the town to follow, and that, as he said at Glogau, the burning of the town may be no reason for capitulation, the commandant having to look exclusively to the defence of the works.",

      "rationale": "The King's order as Höpfner prints it, and Höpfner's account, read from the page images. The aims moved from defence to the utmost under the King's order, in expectation of relief, to a capitulation once relief failed; they came from the King's order and from the governor and government, so the phase is left unresolved. The governor's reasons are given as Höpfner quotes them; reasons 3-5 are on p. 113, and the end of reason 9 with Höpfner's answer to it on p. 115, read in the OCR only and not used. Höpfner's answers are his judgement. The passage read addresses the order of 22 November to the commandants' offices and does not name Breslau (our reading). English renderings (ours): 'under 22 November the King communicated to the commandants' offices the appointments of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless and of Count Götzen, and added:'; '\"I charge you repeatedly, in case of an enemy attack, to defend the fortress entrusted to you most obstinately on your honour and duty, until it is relieved with the help of the Russian operations, and on pain of losing your head you must so use and apply all the means at your command for this purpose that you need not surrender the fortress, or, in case of a misfortune, can submit yourselves on that account to the strictest court-martial after peace has been restored, etc.\"'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'the clearing of the suburbs, which hindered a vigorous defence, was not done, partly in the hope of a relief by the Russian operations, partly because the government feared the mood of the numerous burghers if it destroyed these extensive buildings before the enemy forced it to, and partly, finally, because it was believed that when the enemy actually appeared it would still be possible to shoot them down and burn them'; 'the arrival of the Prince of Anhalt-Pless was unfortunately delayed until 18 December; the enemy had by now already reinforced himself, but seemed not yet to have all his forces together; if a formal relief was therefore no longer to be thought of, it still seemed possible by a surprise attack to enter into communication with Breslau for long enough to throw in 1 or 2 battalions of good troops and the necessities the town perhaps already lacked, and to bring out the considerable cash holdings, the horse artillery and the muskets handed in by the burghers'; 'at 4 in the afternoon Colonel Duveyrier came, empowered to negotiate the surrender. The bombardment still went on even now. The governor could no more obtain the armistice of 8 days he asked for, to give the Prince of Pless time for a new attempt at relief, than the dispatch of an officer to Kalisch, by whom he wished to make sure whether Russians were approaching or not. Only for arranging the affairs of the town and the garrison were 3 days granted'; 'the governor gave as reasons for the capitulation:'; '\"1) the weakness and' (the sentence continues in the next paragraph); '\"2) the bad quality of the garrison, which showed itself in insubordination and heavy desertion\"' (the end of the sentence begun in the preceding paragraph); '- insubordination on a larger scale, however, showed itself only 2 days before the surrender of the town, when the garrison regarded itself as sold and nothing was done on the government's side to meet such suspicion'; '\"6) the lack of meat and of wood for baking\"'; 'since the commissariat office showed that it had used 40 Klafter of wood for baking in 10 weeks, and 12 Klafter more were handed over to the enemy, there would by this reckoning still have been a 3-week supply of wood'; 'so only the lack of meat would remain as a reason for the capitulation. The governor was anxious about imposing considerable privations on the weak, fatigued garrison, inclined to desert, and feared that the garrison, which no longer counted on any relief since the news of the Prince of Pless's defeat had spread in the town, would at the decisive moment of the enemy's storm think more of excesses than of resistance, and that a plundering of the town would be the inevitable consequence'; '\"7) the burning down of the town that was to be expected, since it had not been possible to destroy the enemy's mortar batteries placed behind the ruins of houses in the suburbs\"'; 'we have already stated at Glogau that the burning down of the town may be no reason for capitulation, but that the commandant has to direct his attention exclusively to the defence of the works'; '\"8) the nearness of the large suburbs, which made all operations easier for the enemy and made the defence very difficult\"'; '\"9) the frost that had set in, since the complete freezing of the Oder and the ditches made a general storm to be feared.       "value": "Side B held a permanent fortress. Höpfner: the arming began on 19 October; time was too short to restore the works fully, raise the parapets and make bonnets, cover and banquette, and the fortress had only two engineer officers; the defence was restricted on 6 November to the main wall with its wide water ditches and a few outworks, the Dom and the Springstern being drawn in later and the enveloppe held only by day by marksmen and Jäger; the Bürgerwerder works were held as an outpost; the main wall was unrevetted at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates, and the enveloppe, the bridge and the batardeau near the Ohlau gate were secured by palisade retrenchments under the canister fire of the adjacent works; the munition lay mostly in a single magazine with weak vaults. Side A: from the night to the 8th it dug two short parallels, one resting on the Oder bank 10-12 feet above the water; it built batteries from the night to the 9th and gun positions on the right bank; from the night to the 12th it extended the parallels and began second parallels and a parallel with a battery on the right bank 400 paces from the Oder crownwork; it laid out the left second parallel in saw-tooth form, dug cuts into the Nikolai suburb and zigzags joining the parallels, and worked at new batteries on the 19th, and Vandamme ordered 4 new batteries. Höpfner judges the siege works very irregular: the batteries were very irregularly built, the guns stood behind embrasures raised toward the front, and the mortars were mostly behind ruins of the suburbs and woodpiles.",

      "rationale": "Coded both_fortified: side B defended permanent works, and side A dug parallels, approaches and batteries under the fortress's fire. A coding that counted only the defended fortress would give B_fortified. Höpfner's Plan XVIII was not inspected. English renderings (ours): 'when on 19 October, at the instance of the engineer brigadier General Lindener, the arming works of Breslau began, the government had at once had the guns taken to the outworks and suitably placed, and had also ordered the palisading of these works, the repair of the drawbridges, etc.'; 'for a complete restoration of the works, for raising the parapets as required, making bonnets and cover, and building the banquette, the time was too short with so extensive an enceinte. The fortress had only two engineer officers, and the garrison was too weak to contribute materially to the works'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'only later, when the garrison had received some reinforcement, were the important and already palisaded outworks, the Dom and the Springstern, also drawn into the defence'; 'the enveloppe that surrounded the fortress was to be occupied only by day, by single marksmen and Jäger'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'the storm could hardly succeed unless the garrison was very inattentive or treachery was counted on. The enveloppe near the Ohlau gate, the Ohlau bridge and the batardeau over the main ditch near the Ohlau gate were secured by palisade retrenchments and lay under the strongest canister fire of the adjacent works'; 'of finished munition, and of loose powder and iron munition, there were very considerable stores, which for the' (the sentence continues on p. 49); 'greater part were housed in a single magazine under the cavalier of the Taschen bastion. Light fell into this magazine through an open tower, and the vaults were weak, so that a bomb, if it fell unluckily, could blow the magazine and with it a great part of the town into the air' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 48); 'the siege works began as early as the night to the 8th, with so small a number of workers that they had to be limited to building two short parallels toward the projected batteries; one parallel was to rest on the left on the Oder, the other on the left on the Nikolai suburb'; 'since the bank of the Oder where the first-named parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water level, and from the parallel one could reach a sandbank lying there unseen from the Bürgerwerder, this junction gave the besieger great advantages'; 'in the night to the 9th the besieger began building the projected batteries, and a third battery was worked at in the prolongation of the street of the Nikolai suburb; on the right bank of the Oder too, at the Elbing and behind the Mönchswiese, gun positions were completed'; 'in the night to the 12th the enemy extended the left parallel nearer to the Oder and the right parallel to the capital of the Hunde bastion, and began a second parallel on the left at the Oder and on the right of the suburb. A parallel with a battery was also laid out on the right side of the Oder, 400 paces from the Oder crownwork'; 'in the night to the 13th the besieger extended the two second parallels begun the night before and laid out the one on the left in saw-tooth form, to place in it light guns that were to take the artillery on the Bürgerwerder in the rear'; 'on 13 December 2 companies of French sappers and miners, of 66 men each, arrived, and were used at once to dig cuts into the Nikolai suburb and to the right of the churchyard there, and to build batteries in the second parallels'; 'in the nights to the 14th and the 15th the besieger worked at the zigzags connecting the two parallels right of the suburb of St. Nikolai, and in the latter night the batteries built one after another were armed: the 2 batteries of the first parallel right of that suburb, counted from the left wing, with 2 heavy mortars and 3 light howitzers, and with 2 light mortars and 3 heavy howitzers; the batteries of the second parallel with 2 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders and with 4 light howitzers and 4 6-pounders respectively, these last batteries for firing on the batteries of the place. On the right bank of the Oder 8 field howitzers could be brought into action. Two 24-pounders and a heavy mortar had not yet arrived from Glogau'; '19 December passed quietly; the enemy worked only at extending the second parallel to the right and at new batteries'; 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'as for the siege works of the French, they were conducted very irregularly and could probably lead to the goal only under such peculiar circumstances'; 'the French batteries were built very irregularly; the guns in them, for the majority cannon and howitzers and mostly Prussian, stood behind embrasures raised toward the front; the elevating wedges had been taken out and the barrels laid on the transoms of the carriages, so that the guns were elevated between 15 and 20 degrees and their projectiles went at random into the town'; 'the mortars were mostly placed behind ruins of the suburbs and woodpiles, especially in the area of the burnt-down church of St. Nikolai'.",
